parts.problemMd:
Explore how Dickens presents ambition in Great Expectations.

You must consider language, form and structure and refer to the context of the novel in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
### Model answer

Dickens presents ambition as a powerful but dangerous force in Great Expectations, showing how Pip's longing to rise in class makes him ashamed of those who love him before he learns that true worth has nothing to do with status.

Pip's ambition is sparked at Satis House. When Estella sneers at his "coarse hands" and "thick boots", Pip is suddenly ashamed of himself, and Dickens uses her cruel words to plant the desire to become a gentleman. The first-person retrospective narration, told by an older Pip looking back, lets Dickens show both the boy's painful longing and the adult's regret at once. In a rigidly class-divided Victorian society, where a blacksmith's apprentice could almost never rise, Estella makes Pip feel that being "coarse and common" is something shameful he must escape.

Dickens shows that ambition makes Pip ashamed of his own family. Once he dreams of being a gentleman, Pip becomes embarrassed by Joe, the kind blacksmith who raised him, and by the forge that was once his home; he admits that his old life now seems "coarse and common". Dickens uses the symbol of the forge, once a place of warmth and honest work, to measure how far ambition has corrupted Pip's values. Through this he criticises a society that judged people by manners and money rather than goodness, showing how ambition can poison love and loyalty.

Dickens also uses Joe as a quiet contrast that exposes the emptiness of Pip's ambition. Even as Pip climbs socially, he privately calls Joe "a dear good fellow", admitting his guardian's real worth at the very moment he is ashamed of him. Dickens uses this contrast between Joe's contentment at the forge and Pip's restless craving for status to suggest that ambition is not the only path to a good life. In a Victorian culture that prized self-improvement and "getting on", Joe embodies an older, humbler ideal of honest labour, and Dickens makes the reader feel that Pip's ambition costs him more than it gains.

The cruellest twist is that Pip's gentlemanly ambition rests on a lie. He assumes his fortune comes from Miss Havisham and is meant to win Estella, but his secret benefactor is really the convict Magwitch, the "fearful man" he once fed on the marshes. Dickens uses this structural irony to attack Victorian snobbery: the "low" criminal is more generous than the respectable rich, and the gentleman Pip is built entirely on convict money. Pip's horror when he learns the truth exposes how shallow and snobbish his ambition has become.

Dickens shows that ambition brings Pip misery, not happiness. In London he falls into debt, grows vain, and neglects Joe, yet feels increasingly empty. Much of his ambition is driven by his hopeless love for Estella, the "poor dreams" of winning her that Dickens later shows to be founded on illusion. The contrast between the warm forge and the cold, fashionable city suggests that climbing the social ladder has cost Pip everything that truly mattered. Through this, Dickens questions the Victorian dream of self-improvement, suggesting that ambition without love and integrity leads only to dissatisfaction and shame.

By the end, Pip's ambition is humbled and reshaped. After Magwitch's death and the loss of his fortune, Pip learns to value Joe's goodness and to work honestly for his living. Dickens uses Pip's three-stage journey — from forge to false gentleman to humbled man — to redefine what it means to be a true gentleman: not wealth or class, but kindness and loyalty. The mature Pip who narrates the novel judges his younger self's ambition with shame, guiding the reader towards Dickens's moral.

Through Pip's rise and fall, Dickens presents ambition as a force that can blind us to real worth. By making his hero rise and then fall, Dickens warns his Victorian readers that the dream of "bettering" oneself can quietly destroy the values that matter most. In a class-obsessed Victorian world, Pip's longing to become a gentleman brings only shame and emptiness, until he learns that true value lies in love and integrity, not status.

parts.problemMd:
Explore how Dickens presents guilt in Great Expectations.

You must consider language, form and structure and refer to the context of the novel in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
### Model answer

Dickens presents guilt as a force that haunts Pip from childhood, using it to explore conscience, class and the moral growth that turns a frightened boy into a better man.

Pip's guilt begins when he steals food and a file for the convict Magwitch. Dickens fills the opening chapters with images of guilt: Pip feels watched by the cattle and the marshes, and imagines the man "with the iron on his leg" pursuing him in the dark. The first-person narration makes the reader share the terrified boy's overwhelming sense of having done wrong, even though he acts out of fear and pity. In a strict Victorian world that punished even small thefts harshly, Pip's guilt feels enormous and inescapable, and Dickens uses the gloomy marsh setting to mirror his troubled conscience.

Dickens makes the boy's guilt feel physical and inescapable through the imagery of the home itself. As Pip dreads the theft he must commit, he sees his crime "rose before me in the avenging coals", as if the fire of Joe's own forge were accusing him. Dickens uses this image of the "avenging coals" to show guilt turning everyday things into reminders of wrongdoing, while the phrase "guilty knowledge" names the secret burden the boy carries alone. Because the harsh Victorian law could transport or hang a thief, even a child's small theft becomes a source of terror, and Dickens makes the reader feel how a frightened conscience magnifies guilt out of all proportion.

Dickens links guilt closely to class and shame. Pip describes the "guiltily coarse and common thing it was, to be on secret terms of conspiracy with convicts", showing how he feels tainted by his connection to crime. As his ambition grows, this guilt mixes with snobbery: he is ashamed both of having helped a criminal and of his own humble background. Dickens uses this to expose how Victorian society made people feel guilty about poverty itself, as though being "common" were a kind of crime.

Pip's deepest guilt is towards Joe, the loving blacksmith he abandons. Once Pip becomes a gentleman, he neglects and is ashamed of Joe, and the older narrator looks back on this with painful regret. Joe's unfailing affection, calling Pip "dear old chap" even after being slighted, only deepens that guilt, since Pip knows he has wronged a man who never stops loving him. Dickens uses the retrospective narration so that the adult Pip judges his younger self harshly, turning the whole novel into a kind of confession. This guilt is moral rather than legal, and Dickens presents it as far more serious than the childhood theft.

Pip's guilt is finally transformed through Magwitch. When Pip learns that the convict is his secret benefactor, he is at first horrified, but as he cares for the dying man he feels guilty for his earlier disgust and learns to love him. Dickens uses this change to show guilt becoming a force for good: it teaches Pip humility and compassion. The "fearful man" he once dreaded becomes the person whose love finally redeems him.

By the end, guilt has reshaped Pip into a better person. His shame at how he treated Joe and Magwitch leads him to value loyalty and kindness over class and wealth. Dickens structures the novel so that Pip must lose his fortune and confront his guilt before he can grow, suggesting that a guilty conscience, properly faced, is the path to becoming a true gentleman. The mature narrator's honesty about his own faults models this moral lesson for the reader.

Through Pip's haunted childhood, his shame over class and his betrayal of Joe, Dickens presents guilt as a powerful moral force. By writing the whole story as the older Pip's confession, Dickens makes guilt the engine of the narrative itself, so that the reader is invited to share in Pip's self-judgement and learn the same lesson. Far from being only painful, guilt becomes the means by which Pip learns humility, compassion and the difference between social status and real worth.

parts.problemMd:
How does Dickens present the character of Magwitch in Great Expectations?

You must consider language, form and structure and refer to the context of the novel in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
### Model answer

Dickens presents Magwitch as a figure who seems terrifying but proves deeply loyal and generous, using him to overturn Victorian assumptions about criminals and to question what truly makes a gentleman.

Magwitch first appears as a frightening figure on the marshes. Dickens describes "a fearful man, all in coarse grey, with a great iron on his leg", and gives him the violent command "Hold your noise!", threatening to cut Pip's throat. The harsh, physical language and the bleak graveyard setting make Magwitch seem monstrous and dangerous. Dickens plays on Victorian fears of convicts as brutal outcasts, so that the reader, like Pip, at first judges Magwitch entirely by his rough appearance.

Yet Dickens quickly hints at Magwitch's humanity. Even as he demands food, the convict is starving, hunted and pitiable, and he is touched by the boy's kindness. When a second convict appears, "dressed in coarse grey, too", Dickens uses the contrast between the two men to suggest Magwitch is not simply evil but someone shaped by a hard, unjust life. This early flicker of sympathy prepares the reader for the later revelation that Magwitch is far better than he first seems.

Magwitch's importance becomes clear when he is revealed as Pip's secret benefactor. The convict Pip once feared has secretly worked and saved abroad to make him a gentleman, out of gratitude for that childhood kindness. Dickens uses this twist as the structural turning point of the novel and as a powerful attack on snobbery: the "low" criminal is more generous and loving than the respectable Miss Havisham. Pip's snobbish horror at the truth exposes his own shallowness rather than any fault in Magwitch.

Dickens also presents Magwitch as a man whose deepest pride lies in what he has made of Pip. When he reveals the truth he says, "I've made a gentleman on you", and the rough, ungrammatical speech makes his triumph feel both moving and pitiable. Dickens shows that Magwitch has poured his whole life into raising up the boy who once helped him, treating Pip's rise as his own revenge on a society that cast him out. The same Pip who as a child thought only of "My convict" now owes his entire status to that man, and Dickens uses this bond to argue that loyalty and gratitude, not birth, are the real marks of worth.

Dickens presents Magwitch as fiercely loyal and capable of deep love. He risks execution by returning illegally to England simply to see the gentleman he has made, and he treats Pip almost as a son. As Pip slowly overcomes his disgust and comes to care for the dying convict, Dickens shows Magwitch's rough exterior giving way to tenderness. Tending the wounded man at the end, Pip admits "my repugnance to him had all melted away", and now "I only saw a man" who had loved him faithfully for years. Dickens uses this change in Pip's own feelings to measure Magwitch's true worth: once the snobbery is stripped away, the convict is revealed as gentle and devoted. His loyalty quietly shames the cold, self-interested behaviour of the novel's more "respectable" characters.

Through Magwitch's death, Dickens completes his criticism of Victorian society. The convict dies still loving Pip, and Pip's loyalty to him at the end marks how far Pip has grown morally. Dickens uses Magwitch to argue that goodness is not decided by class or by the law: a transported criminal can be more honourable than a wealthy lady. In a society that harshly punished and exiled the poor, Magwitch stands as Dickens's challenge to readers to look beyond appearances.

Dickens presents Magwitch as far more than the frightening convict of the opening. By making the most feared figure in the novel into its most loving, Dickens forces his Victorian readers to question their easy assumptions about who is "respectable" and who is not. Through his loyalty, generosity and love, Magwitch overturns prejudices about criminals and becomes the means by which Pip learns that true worth has nothing to do with class.

parts.problemMd:
In what ways is Miss Havisham significant in Great Expectations?

You must consider language, form and structure and refer to the context of the novel in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
### Model answer

Miss Havisham is significant as a powerful symbol of the destructive effects of bitterness and revenge, and as the figure whose influence shapes both Pip's false ambition and Estella's coldness.

Miss Havisham is significant first as a striking symbol of a life frozen by heartbreak. Jilted on her wedding day, she has stopped all the clocks "at twenty minutes to nine", still wears her decaying wedding dress, and lives shut away from daylight in the gloom of Satis House. Dickens uses this powerful imagery — the stopped clocks, the rotting bridecake, the locked-out sunlight — to present her as a woman trapped in a single moment of pain. The precise detail "twenty minutes to nine" makes the reader feel that her whole life has frozen at the exact second her heart broke, so that time itself seems to have died with her hopes. She becomes a symbol of how clinging to the past can rot a person from within, and Dickens uses her decay to suggest that refusing to move on is itself a kind of living death.

Miss Havisham is significant because she turns her own pain into revenge. She has adopted Estella and raised her to "break their hearts", whispering "Break their hearts my pride and hope, break their hearts and have no mercy!" Dickens presents her as deliberately twisting a child into a weapon against all men. The fierce repetition of "break their hearts" makes her sound almost like a chant or a curse, showing how completely revenge has taken over her mind. This makes her both villain and victim: she causes terrible harm, yet her cruelty grows from her own deep wound, which gives her real tragic depth.

Miss Havisham is significant for the part she plays in Pip's false ambition. By inviting him to Satis House and allowing him to believe she is his secret benefactor, she encourages his dream of becoming a gentleman worthy of Estella. Dickens uses her to mislead both Pip and the reader, since the real benefactor is the convict Magwitch. Her cold game with Pip's hopes shows how the wealthy in the novel toy with those beneath them, treating people as playthings for their own purposes.

Dickens gives Miss Havisham a powerful moment of change near the end. Seeing the misery she has caused Pip and Estella, she is overwhelmed by guilt and begs Pip's forgiveness, crying out "What have I done!" over and over. Dickens uses this desperate repetition to show her finally grasping the full weight of her revenge, realising too late how far it has gone. Through her remorse he delivers a clear moral: revenge destroys not only its targets but the person who seeks it. Her dramatic death, when her old wedding dress catches fire, works almost as a symbolic punishment for a life wasted on bitterness, as though the past she refused to leave behind at last consumes her.

Miss Havisham's significance reaches across the whole novel. Her coldness helps create Estella's inability to love, which in turn causes Pip lasting pain; she has trained Estella so thoroughly that the girl cannot return the feeling behind Pip's "poor dreams" of winning her. Her decaying house stands throughout as a warning against living in the past, and Dickens uses the parallel with Magwitch to sharpen her significance: where the convict's benefaction comes from love, hers comes from spite. Through her, Dickens explores how heartbreak, if nursed into revenge, spreads its damage from one person to the next. She is one of the novel's clearest examples of a life ruined by refusing to let go.

Miss Havisham is significant, then, as both a haunting symbol and a driving force in the plot. By making her at once frightening and pitiable, Dickens ensures she lingers in the reader's mind as a warning rather than a simple villain. Through her frozen world, her cruel revenge and her final remorse, Dickens warns that bitterness destroys the bitter as surely as their victims, leaving a trail of broken hearts behind.

parts.problemMd:
‘Throughout the play there is a battle between good and evil.’

Explore the theme of good versus evil in Macbeth.

You must consider language, form and structure and refer to the context of the play in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

In Macbeth, Shakespeare presents a conflict between good and evil, which drives the play from the very first scene to the final resolution. The theme is explored through the moral decline of Macbeth, the contrasting actions of noble characters like Banquo and Macduff and the larger impact of evil on the natural and social order of Scotland. The play shows that although evil can corrupt and destroy, it is ultimately defeated by the forces of good.

At the beginning of the play, Macbeth is introduced as a loyal and brave general. His heroic actions in the battle earn him high praise from the Captain, who calls him “brave Macbeth — well he deserves that name”. King Duncan also rewards him with the title of Thane of Cawdor. Macbeth’s alignment with good is clear at this stage, and Duncan’s praise, “I have begun to plant thee, and will labour / To make thee full of growing”, uses a metaphor to suggest that Macbeth will flourish under his rule. Structurally, this positive portrayal makes Macbeth’s later downfall more tragic and highlights the powerful influence of evil.

This influence of evil arrives with the Witches, whose prophecies ignite Macbeth’s ambition. Their greeting, “All hail, Macbeth! that shalt be king hereafter!” plants the idea of kingship in his mind and leads him to believe that he is destined to rule. However, Shakespeare presents the Witches as dangerous figures, aligned with the supernatural and the demonic. Banquo’s reaction to them is more cautious. He recognises that they may be trying to trap them: “The instruments of darkness tell us truths; / Win us with honest trifles, to betray’s / In deepest consequence”. This contrast between Macbeth and Banquo emphasises the moral choice available to them and shows Macbeth beginning to shift towards evil.

Despite his ambition, Macbeth initially struggles with the idea of murdering Duncan. In a soliloquy, he acknowledges the reasons not to go through with the act: Duncan is his guest, his kinsman and a virtuous king. Macbeth describes Duncan’s virtues as “plead[ing] like angels, trumpet-tongued”, suggesting that he is aware of the moral and spiritual consequences of the murder. However, Lady Macbeth’s manipulation proves decisive. She mocks his masculinity, “When you durst do it, then you were a man” and questions his courage, persuading him to commit the murder. Her influence shows how evil can be persuasive.

Once Macbeth kills Duncan, the balance changes in favour of evil. The natural world responds to this disruption: “By the clock ’tis day, / And yet dark night strangles the travelling lamp”. Shakespeare uses this image of darkness to show how Macbeth’s crime has upset the natural order. This would have resonated with a Jacobean audience, who believed in the Divine Right of Kings and the Great Chain of Being. A king was God’s chosen representative, so regicide was not only a political crime but a spiritual one as well.

As Macbeth becomes more tyrannical, Scotland suffers. He continues to commit atrocities, including the murder of Macduff’s family. In response, Macduff joins Malcolm, Duncan’s son, in raising an army to overthrow Macbeth. Macduff’s grief, “My wife and children’s ghosts will haunt me still”, is genuine, but he channels his sorrow into a desire for justice: “let grief / Convert to anger”. Macduff’s desire to “Bleed, bleed, poor country” shows that he is motivated not by personal gain but by the wish to restore peace and order.

The play ends with the defeat of Macbeth, marking the triumph of good. Macduff, representing justice and loyalty, kills Macbeth and declares that “the time is free”. This short statement signals the end of tyranny. Malcolm’s speech after Macbeth’s death mirrors Duncan’s earlier language, using the metaphor of planting again: “What’s more to do, / Which would be planted newly with the time”. This parallel in the language and structure shows that the natural order has been restored.

In conclusion, Macbeth presents the struggle between good and evil as a central theme. Shakespeare explores this conflict through characterisation, imagery and dramatic structure. While Macbeth succumbs to evil through ambition and persuasion, characters like Banquo, Macduff and Malcolm remain firm in their moral convictions. parts.problemMd:
How does Shakespeare present the character of Macbeth in the play?

You must consider language, form and structure and refer to the context of the play in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

Shakespeare presents Macbeth as a tragic figure who begins as a loyal and courageous soldier but descends into tyranny, driven by ambition, supernatural influence and manipulation. Macbeth’s journey is central to the play’s structure and themes and Shakespeare uses language, structure and form to reveal how ambition can corrupt even the most honourable.

At the beginning of the play, Macbeth is admired for his bravery. The Captain praises his role in battle: “brave Macbeth — well he deserves that name”. Duncan also rewards him with the title Thane of Cawdor, affirming Macbeth’s loyalty and worth. This honourable reputation is further emphasised when he is described through the metaphor as “Bellona’s bridegroom”, likening him to Mars, the Roman god of war. In Jacobean society, such loyalty to the king was sacred. Macbeth’s initial status as a brave, trustworthy noble makes his later downfall more tragic and shocking.

Macbeth’s transformation begins when he encounters the Witches. He is fascinated by their strange appearance, “What are these, / So wither’d, and so wild in their attire”, and immediately intrigued by their prophecies. Banquo observes that Macbeth “seems rapt withal”, showing how strongly he is affected. When the prophecy that he will be Thane of Cawdor proves true, Macbeth begins to believe he is destined to be king. However, Duncan names Malcolm as heir: “The Prince of Cumberland!”, which Macbeth sees as an obstacle. The idea of murder first takes hold, showing ambition beginning to override his loyalty.

Despite this, Macbeth initially struggles with the idea of killing Duncan. In a soliloquy, he reflects on Duncan’s goodness and his own responsibilities as “kinsman”, “subject” and “host”. He notes Duncan’s virtues “Will plead like angels, trumpet-tongued”, using religious imagery to show the moral weight of the crime. At first, Macbeth concludes: “We will proceed no further in this business”, showing that his conscience still has power. However, Lady Macbeth mocks his hesitation, questioning his courage: “When you durst do it, then you were a man”. Her manipulation proves successful and Macbeth’s resolve collapses. A Jacobean audience might have been surprised to see a woman exerting such power over her husband, defying expectations of female submissiveness.

Once Duncan is murdered, Macbeth is overwhelmed by fear and guilt. He thinks he hears a voice cry, “Sleep no more! / Macbeth does murder sleep”, symbolising a loss of peace and innocence. Fear begins to dominate him, and he starts to kill to protect himself. He arranges the murder of Banquo not out of necessity but because of jealousy: “For Banquo’s issue have I filed my mind”. Macbeth has no heir and resents that Banquo’s children will inherit the throne.

Banquo’s ghost haunts Macbeth at a banquet, exposing the psychological effects of his crimes. He shouts, “Thou canst not say I did it. Never shake / Thy gory locks at me!”, showing his guilt and loss of control. This is a striking contrast to the fearless warrior portrayed at the start of the play. Shakespeare structures the play so that Macbeth’s psychological unravelling mirrors his moral decline.

When he hears of Lady Macbeth’s death, Macbeth expresses a bleak outlook on life: “Life’s but a walking shadow… a poor player / That struts and frets his hour upon the stage / And then is heard no more”. He views life as meaningless, shaped by ambition and futility. He also begins to doubt the Witches’ promises: “I pull in resolution and begin / To doubt th’ equivocation of the fiend / That lies like truth”, showing his realisation that he has been deceived.

Despite everything, Macbeth regains some bravery in the final act. He declares, “I’ll fight till from my bones my flesh be hack’d”, and asks for his armour, echoing the fearless soldier we saw at the start. He also says, “I had almost forgot the taste of fear”, suggesting he has become numb to emotion. Though he remains defiant, his downfall is inevitable. Indeed, Macbeth’s tragic fall results from his attempt to alter the natural and divine order. According to the Great Chain of Being and Divine Right of Kings, it was sinful to challenge the monarchy. Macbeth’s regicide brings chaos and leads to his destruction. His death allows order to be restored.

In conclusion, Shakespeare presents Macbeth as a tragic figure destroyed by ambition, manipulation and supernatural temptation. From noble beginnings to tragic end, Macbeth’s story serves as a warning of how quickly power can corrupt and how defying the natural order brings only ruin. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 30-mark question. parts.problemMd:
In what ways does Macduff contribute to Macbeth’s downfall in the play?

You must consider language, form and structure and refer to the context of the play in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

In Macbeth, Shakespeare presents Macduff as a critical element in Macbeth’s downfall. A noble and loyal character, Macduff’s commitment to justice, his suspicion of Macbeth and his eventual decision to avenge the murder of his family all contribute to the tyrant’s defeat. Through Macduff, Shakespeare explores themes of loyalty, justice and the restoration of order, using language, structure and form to contrast Macduff with Macbeth and highlight the moral consequences of ambition and betrayal.

Macduff first emerges as a loyal soldier and committed servant of King Duncan. When he discovers Duncan’s murdered body, he reacts with horror and sorrow: “O horror, horror, horror”, calling it a “Most sacrilegious murder”. The adjective “sacrilegious” reflects the Jacobean belief in the Divine Right of Kings, where killing a monarch was not only treason but a crime against God. Macduff recognises this immediately, unlike others who appear more focused on practical matters. His strong moral compass is one of the qualities that sets him apart and foreshadows his future role in exposing and defeating Macbeth.

From early on, Macduff is suspicious of Macbeth. After Macbeth kills Duncan’s guards, allegedly out of anger, Macduff questions his motives: “Wherefore did you so?” His scepticism is further emphasised when he chooses not to attend Macbeth’s coronation, showing his unwillingness to support someone he distrusts. This resistance to blindly following the new king marks him as a character guided by conscience rather than ambition, forming a structural contrast with Macbeth’s rapid descent into tyranny.

Shakespeare presents Macduff as a foil to Macbeth. While Macbeth is consumed by self-interest and willing to kill to secure power, Macduff acts selflessly to protect Scotland. He travels to England to seek help from Malcolm and the English king, leaving his family behind. This action, while noble, leads to devastating consequences as Macbeth orders the murder of Macduff’s wife and children. Lady Macduff condemns his absence, saying, “His flight was madness” and that “He wants the natural touch” suggesting he lacks human feeling. However, Shakespeare later reveals Macduff’s profound grief, reinforcing his humanity and honour.

Macduff’s reaction to the news of his family’s death is deeply emotional. He says, “My wife and children’s ghosts will haunt me still” and vows to turn his grief into revenge. This personal loss fuels his determination to bring Macbeth down, yet his actions are not purely vengeful as they are also about restoring rightful order to Scotland. When Malcolm tests Macduff’s loyalty, Macduff is distraught at the thought of further corruption: “Bleed, bleed, poor country!” This line uses personification to show his deep concern for Scotland.

Macduff’s role becomes even more significant as the play reaches its climax. One of the Witches’ prophecies states that “none of woman born / Shall harm Macbeth” which gives Macbeth a false sense of invincibility. However, during their final confrontation, Macduff reveals that Macduff was “from his mother’s womb / Untimely ripped”. The revelation that Macduff was born by Caesarean section turns the prophecy against Macbeth and leads to his downfall.

In their final battle, Macduff declares, “My voice is in my sword” indicating that he lets action speak for justice. His resolve and righteousness contrast with Macbeth’s desperation and fading courage. Macduff ultimately kills Macbeth, fulfilling the prophecy and ending the tyrant’s rule. In doing so, he restores order to Scotland. He supports Malcolm’s claim to the throne, saying, “I see thee compassed with thy kingdom’s pearl”, which symbolises Malcolm’s noble supporters and the return of rightful leadership.

Shakespeare’s use of structure and form frames Macduff as the moral centre of the play. From the moment he suspects Macbeth to the final battle, Macduff’s journey is one of justice and loyalty. His role mirrors the structure of the tragic hero’s fall for while Macbeth falls from greatness through ambition, Macduff rises through honour and sacrifice. His presence in the final scenes of the play restores the natural order, fulfilling the expectations of a tragic resolution. For a Jacobean audience, Macduff represents the ideal nobleman: loyal to king and country, respectful of divine authority and unafraid to challenge evil.

In conclusion, Macduff contributes to Macbeth’s downfall through his loyalty, suspicion, personal loss and pursuit of justice. Shakespeare uses him as a foil to Macbeth and as a symbol of the righteous force that restores moral and political order. Through powerful language, structure and contextual relevance, Macduff’s role is essential in bringing the tragedy to its necessary end. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 30-mark question. parts.problemMd:
‘Shakespeare makes great use of symbols, such as weather and blood.’

Explore the significance of symbols in Macbeth.

You must consider language, form and structure and refer to the context of the play in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

In Macbeth, Shakespeare makes powerful use of symbolism to explore major themes such as guilt, evil, disruption to the natural order and the struggle between good and evil. Symbols such as blood, weather, animals, light and darkness, sleep, and water help to deepen the audience’s understanding of character motivations and reinforce the play’s tragic and moral aspects. These recurring images are woven through the language, structure and form of the play and would have held particular resonance for a Jacobean audience.

One of the most prominent symbols in the play is blood, which represents guilt and the psychological consequences of murder. After Macbeth kills Duncan, he looks at his hands in horror: “What hands are here?” and later declares, “Will all great Neptune’s ocean wash this blood / Clean from my hand?” The hyperbolic image of the sea turning red emphasises how deeply stained with guilt Macbeth feels. In contrast, Lady Macbeth initially believes that “A little water clears us of this deed”, but her confidence unravels later when she is seen obsessively rubbing her hands in her sleep, crying, “Out, damned spot!” This repeated symbolism of blood and water shows how guilt cannot be easily washed away and reflects the psychological torment that follows immoral actions. While water is used throughout the play to attempt to cleanse guilt, it has contextual links with witch trials, as floating on water was believed to be a sign of witchcraft. This connection adds another layer of irony to Lady Macbeth’s final attempts to wash her guilt away.

Weather is also symbolic throughout the play, particularly in connection with the Witches and unnatural events. The play begins with thunder and lightning, establishing a mood of foreboding. Each time the Witches appear, stormy weather follows, “When shall we three meet again / In thunder, lightning, or in rain?”, linking them to chaos and evil. In contrast, when King Duncan arrives at Macbeth’s castle, the weather is described as “Nimbly and sweetly” symbolising his goodness and the natural order he represents. The disruption of this order is mirrored by unnatural weather later in the play, such as when “dark night strangles the travelling lamp”, showing that the world itself reacts to Duncan’s murder.

Similarly, animal imagery is used to convey the breakdown of the natural order and to mirror characters’ states of mind. After Duncan’s murder, Ross notes that an owl has killed a falcon, “A falcon… / Was by a mousing owl hawked at and killed”. This unnatural reversal symbolises Macbeth, a lower-ranking nobleman, killing the king. The disturbance also spreads to Duncan’s horses, who break out of their stalls and eat each other, which is another clear sign of chaos. Later, Lady Macduff uses a bird metaphor to condemn Macduff’s abandonment: “the poor wren… will fight / Her young ones in her nest, against the owl”, casting Macbeth as the predatory owl and herself as the small, helpless bird. Animal imagery thus links to broader themes of disorder and destruction.

Light and darkness also serve as opposing forces throughout the play. Light is associated with goodness and virtue, as seen when Duncan says “Signs of nobleness, like stars, shall shine / On all deservers”. In contrast, Macbeth seeks darkness to conceal his ambitions: “Stars, hide your fires; / Let not light see my black and deep desires”. Lady Macbeth, too, calls upon the night: “Come, thick night”, hoping that darkness will mask her evil intentions. Later, in her sleepwalking scene, she carries a candle suggesting that in her madness, she now fears the darkness she once embraced. Shakespeare uses light and dark not just as imagery, but to symbolise internal moral conflict.

Sleep functions as another important symbol, representing innocence and peace. After murdering Duncan, Macbeth claims to hear a voice cry: “Sleep no more! Macbeth does murder sleep”. This reflects his sense of having destroyed not only Duncan’s rest but also his own. As the play progresses, both Macbeth and Lady Macbeth are increasingly disturbed by sleeplessness and nightmares. Shakespeare connects sleep to conscience as those with guilt cannot rest, while the innocent, like Duncan or Banquo’s son Fleance, are associated with peaceful sleep.

In conclusion, Shakespeare’s use of symbolism in Macbeth is central to its meaning. Symbols such as blood, weather, darkness and sleep are not only repeated throughout the play but serve to reveal character, reinforce themes and reflect the disruption of the natural and moral order. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 30-mark question. parts.problemMd:
Captain: ‘The merciless Macdonald — / Worthy to be a rebel…’

Discuss the theme of betrayal in Macbeth.

You must consider language, form and structure and refer to the context of the play in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

In Macbeth, Shakespeare explores betrayal as a devastating force, affecting not only political power but also personal relationships and moral integrity. Through acts of treachery against individuals and against Scotland itself, the play highlights how betrayal leads to guilt, grief and tragedy. Many characters suffer as a result of betrayal and Shakespeare encourages sympathy for them through their language, actions and the consequences they face.

One of the first acts of betrayal in the play is committed by the Thane of Cawdor, who supports the Norwegian army against his own king. King Duncan, unaware of his disloyalty until it is too late, expresses sorrow that trust can be so easily broken: “He was a gentleman on whom I built / An absolute trust”. This line foreshadows Duncan’s misplaced trust in Macbeth, who is rewarded with the traitor’s title. Duncan’s generosity and honesty make him a deeply sympathetic figure. When Macbeth murders him, the act is not only a betrayal of loyalty but of hospitality and kinship. Macbeth himself reflects that Duncan’s “virtues / Will plead like angels”, a simile that heightens the audience’s sense of Duncan’s goodness and the horror of the crime. In Jacobean England, betrayal, especially of a monarch, was seen as a deadly sin, disrupting the Divine Right of Kings and the Great Chain of Being.

Banquo also becomes a victim of betrayal. Though he receives prophecies similar to Macbeth’s, he chooses not to act dishonourably, declaring he must keep his “allegiance clear”. His integrity contrasts sharply with Macbeth’s ambition. Despite this, Macbeth views Banquo as a threat and arranges for his murder. When the murderers attack, Banquo exclaims, “O, treachery!”, a powerful reminder of how he has been betrayed. Furthermore, given that Banquo was believed by King James I to be his ancestor, Shakespeare’s sympathetic portrayal may have been a political compliment to the king.

Macduff is another character who evokes sympathy through betrayal. Although his decision to leave Scotland and support Malcolm is patriotic, it leads to the murder of his innocent family. Lady Macduff calls his departure “madness” and says, “Our fears do make us traitors”, suggesting that even good intentions can appear as betrayal. Her bitter complaint, “Wisdom! — to leave his wife, to leave his babes”, emphasises her sense of abandonment. When Macduff learns of their deaths, he is devastated. His reaction, “all my pretty chickens and their dam / At one fell swoop?”, uses a metaphor to express his loss. His grief is raw and sincere and he blames himself: “Sinful Macduff, / They were all struck for thee!” This moment of guilt deepens audience sympathy and underscores the personal cost of betrayal.

While Macbeth is the play’s main betrayer, Shakespeare also invites a degree of sympathy for him. Early in the play, Macbeth is torn between ambition and loyalty. In a soliloquy, he considers Duncan’s virtues and his own roles as “kinsman” and “host”, clearly recognising the moral weight of murder. Yet under the influence of the Witches and Lady Macbeth, he proceeds. As the play progresses, Macbeth becomes increasingly isolated and haunted. After Lady Macbeth’s death, he responds not with grief but weary resignation: “She should have died hereafter”. This line shows how emotionally numb he has become, consumed by guilt and despair.

Lady Macbeth herself also elicits sympathy. Initially strong and persuasive, she unravels under the weight of guilt. In her sleepwalking scene, she imagines blood on her hands, “What, will these hands ne’er be clean?” and obsessively replays the events of Duncan’s murder. Her death is widely believed to be a suicide and her mental decline reflects the consequences of betrayal not just of others, but of conscience and morality. The audience may feel pity for her as someone who encouraged betrayal, but ultimately could not live with its cost.

In conclusion, Shakespeare presents betrayal in Macbeth as a destructive force that corrupts individuals and tears apart families, friendships and the natural order itself. While Macbeth is the central figure who betrays king, country and conscience, it is the impact of his betrayal on others, Duncan, Banquo, Macduff and Lady Macduff, that evokes the greatest sympathy. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 30-mark question. The essay presents a thoughtful and coherent argument, supported by a wide range of relevant examples and close textual analysis. There is insightful discussion of character and motivation, particularly in relation to Duncan, Banquo, Macduff and Lady Macduff and a nuanced exploration of how sympathy is generated through Shakespeare’s language and structure. > > Contextual understanding is effective, with well-integrated references to Jacobean beliefs, such as the Divine Right of Kings and the Great Chain of Being. parts.problemMd:
Discuss the presentation of one character you sympathise with in the play.

You must consider language, form and structure and refer to the context of the play in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

In Macbeth, Shakespeare presents Banquo as a noble and loyal figure whose resistance to temptation and unjust death make him one of the most sympathetic characters in the play. While others around him give in to ambition and deceit, Banquo remains honourable, cautious and morally grounded. Through his language, behaviour and the way other characters treat him, Shakespeare encourages the audience to admire and pity him, especially as his murder reflects the growing corruption in Scotland under Macbeth’s rule.

Banquo is introduced early in the play as Macbeth’s fellow soldier and equal in battle. Like Macbeth, he receives a prophecy from the Witches, but unlike Macbeth, he remains suspicious of them. While Macbeth is “rapt” with attention, Banquo warns, “The instruments of darkness tell us truths... to betray’s / In deepest consequence”. This warning shows Banquo’s wisdom and moral awareness. He immediately senses danger, even when promised greatness. His scepticism stands in contrast to Macbeth’s eagerness, marking him as a character guided by caution and principle rather than ambition. This reluctance to trust the supernatural adds to his noble image.

Banquo’s refusal to betray King Duncan also contributes to the sympathy he inspires. When Macbeth tries to involve him in a private conversation about the Witches, Banquo responds, “So I lose none / In seeking to augment it”, meaning he will not gain power if it costs him his honour. Shakespeare presents Banquo as someone who could choose to chase power but consciously decides not to. This choice seals his fate, however, as Macbeth sees him as a threat, not only because of the prophecy that Banquo’s descendants will be kings, but because Banquo’s honour contrasts so sharply with Macbeth’s guilt.

The decision to murder Banquo is one of Macbeth’s most chilling acts. It marks a turning point in his moral descent, as he plans it without consulting Lady Macbeth and does so purely to secure his power. Macbeth describes Banquo as “royalty of nature” and notes his “dauntless temper” revealing that he envies Banquo’s natural leadership. The audience sees that Macbeth recognises Banquo’s goodness, yet chooses to destroy him. When Banquo realises what is happening, he cries, “O, treachery!”, a powerful single line that encapsulates his shock and betrayal. This moment evokes strong sympathy, as Banquo dies because he remains loyal and refuses to act unjustly.

Banquo’s murder is made even more tragic because of its impact on his son, Fleance. Although Fleance escapes, he is forced to flee alone into the night. Shakespeare’s decision to have Fleance survive suggests that Banquo’s line may still continue, but the emotional toll of Banquo’s death on his family is clear. Banquo’s murder symbolises the complete breakdown of morality in Macbeth’s Scotland. King James I believed he was descended from Banquo, and Shakespeare’s sympathetic portrayal of him as honourable and betrayed would have pleased the monarch. Banquo’s association with future kings, as the Witches predict, reinforces his lasting importance and justifies the audience’s admiration and pity.

Even in death, Banquo continues to influence the play’s events. His ghost appears at Macbeth’s banquet, shaking its “gory locks” at him. This haunting image is a manifestation of Macbeth’s guilt and mental instability. It also reminds the audience of Banquo’s unjust death and strengthens the sense of injustice. Macbeth’s terrified reaction, “quit my sight!”, reveals his inner torment and through this, Shakespeare highlights Banquo’s enduring moral power. For a Jacobean audience, the ghost may also represent a soul denied rest, further deepening the pathos around Banquo’s fate.

Structurally, Banquo’s role highlights the contrast between ambition and restraint. Both he and Macbeth begin the play as loyal warriors and receive prophecies, but only Macbeth acts on them violently. Banquo’s quiet dignity and inner strength are a foil to Macbeth’s moral collapse. Shakespeare uses this contrast to heighten the audience’s sympathy for Banquo, who dies precisely because he resists temptation. His story serves as a tragic example of how goodness is punished in a corrupt world.

In conclusion, Banquo is presented as a principled and courageous character whose moral strength contrasts sharply with Macbeth’s corruption. Shakespeare encourages the audience to sympathise with Banquo through his loyalty, his unjust death and the lasting legacy he leaves behind. Banquo’s quiet heroism and tragic end make him one of the most admirable and pitiable figures in the play, a man destroyed not by his flaws, but by his refusal to be corrupted. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 30-mark question. The essay presents a coherent line of argument, clearly demonstrating why Banquo evokes sympathy. There is thoughtful analysis of his moral integrity, his response to the Witches and his unjust murder, supported by well-chosen textual references. The contrast with Macbeth is effectively developed and Banquo’s role as a moral foil is well explained. parts.problemMd:
Explore the theme of ambition in Macbeth.

You must consider language, form and structure and refer to the context of the play in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
### Model answer

Shakespeare presents ambition as a dangerous, corrupting force that drives Macbeth from loyal hero to murderous tyrant, and which ultimately destroys him.

Shakespeare shows that ambition is Macbeth’s only real motive for murder. In soliloquy he admits he has nothing spurring him on but “Vaulting ambition which o’erleaps itself”. The metaphor of a rider vaulting so hard that he falls off the other side warns that excessive ambition destroys itself. The soliloquy form lets the audience hear Macbeth’s private conscience, so we see that he knows the murder is wrong even as ambition pushes him on. For a Jacobean audience, who believed kings were chosen by God, this ambition to seize the throne was not only a crime but a sin against the natural order.

Shakespeare places the witches at the very start to show how this ambition is awakened. Their prophecy that Macbeth “shalt be king hereafter” plants the idea, yet Shakespeare leaves it unclear whether they create his ambition or simply reveal what is already there. By having Banquo react with caution while Macbeth is immediately gripped, Shakespeare uses contrast to suggest the ambition is Macbeth’s own. King James I’s belief in the genuine danger of witchcraft would have made this supernatural temptation truly frightening for the original audience.

Shakespeare also shows that ambition makes Macbeth deceitful, forcing him to hide his true self. When his path to the throne is blocked by Malcolm being named heir, Macbeth asks the “Stars, hide your fires” so that light will not “see my black and deep desires”. The metaphor of light and darkness shows that Macbeth already knows his ambition is shameful and must be concealed, even from himself. This aside, spoken while Duncan stands nearby, lets the audience share a guilty secret the King cannot see, building dramatic irony. To a Jacobean audience, plotting against an anointed king — only a year or so after the Gunpowder Plot to murder their own king — would have made these “black” desires feel like a real and present treason.

Ambition is not Macbeth’s alone. Lady Macbeth is at first the more ruthless, fearing that he is “too full o’th’ milk of human kindness” to seize the crown. The image of milk presents kindness as something soft she wants to drain out of him. She urges him to “be the serpent under’t”, hiding cruelty beneath a fair face, and calls on dark spirits to strip away any womanly pity that might stop her. Shakespeare uses her to show ambition overriding nature itself, and in a patriarchal society a woman so driven by ambition would have seemed deeply unnatural and disturbing.

Shakespeare also shows that ambition, once acted on, can never be satisfied. After killing Duncan, Macbeth murders again and again — Banquo, then Macduff’s family — to protect his crown, and his ambition curdles into paranoia and tyranny. Shakespeare uses the disordered natural world, where “darkness does the face of earth entomb”, to mirror the moral chaos that ambition has unleashed on Scotland. The murder of a divinely appointed king was believed to upset the whole universe, which is why nature itself seems to rebel.

By the end, ambition has brought Macbeth nothing. His wife is dead and his enemies are closing in, and he reflects bitterly that life is no more than a “brief candle”, soon snuffed out. The metaphor shows how ambition has hollowed out his existence until it feels empty and meaningless. Shakespeare’s tragic structure ensures that ambition leads only to isolation and despair, and Macbeth dies cursing the prophecies that first stirred him. The restoration of the rightful king, Malcolm, reaffirms the natural order that ambition tried to overturn, sending the Jacobean audience a clear warning.

Through soliloquy, the supernatural and the collapse of natural order, Shakespeare presents ambition as a force that promises greatness but delivers ruin. Macbeth’s fall warns that ambition, when it ignores conscience and the proper order of things, destroys not only the ambitious person but everything around them.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> This is a 30-mark question. This answer would be placed in the top band (Level 5) because it is an assured response that analyses how Shakespeare uses language, form and structure to present ambition, with context integrated throughout.
> 
> **Commentary**

parts.problemMd:
How far do you agree with Elizabeth Bennet’s view that Charlotte Lucas should not have married Mr Collins for convenience in Pride and Prejudice?

You must consider language, form and structure and refer to the context of the novel in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

In Pride and Prejudice, Jane Austen presents two contrasting views on marriage through the characters of Elizabeth Bennet and Charlotte Lucas. Elizabeth is shocked when Charlotte accepts Mr Collins and she believes her friend is sacrificing her happiness for security. While Elizabeth’s view is rooted in ideals of love and compatibility, Charlotte’s decision reflects the societal expectations and economic pressures of women in the early 19th century. Austen presents both perspectives with sympathy and while Elizabeth’s ideals are admirable, Charlotte’s pragmatism is understandable and in many ways is justified.

Elizabeth’s reaction to Charlotte’s engagement to Mr Collins is one of disbelief and disappointment. Elizabeth cannot understand how Charlotte could agree to marry “a conceited, pompous, narrow-minded, silly man” simply to secure her future. Elizabeth values emotional connection and mutual respect in a marriage and this informs her rejection of Mr Collins herself. The contrast between the two women is evident. While Elizabeth seeks love and refuses to marry without it, Charlotte takes a more practical approach, stating plainly that she is “not romantic”. From a modern perspective, it may seem that Elizabeth is right to criticise Charlotte’s choice. Mr Collins is clearly absurd and embarrassing, both in his flattery of Lady Catherine and his social awkwardness. He had, after all, proposed to Elizabeth and even considered Jane first, showing a total lack of romantic feeling. Charlotte acknowledges that he is “neither sensible nor agreeable”, but she still accepts him, suggesting that happiness in marriage is “entirely a matter of chance”. Through Charlotte’s words, Austen highlights the lack of agency many women had during this period.

However, Charlotte is 27 and has limited prospects. At a time when marriage was often a woman’s only option for financial security, Charlotte’s decision is not without merit. She makes a calculated, rational choice based on her circumstances and Austen never condemns her for this. In fact, she allows Charlotte to succeed in making the best of her situation. When Elizabeth visits Charlotte and Mr Collins, Charlotte has cleverly arranged her life to avoid much of her husband’s company, placing her sitting room at the back of the house. This shows that she has maintained some independence within the constraints of her marriage. Austen herself never married, though her novels are preoccupied with love and marriage and she understood the limited choices available to women. While the novel promotes the idea that love should be at the heart of marriage, it also recognises that this is not always possible. Charlotte’s honesty, “it is better to know as little as possible of the defects of the person with whom you are to pass your life”, shows her acceptance of reality, not weakness.

Austen uses Charlotte’s marriage to contrast with the eventual union of Elizabeth and Darcy, which is based on love, respect and mutual growth. Structurally, this contrast strengthens the novel’s overall message: that while love should be the foundation of marriage, society often forces women to compromise. Charlotte’s marriage functions as a foil to Elizabeth’s, showing how women with different fortunes must make different choices. Indeed, Charlotte’s brothers are relieved by her marriage, since it removes the financial burden of supporting her. Mr Collins believes the marriage is successful and claims, “My dear Charlotte and I have but one mind”. This is both comical and informative as Austen uses irony here, showing Mr Collins’ inability to see the truth and Charlotte’s achievement in making the best of the marriage.

In conclusion, while Elizabeth’s belief that Charlotte should not have married Mr Collins reflects her own values and emotional courage, Charlotte’s decision is practical, rational and in many ways admirable. Austen presents both perspectives with balance, showing the societal constraints that force Charlotte’s hand, while still allowing the reader to admire Elizabeth’s integrity. I therefore partially agree with Elizabeth, but I also understand and respect Charlotte’s choice. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 30-mark question. parts.problemMd:
‘At the time the novel was written, women were expected to behave in particular ways.’

In what ways do women go against how society expected them to act in the novel?

You must consider language, form and structure and refer to the context of the novel in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

In Pride and Prejudice, Jane Austen presents a range of female characters who either conform to or challenge the expectations of women in Regency England. While society dictated that women should be modest, obedient and concerned with marriage, Austen uses characters such as Elizabeth Bennet and Lydia to show women pushing against these norms, whether through personal convictions or reckless behaviour.

Elizabeth Bennet most clearly defies convention. Unlike many women of her time, she refuses to marry for convenience or status. When Mr Collins proposes, she shocks him by stating directly, “You could not make me happy”. This is remarkable for a young woman in her social position, especially given the economic security his offer represents. Elizabeth’s rejection of Mr Darcy’s first proposal is equally unexpected and his reaction, “mingled incredulity and mortification”, highlights just how rare it would be for a man of his rank to be refused.

Elizabeth’s behaviour also challenges expectations in more subtle ways. She walks alone through muddy fields to visit her sister Jane at Netherfield, a journey of three miles that would have been considered unladylike. Her arrival in “dirty stockings” horrifies Miss Bingley, who judges her for showing “a most country-town indifference to decorum”. However, Austen encourages the reader to admire Elizabeth’s loyalty and independence. Her spirited teasing of Mr Darcy, her intelligence and her refusal to flatter him, even in company, all suggest a woman who is unafraid to voice her views and be herself.

Lydia Bennet, by contrast, breaks society’s rules in a more reckless and dangerous way. She is described as “untamed, unabashed, wild, noisy, and fearless”, traits that might be admired in a man but would have been scandalous in a young woman of the gentry. Her elopement with Mr Wickham nearly destroys the family’s reputation. In Regency England, a woman living with a man outside of marriage would have been shunned and Lydia’s thoughtlessness is shown when she returns to Longbourn with “easy assurance”, entirely unaware of the disgrace she has narrowly escaped. Austen uses Lydia’s behaviour as a warning about the consequences of neglecting propriety and parental responsibility.

Even Jane and Charlotte Lucas, who are more conventional, display their own subtle resistance. Jane chooses not to chase Mr Bingley, but her quiet dignity earns her the respect of the reader and of Darcy. Charlotte’s decision to marry Mr Collins may seem to reinforce society’s expectations, but it is also an act of agency. She knows her chances are slim and makes a pragmatic choice to secure her future, later managing her life to avoid Mr Collins’ company. She is honest about her motives, claiming, “I am not romantic, you know”, showing her realistic expectations.

Mrs Bennet, though a comic figure, also goes against expected behaviour, albeit unintentionally. Her loud remarks about her daughters’ marriages and her willingness to discuss private family matters in public would have been considered highly improper. Her obsession with marriage makes her appear foolish, but it also reveals the pressures placed on women to secure their daughters’ futures. Austen’s readers would have recognised the pressures women faced. Marriage was often the only secure future for women without wealth. Women were expected to be demure, silent in public debate and reliant on men. Austen critiques these norms by showing that women like Elizabeth, who value self-respect and intelligence, are more admirable than those who simply follow society’s rules.

In conclusion, Pride and Prejudice presents a nuanced picture of women in a restrictive society. Through Elizabeth, Lydia and even Charlotte, Austen explores different ways in which women go against expectations, whether through principle, pragmatism or carelessness. In doing so, she encourages her readers to consider the limitations placed on women and the courage it takes to defy them. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 30-mark question. parts.problemMd:
How does Austen present Elizabeth Bennet in the novel?

You must consider language, form and structure and refer to the context of the novel in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

In Pride and Prejudice, Jane Austen presents Elizabeth Bennet as an intelligent, independent and strong-willed heroine whose growth throughout the novel highlights her complexity. Elizabeth is not only the emotional centre of the story but also a progressive figure who challenges the gender and class expectations of her time.

At the start of the novel, Elizabeth is described as having “a lively, playful disposition, which delighted in anything ridiculous”. This reveals her wit and tendency to mock foolishness, which immediately distinguishes her from the more conventional women around her. Her sharp observations and teasing tone, especially with characters like Mr Darcy and Mr Collins, make her both entertaining and admirable to readers. Her language is confident and unapologetic, which would have been unusual for a young woman in Regency England.

Elizabeth’s independence is most evident in her rejections of marriage proposals. She tells Mr Collins, “You could not make me happy” challenging the expectation that women should marry for financial stability. She even turns down Mr Darcy’s first proposal, despite his wealth and status, stating that he was “the last man in the world” whom she “could ever be prevailed on to marry”. This blunt language shocks Mr Darcy and demonstrates Elizabeth’s refusal to compromise her values. Austen uses this moment to assert that personal integrity should matter more than wealth or social advantage.

The structure of the novel supports Elizabeth’s development. Most of the narrative is filtered through her perspective, which allows readers to experience her emotional journey and self-discovery. A key moment in this journey is Mr Darcy’s letter after her first refusal. In a moment of clarity, Elizabeth admits, “Till this moment, I never knew myself,” revealing her growing maturity. Austen uses this turning point to show that Elizabeth is capable of reflection and change which is a crucial quality in a heroine.

Elizabeth’s evolving feelings for Darcy are also shaped by her visit to Pemberley. The house and its grounds reflect Darcy’s true character: reserved, honourable and generous. Mrs Reynolds’ praise, “If I were to go through the world, I could not meet with a better”, contrasts with Elizabeth’s earlier prejudices. Her feelings shift from resentment to admiration: “She respected, she esteemed, she was grateful to him”. Austen uses this change to highlight the importance of looking beyond first impressions, which is one of the novel’s main themes.

Throughout the novel, Elizabeth also challenges the rigid class system. Her refusal to be intimidated by Lady Catherine de Bourgh is particularly striking. When confronted about a supposed engagement to Darcy, Elizabeth responds with dignity and defiance: “You have insulted me, in every possible method”. This moment demonstrates Elizabeth’s moral courage and equality of spirit, reinforcing her position as a woman who values herself regardless of rank. Contextually, Elizabeth’s actions were unconventional for her time. Women were expected to be submissive and marry for security, but Elizabeth insists on marrying for love and personal compatibility. Austen challenges social norms through Elizabeth, presenting her as a woman who refuses to accept a lesser life simply because it is expected. At a time when entailment laws restricted women’s independence, Elizabeth’s eventual marriage to Darcy offers both romantic fulfilment and financial security, but crucially, on her own terms.

By the end of the novel, Elizabeth has grown in self-awareness. Her earlier “playful disposition” is tempered by empathy and restraint, such as when she resists teasing Darcy about Mr Bingley’s return: “She remembered that he had yet to learn to be laughed at, and it was rather too early to begin”. This shift in tone signals her emotional growth and her readiness for a mature relationship based on respect and understanding.

In conclusion, Austen presents Elizabeth Bennet as a complex and admirable character whose strength, independence and personal growth make her a heroine. Through language, form and structure, Austen traces Elizabeth’s journey from confident observer to self-aware partner, celebrating her refusal to conform to societal expectations. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 30-mark question. parts.problemMd:
Explore the role of parents in Pride and Prejudice.

You must consider language, form and structure and refer to the context of the novel in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

In Pride and Prejudice, Jane Austen presents a range of parental figures to explore how different approaches to parenting affect their children’s prospects and behaviour. At a time when a parent’s role was to ensure good upbringing and advantageous marriages, especially for daughters, Austen uses contrast, irony and characterisation to critique both effective and ineffective parenting.

Mr and Mrs Bennet are the central parental figures in the novel, yet Austen presents them as flawed. Mrs Bennet is shown as socially embarrassing, indiscreet and overly obsessed with marrying off her daughters. Her conduct often undermines her daughters’ reputations, as when she openly boasts about Jane’s beauty and prospects, totally ignoring social decorum. Mr Bennet is portrayed as more intelligent and witty, but emotionally detached and ineffective. He confesses to Elizabeth that he married her mother for superficial reasons: “captivated by youth and beauty”. His sarcasm amuses Elizabeth but he fails to check Lydia’s reckless behaviour.

Austen uses language to emphasise Mr Bennet’s shortcomings. He refers to Lydia and her sisters as “the silliest girls in the country” and the superlative here shows his exasperation but also his lack of effort to guide them. His indifference contrasts with Mrs Bennet’s anxious, though misguided, involvement. Together, they fail to provide their younger daughters with the structure and guidance expected of middle-class parents in Regency society. The consequences of their parenting can be seen in Lydia’s elopement with Mr Wickham. With little supervision or moral guidance, Lydia acts irresponsibly, nearly ruining the family’s reputation. Mr Bennet admits his failure, telling Elizabeth: “Let me once in my life feel how much I have been to blame”. This moment of self-awareness comes too late, but signals Austen’s criticism of neglectful parenting. Austen also shows that Elizabeth’s closeness to her father is both a strength and a limitation. They share a bond based on intelligence and wit, but Mr Bennet’s approval can lead Elizabeth to overlook his failures as a parent. While their relationship may have seemed unusual for the time, it highlights Elizabeth’s sharp mind and individualism, traits encouraged by Mr Bennet’s favouritism but not necessarily supported by effective guidance.

In contrast, the Gardiners serve as examples of positive parental influence. Mr Gardiner is described as “a sensible, gentlemanlike man, greatly superior to his sister” and both he and Mrs Gardiner provide Elizabeth and Jane with guidance and emotional support. When Lydia elopes, it is Mr Gardiner, not Mr Bennet, who takes practical steps to resolve the situation, working with Mr Darcy to locate the couple. The Gardiners’ involvement and good judgment show how responsible parenting can protect and support young women in society. In Regency England, parents played a significant role in shaping their children’s futures, particularly daughters who relied on marriage for social and financial stability. Fathers had legal and social authority over marriage choices and good parenting was considered essential to a family’s reputation. Austen reflects and critiques this through the Bennets’ failings and the Gardiners’ successes and the structure of the novel enhances these contrasts. Mr Bennet and Mr Gardiner are deliberately juxtaposed, showing the difference between neglect and competence. Similarly, the marriages of the Bennet daughters reflect their upbringing: Jane and Elizabeth, more mature and self-aware, succeed in marrying well, while Lydia’s lack of restraint nearly leads to disaster.

Lady Catherine de Bourgh represents an extreme example of a parent as she is overbearing and controlling. She attempts to dictate her daughter Anne’s future, stating that Anne and Mr Darcy have been intended for each other. Her domineering attitude contrasts sharply with Elizabeth’s independence and Mr Bennet’s passive approach. Austen uses Lady Catherine’s snobbery and sense of entitlement to critique the obsession of the upper classes with family alliances and status.

In conclusion, Austen presents parenting as a central influence on the behaviour, choices, and fates of young women. Through characters such as Mr and Mrs Bennet, the Gardiners and Lady Catherine, she explores the consequences of neglect, overcontrol and guidance. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 30-mark question. parts.problemMd:
‘Journeys, including Elizabeth’s journey to visit the Collinses, are significant in the novel.’

Explore the significance of journeys in Pride and Prejudice.

You must consider language, form and structure and refer to the context of the novel in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

In Pride and Prejudice, journeys are significant as they not only move characters through different locations but also act as key catalysts for emotional and moral change. Austen uses physical travel to reflect the inner journeys of her characters, especially Elizabeth, whose opinions and prejudices are frequently challenged while away from Longbourn.

Elizabeth’s journey to visit Charlotte and Mr Collins at Hunsford is particularly pivotal. Her arrival at Rosings and exposure to Lady Catherine's aristocratic world offer a stark contrast to her modest home life and this setting becomes crucial to her evolving view of Mr Darcy. As a result of her journey, she starts to understand some of the reasons for Mr Darcy’s unsociability. Her first proposal from Darcy occurs here, marking a significant turning point. The narrative uses the structure of the journey to initiate a shift in Elizabeth’s perception, not only of Darcy but of her own limitations and pride. Her emotional journey begins with indignation but gradually leads to introspection.

The subsequent journey to Pemberley is even more significant. Described in romanticised terms, with Elizabeth admiring the natural beauty of the estate, this setting provides a visual metaphor for Darcy’s true character. The journey physically removes Elizabeth from the gossip and prejudices of Hertfordshire and places her in a neutral environment, where she can judge Darcy for herself. Austen describes how “to be mistress of Pemberley might be something!”, signalling Elizabeth’s shift from disdain to admiration. The stately home becomes symbolic of Darcy’s hidden virtues, his honour, refinement and generosity, which had been previously obscured by his pride.

Other characters’ journeys also serve as plot devices that reveal personality and provoke consequences. Jane’s journey to Netherfield, on horseback in the rain, leads her to fall ill and stay under the Bingleys’ roof. The context of this event reveals the vulnerability of women in Regency England, reliant on proximity and social manoeuvring to secure marriage prospects. When Elizabeth walks to visit her sister, Jane, at Netherfield, Miss Bingley speaks of Elizabeth in derogatory terms and mocks Elizabeth’s “abominable sort of conceited independence”. During this period, a woman walking that distance alone was putting her reputation at risk and questions would possibly have been raised about her virtue. Elizabeth’s choices reflect her spirited independence in a society that prized female decorum and obedience.

In contrast, Lydia’s journey to Brighton leads to scandal and disgrace. Despite Elizabeth’s appeals to Mr Bennet to prevent it, Lydia’s unchecked freedom results in her elopement with Mr Wickham, a crisis that nearly destroys the family’s reputation. Here, Austen critiques not just individual recklessness but also parental negligence and social structures that allow such danger. The Marriage Act of 1753 prevented marriage for those under 21 who did not have the consent of their parents or guardians, therefore the only alternative for couples in England and Wales was to apply for a licence from the Archbishop of Canterbury in London. This meant that many couples eloped to Scotland, where the Marriage Act did not apply. Wickham and Lydia’s own journey to London, followed by Mr Darcy’s pursuit of them, is another example of how a journey leads to transformation. Darcy’s selfless intervention, hidden from Elizabeth until much later, demonstrates his honour and sets up the final reconciliation. Mrs Gardiner’s letter recounting Darcy’s movements acts as a narrative device, revealing his character indirectly.

Journeys in Pride and Prejudice are significant because they drive the emotional and moral development of key characters, particularly Elizabeth. Austen uses travel not just to move her plot forward, but to challenge assumptions, shift relationships and expose the rigid class and gender norms of Regency society. Each journey marks a turning point, reinforcing how movement is central to the novel’s exploration of pride, prejudice and personal growth. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 30-mark question. parts.problemMd:
How does Austen present the relationship between Jane and Mr Bingley in the novel?

You must consider language, form and structure and refer to the context of the novel in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

In Pride and Prejudice, Austen presents the relationship between Jane Bennet and Mr Bingley as one of harmony, affection and compatibility. Their courtship is shaped by the influence of others, especially Bingley’s family and Mr Darcy, yet Austen uses their love story to contrast with the more dramatic relationship between Elizabeth and Darcy. While not the most emotionally complex couple in the novel, Jane and Bingley’s union reinforces Austen’s theme that good character should triumph over social interference.

Jane and Bingley are first introduced at the Meryton assembly, where their immediate mutual attraction is made clear. Jane dances with Bingley twice and Bingley later refers to her as “the most beautiful creature I ever beheld!” His admiration is simple and direct, setting the tone for their relationship. Jane is equally impressed and tells Elizabeth that Bingley is “just what a young man ought to be”. Austen’s use of straightforward, sincere language reveals the natural compatibility between the two characters.

However, their relationship faces obstacles, largely imposed by external forces. Miss Bingley and Mr Darcy, concerned about Jane’s lower social standing, persuade Bingley to leave Netherfield. Mrs Hurst’s comment, “with such a father and mother, and such low connections”, reflects Regency attitudes towards class and marriage. Austen uses this conflict to show how social expectations can interfere with genuine affection. Jane’s response is dignified and restrained, revealing her modesty and emotional resilience, even when she is deeply hurt.

The structure of the novel reinforces the contrast between Jane and Bingley’s calm, steady relationship and the more volatile romance between Elizabeth and Darcy. Jane and Bingley’s love story develops in the background, with fewer dramatic moments, which mirrors their personalities. Mr Bennet comments humorously on this when he says, “You are each of you so complying, that nothing will ever be resolved on”. This light-hearted observation points to the ease and amiability that characterise their bond.

Jane’s character is consistently generous and forgiving. When Bingley returns after Darcy’s confession and resumes his courtship, Jane welcomes him without hesitation. Even Miss Bingley, who actively tried to keep them apart, is met with Jane’s kindness. Austen presents Jane as the moral centre of the novel and her happiness serves as part of the story’s resolution. Her reunion with Bingley at Netherfield contributes to the novel’s uplifting ending: “I am certainly the most fortunate creature that ever existed!” Contextually, their match would have been seen as successful. Mr Bingley, a wealthy gentleman with “four or five thousand a year”, is extremely eligible. Jane, as the eldest daughter, would have been expected to marry first, and her beauty, modesty and manners make her an ideal partner. Austen follows societal norms by allowing the eldest daughter to marry well, but also subtly critiques the social pressures that nearly prevented the union.

Austen presents Jane and Bingley’s relationship as one of quiet affection and moral virtue. While it lacks the emotional complexity of Elizabeth and Darcy’s, it represents a different kind of romantic success and it is one based on mutual respect, simplicity and goodness. Their eventual marriage offers resolution and reinforces Austen’s belief that character, not social standing, should guide the choice of a life partner. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 30-mark question.
