parts.problemMd:
How does Miller present Eddie Carbone in A View from the Bridge?

You must consider language, form and structure in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
### Model answer

Miller presents Eddie Carbone as a tragic hero whose love for his niece curdles into an obsession he cannot admit, destroying him and those around him.

Miller frames Eddie’s story through the lawyer-narrator Alfieri, who introduces him as an ordinary longshoreman before warning that the story will run its “bloody course”. This structural device gives the play the shape of a Greek tragedy: the audience knows from the start that Eddie is doomed, so we watch not what will happen but how and why. Alfieri’s later image of “a passion that had moved into his body, like a stranger” presents Eddie’s downfall as something beyond his control, inviting our sympathy even as we judge him.

At first Eddie seems a caring guardian to his niece Catherine, but Miller’s dialogue slowly reveals something darker. His objections to her growing up — her high heels, her new job, the way she walks — are obsessive in their detail, and his constant focus on Catherine betrays a possessiveness he refuses to name. Miller makes Eddie’s inability to say what he feels the heart of the tragedy: the more fiercely he denies his desire, the more violently it leaks out in his behaviour towards Rodolpho.

That jealousy drives the central conflict. Eddie tries to undermine Rodolpho by mocking his blond hair, his singing and his dressmaking, hinting that he “ain’t right” — that he is not a real man. Miller uses these attacks to show Eddie projecting his own anxieties: unable to compete with Rodolpho for Catherine, he attacks his masculinity instead. The shocking moment when Eddie kisses both Catherine and Rodolpho is an action rather than a speech, and Miller lets Eddie’s body reveal the desire and aggression his words keep hidden. Because this happens in front of the audience as stage action, it carries a force no dialogue could, exposing in seconds the truth Eddie has spent the whole play denying.

Eddie’s flaw leads him to break the community’s deepest code by reporting the cousins to the Immigration Bureau. Miller foreshadows this through the earlier story of Vinny Bolzano, the boy who informed on his own family and was spat on in the street. By having Eddie tell this cautionary tale himself, Miller makes his later betrayal bitterly ironic: Eddie becomes the very figure he despises. The act shows how completely his obsession has overridden his judgement and his loyalty.

Miller also uses Alfieri to define exactly what is wrong in Eddie. Alfieri admits that, like most people, he has learned to “settle for half”, and he repeatedly begs Eddie to accept that Catherine must be let go. Eddie’s tragedy is that he cannot settle for half: he wants all of Catherine and will not compromise. Miller uses Alfieri’s reasonable, measured voice as a contrast to Eddie’s rising desperation, so that we see how far Eddie has slipped beyond ordinary good sense. This structural pairing of the calm narrator and the man who will not listen makes Eddie’s destruction feel both avoidable and inevitable, which is the essence of tragedy.

At the end, Eddie cares only about his “name”, demanding that Marco publicly take back his accusation. Beatrice finally says the truth he cannot face — “you want somethin’ else, Eddie, and you can never have her!” — but he would rather die than admit it. He is killed with his own knife, a fitting image of a man destroyed by his own desires. Alfieri’s closing verdict, that Eddie “allowed himself to be wholly known”, suggests a strange dignity in the total, destructive honesty of his feeling, even as Alfieri mourns the waste of it.

Miller presents Eddie as both guilty and pitiable: a man undone by a love he cannot understand or control. Through Alfieri’s framing, the slow exposure of Eddie’s obsession and the tragic structure of the play, Miller turns one man’s private shame into a powerful drama about desire, denial and the cost of refusing to know yourself.

parts.problemMd:
How does the character of Eric Birling change in An Inspector Calls?

You must consider language, form and structure in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

Priestley presents Eric as a character who undergoes a significant transformation in his attitudes towards himself and others in the play. Initially depicted as immature and irresponsible, he becomes more morally conscious and responsible.

As a character, Priestley first presents Eric as a reckless and self-centred young man, illustrating his lack of awareness and irresponsible attitude towards himself and others. He is first portrayed as “not quite at ease, half shy, half assertive” denoting his lack of confidence and social awkwardness, which sets him apart from more self-assured characters like Gerald. He is presented as a weak character and although he attempts to challenge some of his parents’ views in the early stages of the play, he struggles to confront them to any great extent and they are largely dismissive of his opinions. They also ignore Eric’s alcoholism which perhaps alludes to his wish to escape the responsibilities placed upon him or to avoid uncomfortable truths, though this may also reflect his parents’ tendency to ignore his problems. While Eric contradicts his parents on many occasions in Act 1, actions which could be perceived as showing some empathy towards the strikers in his father’s factory, his retorts to his parents may simply be due to his hostility towards them. Eric remains on the fringes of the action in the first two acts and this enables the other characters in the play to dominate proceedings, which further highlights his immaturity. Indeed, Eric attempts to leave when he suspects the Inspector may want to question him and thus initially avoids taking any responsibility for his actions.

As the play progresses, Eric’s attitude begins to change as he becomes increasingly aware of his responsibility to others. His guilt for his actions towards Eva in Act 3, when he confesses his affair and admits Eva was pregnant with his child, shows some attempt at responsibility when he suggests marriage to Eva. However, as the father of her child, he ultimately fails in his duty to protect both of them. While an audience may also view Eric as a somewhat sympathetic character, his treatment of Eva also reveals his exploitation of her. Like Gerald, Eric abuses his power and status as a middle-class man with Eva and discards her when it suits him. He also hints at the potential for sexual violence and shows that Eva resisted him, his behaviour became threatening: “I was in that state when a chap easily turns nasty”. He fails to acknowledge the fundamental social and economic vulnerability of women like Eva, who could be easily exploited by wealthy men like Eric. While Gerald hints that he may have been in love with Eva, Eric admits he was not, and so his behaviour could also be viewed as more malicious.

By the end of the play, Priestley presents Eric as a significantly altered character, one who is ashamed and regretful over his conduct with Eva. During his confession, he uses emotive language and repetition, “you killed them both — damn you, damn you”, to reveal his anger and condemnation which is juxtaposed with his parents’ dismissive reactions, and he heavily criticises his mother’s treatment of Eva. While he could appear to express a stronger sense of guilt than the others (through his emotional outburst), his emotional outburst may reflect immaturity rather than deep remorse, especially when compared to his sister’s response. While Arthur, Sybil and Gerald rejoice at having discovered the Inspector was a fraud, in contrast, both Eric and his sister are at pains to focus on the lessons that they all must now learn, regardless of whether the Inspector was real. Eric and Sheila do not share the same sense of relief as the others when the Inspector is discovered to be a fraud, as this is irrelevant to them. Through Sheila and Eric, Priestley offers the audience a more optimistic view of the future, that the younger generation is capable of change as he depicts them as more compassionate and empathetic, incapable of avoiding their social responsibilities. In doing so, Priestley suggests the younger generation will avoid the errors of the previous generation, suggesting that the selfish and exploitative capitalist system will be replaced with a more socialist agenda. In part, Eric therefore presents a symbol of hope for the changing attitudes of the younger generation.

Initially presented as an immature character, Priestley uses the character of Eric to demonstrate the possibility of personal growth and social responsibility. Priestley uses Eric’s personal development to encourage others to change their attitudes, and to look after one another, in order to strive for a society where all members are treated more equally and fairly. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 30-mark question. The essay presents a coherent argument supported by relevant textual references, including powerful quotes that highlight Eric’s emotional conflict and moral growth. parts.problemMd:
‘Things are not always what they appear to be in the Birling household.’

Explore the theme of appearance and reality in the play

You must consider language, form and structure in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

In An Inspector Calls, Priestley explores the theme of appearance and reality to expose the hypocrisy, deceit and social prejudices of the upper classes. The Birlings present themselves as a respectable, successful family, but the Inspector’s arrival gradually reveals a darker, more selfish reality beneath their polished surface. Through language, structure and form, Priestley uncovers the difference between who the characters claim to be and who they truly are.

At the start of the play, the Birlings appear to be a close-knit, respectable family. The stage directions describe them as being “pleased with themselves” after a celebratory dinner. Gerald even comments that they “seem to be a nice well-behaved family”. However, Priestley uses irony and contrast to undermine this false reality. The audience soon discovers that each family member has played a part in Eva Smith’s downfall and that the unity of the Birlings is superficial. The luxurious setting of the house, described as “substantial and heavily comfortable but not cosy and homelike”, symbolises their external wealth but also their internal emotional coldness.

Sheila and Gerald’s engagement initially appears to be a happy union, but cracks soon emerge. Sheila’s seemingly innocent question, “is it the one you wanted me to have?” — suggests a lack of agency and a concern with appearances. Her reference to “last summer, when you never came near me” introduces doubt. The truth about Gerald’s affair with Eva/Daisy confirms that their relationship was built on an illusion. However, Sheila’s decision to break off the engagement and her later maturity contrast with Gerald’s attempts to dismiss the Inspector’s importance, reinforcing her journey from appearance to reality.

Mr Birling’s self-presentation as a successful businessman and future knight is also revealed to be hollow. He confidently makes pronouncements that are proven wrong by the audience’s knowledge of history, such as the claim that the Titanic is “absolutely unsinkable”. His decision to sack Eva for demanding better wages contradicts his public image as a rational, fair employer. Priestley uses this dramatic irony to show how the appearance of authority and respectability can mask exploitation and selfishness.

The gap between appearance and reality is especially apparent through Mrs Birling, who presents herself as a charitable, moral woman. She is part of a women’s charity supposed to support those in need, yet she denies Eva help for the “gross impertinence” of using the Birling name. Priestley uses irony here: although she sees herself as morally superior, her actions directly contribute to Eva’s fate. Her condemnation of the baby’s father becomes tragic when she learns it is Eric, her own son.

Priestley extends the theme of illusion to the Inspector himself. At first, he seems like an ordinary police inspector, but his name, Goole, sounds like “ghoul” and his prophetic language introduces a supernatural element to proceedings. He possesses an unnatural knowledge of the family’s secrets and delivers moral lessons with authority. Structurally, Priestley never allows the Inspector to show the photograph to more than one person at a time, creating ambiguity. The Inspector’s warning, “if men will not learn that lesson”, is both prophetic and symbolic, hinting at war and social upheaval.

The ending of the play reinforces the theme of appearance versus reality. Once the Birlings believe the Inspector was a fraud, they return to their old attitudes. Gerald uncovers that “there wasn’t any Inspector Goole” and triumphantly declares it “a hoax”. However, the final twist — a phone call announcing that a girl has actually died and an inspector is on his way — underlines Priestley’s warning. The false sense of relief is shattered and the characters are forced to confront the real consequences of their actions once more.

In conclusion, Priestley uses the contrast between appearance and reality to expose the moral flaws of the upper class and the dangers of ignoring social responsibility. Through dramatic irony, symbolism and the structure of the play, he reveals that beneath the Birlings’ respectable exterior lies selfishness, hypocrisy and guilt. This theme remains central to Priestley’s call for greater honesty, compassion and change in society. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 30-mark question. There is a thoughtful analysis of stage directions, character development and the Inspector’s role, supported by relevant quotations and contextual understanding. parts.problemMd:
Mr Birling (talking about Eva/Daisy): ‘She’d had a lot to say, I remember — far too much.’

What does the audience learn about Eva Smith/Daisy Renton from how other characters treat her in the play?

You must consider language, form and structure in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

Through the way other characters describe and treat Eva Smith/Daisy Renton, Priestley presents her as a vulnerable yet principled woman who is repeatedly exploited by those with power. Although she never appears on stage, Eva/Daisy is a central figure in the play, symbolising the wider suffering of working-class women and functioning as an “everywoman” whose fate critiques the selfishness of Edwardian society.

Mr Birling is the first to speak about Eva, revealing that she worked at his factory and was dismissed for leading a strike for better wages. His comment, “She’d had a lot to say — far too much”, highlights his discomfort with being challenged and shows how Eva was punished simply for speaking up. He sees her only as part of the workforce, someone who is expendable, and proudly states it was his duty to “keep labour costs down”. His language is dismissive, reflecting the wider capitalist view that values profit over people.

The audience learns that Eva was not only hard-working but also independent. After being dismissed by Mr Birling, she finds a job at Milwards, only to lose it because Sheila, in a moment of jealousy, uses her influence to have Eva sacked. Priestley uses this moment to show how even those with limited power, like Sheila, can still exploit those below them in the social hierarchy. Sheila admits she was impolite to the shop assistant and Eva, “I was very rude to both of them”, and later expresses deep regret. This contrast between Sheila’s remorse and her parents’ denial highlights the extent of Eva’s suffering and strengthens Priestley’s message about generational responsibility.

Eva’s downward spiral continues as she encounters Gerald, who initially rescues her from the unwanted attention of Alderman Meggarty. Gerald describes how Meggarty had wedged Eva “into a corner with that obscene fat carcass of his” which highlights how trapped and powerless she was. However, while Gerald provides her with only temporary comfort, he ultimately uses her and ends the affair when it no longer suits him. Priestley uses the structure of the play to reveal Gerald’s treatment of Eva before he learns of the Inspector’s investigation, heightening the dramatic irony and audience awareness of his hypocrisy.

Eric’s treatment of Eva is arguably the most disturbing. He admits to forcing himself into her room, stating: “I was in that state when a chap easily turns nasty”. His casual, euphemistic language masks what was clearly an act of sexual violence. He later tries to support Eva by giving her stolen money, but again, she refuses to rely on a man who disrespected her. Eric’s confession and his later emotional reaction, shows that while he feels guilt, his initial actions were self-serving and destructive. Eva’s refusal to marry Eric or accept more money reveals her strong principles as she is not willing to compromise her values, even in desperation.

Mrs Birling’s treatment of Eva is perhaps the coldest. As head of a women’s charity, she refuses to help Eva when she seeks aid, because Eva used the name “Birling” and refused to take money from the child’s father. Mrs Birling accuses her of having “elaborate fine feelings” which she claims are inappropriate for “a girl in her position”. Mrs Birling’s condescending tone and dismissive language show how the upper class viewed working-class women as morally inferior. Ironically, Mrs Birling’s insistence that the father of the child should take full responsibility directly condemns her own son, Eric.

Priestley uses form and structure to convey Eva's presence despite her physical absence. The play’s events are revealed through flashbacks and testimonies, gradually building a picture of Eva as a decent and dignified woman repeatedly let down by a corrupt society. The Inspector’s final speech uses graphic and emotive language, “she died in misery and agony — hating life”, which leaves a lasting impression of the harm the characters have caused. His use of repetition and listing, “millions and millions and millions of Eva Smiths and John Smiths”, positions her as a symbolic figure for all those who suffer due to inequality and exploitation.

In conclusion, through the accounts of others, the audience learns that Eva Smith/Daisy Renton is not just a victim, but a symbol of resilience, principle and injustice. Priestley uses her treatment to expose the moral failings of each character and to deliver a powerful message about social responsibility, class inequality and the need for change. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 30-mark question. parts.problemMd:
Explore the differences between the older and younger generations in An Inspector Calls.

You must consider language, form and structure in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

In An Inspector Calls, J.B. Priestley presents a clear generational divide in how the characters respond to the Inspector’s message of social responsibility. While the older generation, Mr and Mrs Birling, are portrayed as stubborn, morally complacent and resistant to change, the younger generation, especially Eric and Sheila, are shown to be more emotionally affected, open to learning and capable of change.

Priestley first presents Eric as a symbol of youthful irresponsibility, portraying him as immature, secretive and awkward: “not quite at ease, half shy, half assertive”. He struggles to express himself and lacks the confidence to challenge his parents. His early behaviour, including drinking heavily and trying to avoid interrogation, reflects his desire to escape both the truth and adult responsibilities. However, as the play progresses, Eric becomes increasingly affected by the Inspector’s interrogation and begins to show a growing sense of moral awareness. He admits to his role in Eva’s pregnancy and offers to marry her, though even this gesture reveals a failure to fully grasp the seriousness of his actions.

Despite his flaws, Eric’s emotional transformation is significant. His confession is marked by guilt and self-reproach, especially in the line: “I was in that state when a chap easily turns nasty”. Priestley uses this line to expose the entitlement and danger of unchecked male privilege, especially towards vulnerable women. Yet by Act 3, Eric displays genuine remorse and recognises the shared responsibility in Eva’s death: “You killed them both — damn you, damn you”. His emotional outburst reveals his anger and the weight of his guilt, contrasting sharply with the cold detachment of his parents. This moment is key in highlighting the moral divide between both generations: while Eric begins to grasp the Inspector’s message, his parents remain unmoved.

By contrast, Mr and Mrs Birling are portrayed as symbolic of a complacent and outdated upper class, unwilling to take responsibility. Mr Birling is obsessed with his status and business interests and dismisses Eva Smith’s plight as irrelevant. His reaction to the Inspector’s visit centres on the risk of reputational damage, rather than guilt: “There’ll be a public scandal”. Similarly, Mrs Birling coldly denies aid to Eva and shows no remorse even after discovering Eva was pregnant with her grandchild. She insists: “I accept no blame for it at all”. Priestley uses these responses to critique the selfishness and moral blindness of the older generation, who are more concerned with appearances.

Sheila also undergoes a transformation. Initially portrayed as “very pleased with life”, Sheila quickly recognises the consequences of her actions and vows not to repeat them: “I’ll never, never do it again”. Her character, like Eric’s, demonstrates the capacity for growth and empathy and these are qualities that Priestley associates with the younger generation. Both Eric and Sheila reject their parents’ attitudes and align themselves with the Inspector’s message, showing Priestley’s belief that social progress depends on the willingness to change.

While Gerald is part of the younger generation, Priestley aligns him more closely with the values of the older characters. Although Gerald initially appears remorseful, he is quick to discredit the Inspector and dismiss the experience once it becomes convenient: “Everything’s all right now, Sheila”. Gerald’s position reinforces the idea that change is not determined by age alone, but by the willingness to accept responsibility.

By the end of the play, the generational divide is sharply defined. The older characters are relieved to learn that the Inspector might not be real, seeing it as a way to erase their guilt. Eric and Sheila, however, refuse to let go of what they have learned. The cyclical ending, with the arrival of a second inspector, serves as Priestley’s warning: without genuine moral growth, society is doomed to repeat its failures.

In conclusion, Priestley uses Eric and Sheila to symbolise the hope of a more just and responsible society, while Mr and Mrs Birling represent the stubbornness and moral failings of the past. The generational divide in An Inspector Calls is central to Priestley’s message: that real change can only come through accountability, empathy and a willingness to challenge outdated attitudes. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 30-mark question. parts.problemMd:
How far do you agree with the view that the ending of An Inspector Calls is successful?

You must consider language, form and structure in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

The ending of An Inspector Calls can be seen as highly successful in reinforcing Priestley’s social message and delivering a powerful dramatic conclusion. Through a combination of language, structure and form, Priestley leaves the audience with a final twist that not only re-establishes tension but also re-emphasises the moral consequences of ignoring collective responsibility.

The play’s cyclical structure contributes to the success of its ending. The sharp ring of the telephone in the final line echoes the “sharp ring” of the doorbell from the opening, creating a dramatic parallel. This suggests that the characters, particularly the older generation, have learned nothing from their experience and that the same lesson is about to begin again, but this time for real. The effect is to reinforce Priestley’s warning that if people fail to change, they will be forced to face the consequences.

The ending also powerfully restores tension just as it begins to fade. Mr and Mrs Birling, along with Gerald, quickly revert to complacency and celebration after learning that there may be no real Inspector and they are described as behaving “triumphantly”. They call it a “hoax” and declare that they’ve “been had”. This false sense of relief lulls both characters and audience into a moment of calm, which is then shattered by the news of a real inspector’s imminent arrival. The shock twist that “a police inspector is on his way here — to ask some questions” is made even more dramatic by Birling’s reaction: he puts the phone down “slowly” and is “panic stricken”. The sudden shift in tone makes for a highly successful dramatic ending, filled with suspense and irony.

The language of the Inspector’s final speech, delivered just before his exit, is also key to the impact of the ending. His use of religious and prophetic language, “Fire and blood and anguish”, acts as a stark warning. It suggests that if society does not learn to care for others, it will suffer through war and social upheaval. This speech is powerful as it successfully ensures the audience leaves the play reflecting on the consequences of ignoring social responsibility.

From a structural point of view, the division between generations is left unresolved, further adding to the tension. While Sheila and Eric show genuine remorse and are determined to change — “It frightens me the way you talk” — the older generation clearly has not. Mr Birling, Sybil and Gerald cling to the belief that the Inspector was a fraud and treat the whole experience as a joke. This reinforces Priestley’s belief that only the younger generation are capable of reform, while the older generation are too entrenched in their selfish, capitalist views.

However, some may argue that the ending is less successful because it raises more questions than it answers. For example, the audience never learns who the Inspector really is. Gerald tries to unpick the Inspector’s identity and Mr Birling phones the Chief Constable, only to be told there is no Inspector Goole. For some, this unresolved mystery might feel unsatisfying. Yet, this ambiguity is arguably intentional: Priestley is less concerned with who the Inspector is and more with what he represents. Sheila herself says: “It doesn’t much matter who it was… The point is, you don’t seem to have learnt anything”. Moreover, the ending’s lack of closure serves to involve the audience, prompting them to reflect on their own values. It also mirrors real life, where consequences are not always immediate.

In conclusion, I think the ending of An Inspector Calls is highly successful. Through dramatic structure, language and a moral message, Priestley creates a conclusion that is both shocking and thought-provoking. The final twist creates further tension, the Inspector’s words echo with an urgency and the contrast between generations is heightened. By ending the play in this way, Priestley ensures it ends not with resolution, but with reflection. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 30-mark question. parts.problemMd:
Sheila: ‘He never seemed like an ordinary police inspector.’

How far do you agree with this view of the Inspector in the play?

You must consider language, form and structure in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

J.B. Priestley presents Inspector Goole as a figure who appears to be more than just an ordinary police inspector. While some aspects of his behaviour align with a traditional inspector, his manner, language and message all suggest that he serves a deeper symbolic and moral purpose. Sheila’s observation that “He never seemed like an ordinary police inspector” captures the audience’s growing suspicion that Inspector Goole represents something much more profound and is perhaps a supernatural force or Priestley’s own voice within the play.

When the Inspector first enters, the stage directions highlight his imposing presence: he “creates at once an impression of massiveness, solidity and purposefulness”. This language immediately distinguishes him from the casual, celebratory tone established in the opening scene. The sense that he is not a conventional inspector is reinforced by Mr Birling’s failed attempts to impress him, including his reference to playing golf with the Chief Constable. Rather than being intimidated or deferential, the Inspector remains calm and assertive, showing no concern for Mr Birling’s status or influence. This challenges expectations of class deference and authority, hinting that Goole operates on a moral level rather than a legal one.

While the Inspector follows a clear and methodical line of questioning, with one line of inquiry at a time, he goes beyond merely gathering evidence. His questions are emotionally charged and morally focused, often pushing the characters to confront uncomfortable truths about their actions. Sheila recognises this, noting that “he’s giving us the rope — so that we’ll hang ourselves”. This phrase reveals that the Inspector is less interested in constructing a legal case and more concerned with guiding the characters towards moral self-realisation.

Goole’s language further suggests that he is no ordinary inspector. In his final speech, he delivers a powerful moral warning about the consequences of ignoring social responsibility: “We are members of one body. We are responsible for each other.” The use of first-person plural pronouns reinforces the idea of collective responsibility, a concept at the heart of Priestley’s socialist message. The speech becomes increasingly dramatic and almost sermon-like, with vivid and apocalyptic imagery: “Fire and blood and anguish”. This tone gives the impression that Goole speaks not just for the law, but for a kind of religious conscience and morality.

The structure of the play also supports the view that Goole is extraordinary. After his sudden and unexplained departure, the characters begin to investigate his identity and realise he is not a real police inspector. Gerald confirms this by speaking to a local constable and triumphantly declares it a “hoax”. Yet, this relief is short-lived. The final twist, a phone call announcing that a girl has actually died and an inspector is on his way, restores tension and deepens the mystery. This dramatic structure leads the audience to question whether Goole was ever meant to be a literal inspector or something more symbolic: a supernatural force, a ghostly figure, or even Priestley’s embodiment of conscience.

Even Goole’s name hints at his unusual nature. Goole sounds phonetically similar to “ghoul”, suggesting a supernatural or ghostly presence. This aligns with interpretations of the play as a modern morality play, where the Inspector serves as a judge, exposing the moral failures of the characters and warning of the consequences of selfishness and injustice. Priestley’s choice to make the Inspector mysterious ensures that the audience focuses not on who he is, but on what he represents.

In conclusion, Sheila’s comment that the Inspector “never seemed like an ordinary police inspector” is entirely justified. Priestley uses the Inspector as more than just a plot device. He is a symbol of moral authority, a mouthpiece for social justice and a warning of a potential future. Through language, form and structure, Priestley creates a character who challenges the audience as much as he challenges the Birlings. The Inspector’s purpose is not to solve a crime, but to expose wrongdoing and demand reflection, both on stage and beyond it. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 30-mark question. parts.problemMd:
Explore the theme of responsibility in An Inspector Calls.

You must consider language, form and structure in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
### Model answer

Priestley uses An Inspector Calls to argue that everyone is responsible for one another, dramatising this idea through the Inspector’s investigation, which forces each character — and the audience — to confront the consequences of their actions.

Priestley opens by establishing the opposite of responsibility. Mr Birling lectures his family that “a man has to mind his own business and look after himself and his own”, dismissing the idea that everybody should look after everybody else as “community and all that nonsense”. Priestley uses dramatic irony here — Birling’s confident predictions that the Titanic is “unsinkable” and that war is impossible are things the audience knows are wrong — so we distrust his selfish philosophy from the start. By making the spokesman for irresponsibility a fool, Priestley discredits his whole worldview before the Inspector has even arrived.

The Inspector is Priestley’s main tool for exploring responsibility. Structurally he controls the play, questioning the family one at a time and forcing each to admit their part in Eva Smith’s death. His role is closer to that of a moral judge than a policeman, and his name, Goole — a homophone of “ghoul” — hints that he may be something more than human. Priestley uses this single, relentless figure to build the argument that every individual action has a consequence for someone else.

Priestley presents responsibility as a chain. Each character adds a link to Eva’s downfall: Birling sacking her, Sheila having her dismissed out of jealousy, Gerald’s affair, Mrs Birling refusing her charity and Eric’s exploitation. Through this structure Priestley shows that responsibility is shared — no single person killed Eva, but together they destroyed her. Sheila grasps this when she insists that “these girls aren’t cheap labour — they’re people”, a line whose dash forces a pause that gives the word “people” real weight. Priestley uses her dawning understanding to model the change he wants the audience to undergo.

Priestley dramatises the theme further through the contrast between the generations. The younger characters, Sheila and Eric, accept their guilt and are changed by it, while the older Birlings and Gerald try to escape it, seizing on the idea that the Inspector was a hoax. Priestley uses this divide to suggest that hope lies with the young, who are still open enough to learn. The parents’ relief that they might avoid a scandal exposes that they have understood nothing about responsibility — only about protecting their reputation.

The theme reaches its climax in the Inspector’s final speech, where he warns that we are “members of one body” and “responsible for each other”. His prophecy that those who refuse this lesson will be taught it in “fire and blood and anguish” lifts a domestic drama into a warning for society as a whole. Priestley then uses the play’s cyclical structure — the final phone call announcing that a real inspector is on his way — to give the characters, and the audience, a second chance to take responsibility. The ending deliberately leaves us asking whether we would change.

Through the Inspector’s investigation, the chain of guilt and the play’s circular structure, Priestley turns responsibility from an abstract idea into a gripping moral test. He argues that no one can live alone, and that ignoring our responsibility for others leads only to suffering — a lesson he is determined his audience will not forget.

parts.problemMd:
“Iyaloja is determined that things are carried out in accordance with Yoruba traditions.”

How is Iyaloja presented as a character who wants the right thing to be done in the play?

You must consider language, form and structure in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
### Model answer

Soyinka presents Iyaloja as the guardian of Yoruba tradition: a wise and powerful woman who is determined that the sacred ritual is carried out properly, even when it costs her dearly.

Iyaloja is presented as a figure of great authority. As "mother" of the market, she commands respect from the women and speaks for the community's values. Soyinka gives her dignified, proverb-rich language that sets her apart from the lighter talk around her and marks her out as wise and serious. Through her control of the market women, who together drive out the colonial messenger Amusa — scorning him as an "eater of left-overs" — Soyinka shows Iyaloja upholding the community's order and refusing to let outsiders interfere with what is sacred. From her first appearance she is the steady centre of the community's moral world.

Iyaloja wants, above all, for Elesin to complete his sacred duty. She understands that the King's Horseman must die to accompany the dead King and keep the world in balance, and she is determined that nothing should prevent this. Soyinka presents her as the voice of tradition, constantly reminding Elesin of the weight of what he must do. Her seriousness contrasts sharply with Elesin's pleasure-seeking, and this contrast is one of Soyinka's main methods: it shows that Iyaloja grasps the cost of the ritual far more clearly than the horseman himself.

Iyaloja reveals how far she will go to do the right thing when she grants Elesin's request to take a young bride on his final night — even though the girl is betrothed to Iyaloja's own son. Soyinka uses this painful decision to show Iyaloja sacrificing her family's happiness for the sake of the ritual and Elesin's peace of mind. Her willingness to give up something so personal proves how completely she places duty and tradition above her own feelings, and it deepens our sense of her as a woman of principle. That she makes the choice without bitterness, treating the girl's future child as the community's gain rather than her family's loss, shows how completely she thinks in terms of the whole people rather than herself.

Iyaloja is also presented as clear-eyed and warning. She senses the danger in Elesin's hunger for life and his marriage, and she cautions him not to let earthly pleasures weaken his resolve. Soyinka gives her a solemn, almost prophetic tone, so that when Elesin later fails, her fears are shown to have been right all along. This dramatic irony — the audience remembering her warnings as disaster unfolds — makes Iyaloja seem wiser than every other character, including the horseman she serves.

When Elesin fails to die and is arrested, Iyaloja turns on him with fierce contempt. "You have betrayed us," she tells him, accusing him of choosing to "eat the world's left-overs" rather than the "sweetmeats" the community had prepared for his honourable death. Soyinka gives her bitter food imagery that throws Elesin's hunger for life back at him, turning the appetite he indulged throughout the play into the proof of his shame. For her, his failure is a betrayal of the living, the dead and the unborn, and her harsh judgement confirms that she has always wanted the right thing done and cannot forgive its undoing.

Even amid this ruin, Soyinka shows Iyaloja thinking of the community rather than herself. Her command "Now forget the dead, forget even the living. Turn your mind only to the unborn" redirects everyone's grief towards the future, and the steady imperative verbs give her the calm authority Elesin has lost. As she arranges what must follow, she is the leader still holding the world together after the horseman has let it fall, so that by the end it is she, not Elesin, who carries the dignity of tradition.

Through her authority, her painful sacrifices and her fierce condemnation of failure, Soyinka presents Iyaloja as the determined guardian of tradition. She is the character who most clearly wants the right thing done, and who suffers most deeply when it is not.

parts.problemMd:
In what ways is the death ritual significant in Death and the King’s Horseman?

You must consider language, form and structure in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
### Model answer

The death ritual is the centre of the entire play: Soyinka makes Elesin's required death the act on which the balance of the Yoruba world depends, and its failure becomes the source of the tragedy.

The ritual is significant first as a sacred duty. As the King's Horseman, Elesin must die in order to follow his dead master and keep the cosmos in order. Soyinka presents this not as a simple act of suicide but as a profound matter of faith, using the Praise-Singer's chants and the steady drumming to surround it with ceremony and weight. From the opening scene, the whole community's attention is fixed on this single sacred event, so that the ritual shapes the form and atmosphere of the play from the start.

The ritual's significance is shown through Elesin's apparent willingness. He boasts that he does not fear death, telling the famous story of the "Not-I bird" from which everyone else flees, and declaring "My rein is loosened" as he prepares to go. Soyinka uses Elesin's vivid, confident language to show that the horseman is meant to embrace the ritual gladly. This makes the ritual feel noble rather than grim — and makes Elesin's later failure all the more shocking.

Soyinka also makes the ritual significant through the proverb-rich language that surrounds it. Elesin sums up its whole meaning in the short creed "Life is honour. / It ends when honour ends", and the women answer "We know you for a man of honour". The plain, balanced phrasing of this creed presents the ritual not as death for its own sake but as the highest form of honour, so that to refuse it is to lose everything that gives life value. Soyinka uses this weight of proverb and shared response to show that the ritual is woven into the community's very language and beliefs.

The ritual is also significant as a piece of theatre, not just an idea. Soyinka fills the early scenes with drumming, dance and song, so that the audience experiences the approaching death as a living ceremony rather than a discussion. The drums in particular act almost as a second voice, building a trance-like rhythm that is meant to carry Elesin gently towards his death. By making the ritual so physical on stage, Soyinka shows how completely it belongs to the whole community, drawing the audience into the same atmosphere of solemn celebration that the Yoruba characters feel.

The ritual becomes the play's central conflict when the colonial officer Pilkings tries to stop it. To the British it looks like barbaric self-destruction, but Soyinka presents their interference as a dangerous failure to understand the Yoruba world. The play warns that to halt the ritual is to "push our world from its course and sever the cord that links us to the great origin", an image that shows the ceremony holding the whole community's universe together. The clash between these two views of the ritual drives the drama.

The ritual's importance is proved by the disaster its failure causes. Distracted by his marriage and weakened by his love of life, Elesin hesitates, and Pilkings arrests him before he can complete the duty. Soyinka structures the play so that this single failure throws everything into crisis: the dead King is left unaccompanied and the community is shamed. The unfinished ritual becomes a wound in the world that the rest of the play must somehow answer.

Finally, the ritual's significance is shown when Elesin's son, Olunde, dies in his father's place. Having studied in England, Olunde nonetheless understands the duty his father abandoned, and his death restores the ritual at terrible cost. Soyinka uses this reversal — the Western-educated son completing the sacrifice the traditional father failed to perform — to show how vital the ritual is, and how its meaning passes down to the next generation rather than dying out.

The death ritual is significant, then, as the spiritual heart of the play. Soyinka makes it the duty that holds the Yoruba world together, the source of the central conflict, and the measure by which every character is finally judged.

parts.problemMd:
Iyaloja: “Now forget the dead, forget even the living. Turn your mind only to the unborn.”

Explore the idea of hope in the play.

You must consider language, form and structure in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
### Model answer

Although the play ends in death and failure, Soyinka threads hope through it, locating that hope not in the living but in duty fulfilled and in the future carried by the unborn.

At first, hope lies in the proper completion of the ritual. The community believes that if Elesin dies as he should, the world will stay in balance and life will continue safely. Soyinka surrounds the early scenes with celebration, song and dance, creating a hopeful, festive mood built on faith that tradition will hold. This opening hope depends entirely on Elesin doing his duty, and Soyinka's bright, ceremonial staging makes the audience share the community's confidence.

This early hope rests on a belief that the world has always held together. The Praise-Singer reminds Elesin that "Our world was never wrenched from its true course", and that in the ancestors' time it was never "tilted from its groove". Soyinka uses these proverb-like images of a world kept steady to suggest that the community's hope is grounded in an unbroken line of duty stretching back through the generations. The hope is not blind optimism but trust in a tradition that has never yet failed — which makes the threat to it feel all the more serious.

Iyaloja's instruction to "forget the dead, forget even the living" and "turn your mind only to the unborn" places hope firmly in the future. Soyinka uses her words to show that, in the Yoruba worldview, the living, the dead and the unborn are bound together, and that hope lies in protecting the generations still to come. Even as death approaches, Iyaloja points beyond it, and Soyinka gives her the play's calm, proverb-like wisdom so that her vision of hope feels deep and lasting rather than naive.

Elesin's failure seems to destroy this hope. When he hesitates and is arrested, the ritual is broken and the community is left shamed and endangered. Soyinka structures the play so that the bright hope of the opening collapses into darkness, suggesting that hope built on one weak man is fragile. The contrast between the festive beginning and the grim later scenes is one of Soyinka's strongest structural methods, and it makes the loss of hope feel devastating. By placing the brightest hope at the very start, Soyinka ensures that its collapse falls hardest, so that the structure itself teaches the audience how fragile a hope resting on one person can be.

Hope returns, painfully, through Olunde. By dying in his father's place, Olunde proves that the community's values survive even in a young man educated abroad. Soyinka uses Olunde's sacrifice to suggest that hope lies in the next generation's willingness to honour duty, even when their elders fail. His death is tragic, but it restores the broken order, showing that hope can outlive even terrible failure.

Olunde even gives this hope words before he acts on it. Talking to Jane Pilkings, he calls a willing death "an affirmative commentary on life", arguing that a sacrifice freely made does not deny life but gives it meaning. Soyinka uses this calm, reasoned line to show that, for Olunde, hope and death are not opposites: the right death can be a way of affirming the community's future. His own sacrifice then proves the point, so that the most hopeful idea in the play is spoken by the character who is about to die for it.

The hope Soyinka finally offers is hard-won and bitter. Elesin dies at last, shamed, while the community's attention turns, as Iyaloja urges, towards the unborn — the children who must carry the world forward. Soyinka refuses any easy comfort, but he leaves the audience with the sense that the community's deepest values, though wounded, will endure. Hope here survives not in any one person but in tradition passed on to those not yet born.

Soyinka presents hope as something rooted not in the survival of individuals but in duty done and in the unborn future. Through Iyaloja's words and Olunde's sacrifice, the play suggests that even amid death and failure, the community's values can be carried forward.

parts.problemMd:
How does Soyinka present the Praise-Singer in Death and the King’s Horseman?

You must consider language, form and structure in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
### Model answer

Soyinka presents the Praise-Singer as Elesin's devoted companion and the voice of Yoruba tradition, using him to celebrate, guide and finally mourn the King's Horseman.

The Praise-Singer is presented as Elesin's constant companion. From the opening he chants "Elesin O! Elesin Oba!", praising and following the horseman through the market. Soyinka uses him almost like a chorus in classical drama, weaving music and proverb around Elesin's words, so that the audience hears the community's voice praising its hero. His presence makes Elesin seem larger than life and surrounds him with ceremony, establishing the play's ritual atmosphere from the very first lines.

The Praise-Singer is significant for the rich, poetic language Soyinka gives him. He speaks in vivid images, promising that Elesin's name will be "like the sweet berry a child places under his tongue", and reminding him that in the ancestors' time the world was never "tilted from its groove". Soyinka uses this proverb-laden style to carry the wisdom and beauty of Yoruba oral tradition, making the Praise-Singer the play's most poetic voice and a living link to the past.

The Praise-Singer also acts as a guide and gentle conscience. He warns Elesin about the dangers of his appetite for life and women, hinting that pleasure may weaken his resolve. Soyinka uses him to voice the community's expectations, reminding Elesin of his duty even as he flatters him. In this way the Praise-Singer is both admirer and warner, holding Elesin to the high standard that tradition demands and quietly preparing the audience for the danger ahead.

Soyinka also uses the Praise-Singer to create dramatic irony. Early on he asks Elesin, "Are you sure there will be one like me on the other side?", a question meant only to praise the bond between them. By the end, after Elesin has failed, the question takes on a darker meaning, since there will now be no companion to follow at all. Soyinka plants this line so that the audience, looking back, feels the gap between the Praise-Singer's confident hope and the failure to come, deepening the sense of tragedy.

Soyinka also uses the Praise-Singer to give the play its distinctive sound. His chants work as call and response, with the community echoing his words, so that his voice never feels like a single speaker but like the voice of a whole people. Soyinka uses this shared music to bind the Praise-Singer to the community he speaks for, making him sound less like a character and more like tradition itself given a voice.

As the ritual approaches, the Praise-Singer becomes the voice meant to carry Elesin into death. He even imagines following the horseman, hoping for someone like himself on "the other side". Soyinka uses the Praise-Singer's chanting, together with the drumming, to create the trance-like atmosphere of the ritual, making him essential to the ceremony's spiritual power. His voice is the thread that should lead Elesin across into the world of the ancestors.

When Elesin fails, the Praise-Singer's tone turns from praise to grief and reproach. The companion who once sang Elesin's glory now mourns the broken ritual and the shame it brings. Soyinka uses this shift in the Praise-Singer's voice to measure the scale of Elesin's failure: even his most loyal admirer is filled with sorrow. Through the Praise-Singer, the audience feels the depth of the community's disappointment.

This change is sealed in the Praise-Singer's bitter farewell. He tells Elesin, "I call you by that name only this last time", reminding him that he once had "a tongue that darted like a drummer's stick". Soyinka contrasts this memory of Elesin's old eloquence with his present silence and shame, so that the Praise-Singer's grief becomes a kind of verdict. The voice that existed to praise him can now only say goodbye, which shows just how completely Elesin has fallen from the honour the Praise-Singer once celebrated.

Soyinka presents the Praise-Singer as Elesin's poetic shadow and the voice of tradition — celebrating, guiding and finally grieving for him. Through him, the play carries the beauty of Yoruba oral culture and measures the tragedy of the horseman's fall.

parts.problemMd:
“Despite living in the Yoruba community, Simon Pilkings only respects British law and order.”

In what ways is respect important in Death and the King’s Horseman?

You must consider language, form and structure in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
### Model answer

Soyinka presents respect as central to the play, contrasting the deep respect the Yoruba community holds for tradition and the dead with Pilkings's narrow respect for nothing but British law and order.

The Yoruba community is presented as bound together by respect for sacred duty. They honour the dead King, the ritual and the roles each person must play, and they treat Elesin's coming death as a matter of the highest importance. Soyinka uses the ceremony, song and proverb of the opening to show a society in which respect for tradition shapes everything. When the women declare that "tonight our husband and father will prove himself greater than the laws of strangers", Soyinka shows how completely the community respects its own values over colonial authority.

This respect is bound up with the idea of honour. Elesin states the community's creed plainly — "Life is honour. / It ends when honour ends" — and the women answer "We know you for a man of honour". Soyinka uses this exchange to show that respect in the Yoruba world is earned by living up to duty, not by holding power. The short, balanced phrasing of the creed makes respect feel like a shared law that everyone accepts, so that to lose honour is to lose the community's respect entirely — which is exactly what happens to Elesin.

Against this, Soyinka presents Pilkings as a man who respects only British power. He cannot see the ritual as anything but barbaric, and he moves to stop it without ever trying to understand its meaning. Most strikingly, Pilkings and his wife wear a confiscated ancestral egungun costume to a colonial ball, treating a sacred object as mere fancy dress. Soyinka uses this casual act of desecration as a powerful visual symbol of Pilkings's total lack of respect for the Yoruba world.

Respect is closely tied to power in the play. The colonial officials expect respect simply because they hold authority, while dismissing the community's own forms of respect as superstition. Soyinka exposes the cruelty and absurdity of this through the messenger Amusa, who is caught between two worlds and mocked by the market women as an "eater of white left-overs". This sharp, comic insult shows how the community withholds respect from those who serve the colonial power, even as that power demands respect it has not earned.

Olunde, Elesin's son, embodies a deeper respect that crosses cultures. Educated in England, he nonetheless respects the duty his father must perform, and he is appalled by the British failure to understand it. Soyinka uses Olunde's calm, reasoned speech to show that real respect means understanding the values of others — something Pilkings never manages. The contrast between Olunde's dignity and the officials' ignorance makes Soyinka's point about respect unmistakable.

Soyinka sharpens this through Olunde's defence of self-sacrifice. Olunde reminds Jane Pilkings that the British honour their own soldiers who die for others, calling such a death "an affirmative commentary on life". Soyinka uses this to expose how selective British respect really is: they admire sacrifice in their own people but condemn it in the Yoruba. By having Olunde turn their values back on them, Soyinka argues that true respect means judging another culture by the standards you accept for yourself, which Pilkings and his world consistently refuse to do.

The play finally turns on respect lost. Elesin forfeits the community's respect when he fails his duty, and his shame is unbearable precisely because respect matters so much in this world. Soyinka structures the ending so that Olunde's sacrifice restores some of the honour his father lost, showing that respect, once broken, can only be repaired at great cost. The whole tragedy grows from how much respect the failure destroys.

Through the community's profound respect for tradition, Pilkings's narrow respect for British law and Olunde's wider understanding, Soyinka makes respect the value that divides the two worlds of the play. The tragedy grows from the colonial failure to respect a world it does not even try to understand.

parts.problemMd:
Discuss the presentation of one character you find interesting in the play.

You must consider language, form and structure in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
### Model answer

Olunde is the play's most interesting character because he overturns every expectation: the Western-educated son who, far from rejecting tradition, understands and finally embraces the duty his father abandons.

Olunde is interesting first because of how Soyinka uses him to surprise the audience. Having gone to England to study medicine, he might be expected to scorn the ritual as primitive. Instead he returns home calm and resolute, prepared for his father's death. Soyinka uses Olunde to challenge the colonial assumption — shared by characters like Pilkings — that a Western education must make a person abandon their own culture. From his first entrance, Olunde quietly defies what both the British and the audience might expect of him.

Olunde is presented as unusually clear-sighted. In his conversation with Jane Pilkings, he calmly defends the ritual and points out the hypocrisy of a Britain that honours soldiers who die for their country while condemning the Yoruba sacrifice. Soyinka gives Olunde measured, intelligent speech that makes him the character who sees both worlds most clearly. This composure makes him far more thoughtful and dignified than the colonial officials who casually dismiss his culture.

Soyinka deepens this clear sight through Olunde's defence of self-sacrifice. Recalling a British captain who blew himself up to save his men, Olunde calls the act "an affirmative commentary on life", arguing that a willing death can give life meaning rather than deny it. Soyinka uses this to show Olunde turning the colonists' own values back on them: the very sacrifice the British admire in their own people is what they condemn in his. There is a quiet dramatic irony here, since the audience knows Olunde will soon prove his argument with his own life.

The same irony runs through Olunde's calm acceptance of his father's death. He tells Jane simply, "I came home to bury my father", expecting Elesin to die that night as duty demands. Soyinka loads this quiet line with dramatic irony, because Olunde will indeed bury a horseman — but it will be himself, dying in his father's place, while Elesin lives on in shame. By making Olunde so composed about a death he believes is certain, Soyinka shows how completely he has accepted the values his father will betray, and prepares the audience for the terrible reversal to come.

What makes Olunde compelling is his loyalty to a duty that is not even his to perform. When his father fails, Olunde steps into the role himself, choosing to die so that the ritual is completed and the community's world restored. Soyinka presents this as a profound act of love and duty, made more striking because Olunde, as a modern young man, has every reason to refuse. His decision is the moral high point of the play, and it gives the tragedy its terrible weight.

Olunde is also memorable for his devastating rejection of his father. Looking on the shamed, still-living Elesin, he declares "I have no father, eater of left-overs", before walking calmly away to his own death. Soyinka uses this cold, controlled line to show how completely Elesin has fallen in his son's eyes, and how seriously Olunde takes the duty his father betrayed. The reversal of roles between father and son — the son now the keeper of honour — is one of the play's most powerful moments.

Olunde's importance reaches across the whole play. His death restores the honour Elesin loses and proves that the community's values survive in the next generation. Soyinka uses him to give the tragedy its meaning: the future, it seems, lies not with the weak elder but with the son who understands. Olunde is interesting precisely because he carries the play's hope and its heartbreak at the same time.

Olunde is the play's most interesting character, then, because he defies every expectation, combining a Western education with a deep loyalty to tradition. Through his clear sight, his sacrifice and his rejection of his father, Soyinka makes Olunde the moral centre of the tragedy.

parts.problemMd:
How does Soyinka present Elesin in Death and the King’s Horseman?

You must consider language, form and structure in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
### Model answer

Soyinka presents Elesin as a magnificent but flawed figure: a man of huge vitality and pride whose love of life finally betrays the sacred duty he was born to perform.

Elesin is presented from the start as a man of enormous life. A stage direction describes his "infectious enjoyment of life", and he sweeps through the market dancing and singing, adored by the women and praised by the Praise-Singer. Soyinka uses this vitality to make Elesin magnificent and commanding, but it also plants a quiet warning: a man so in love with the world may find it hard to leave. From his first entrance, his greatness and his weakness are bound together.

Elesin presents himself as utterly fearless of death. He tells the story of the "Not-I bird", from which everyone else flees in terror, and insists that he alone does not run, declaring "My rein is loosened" as he prepares for the ritual. Soyinka gives him bold, confident, image-rich language so that the community — and the audience — believe he will die willingly. His pride in his own courage is part of what makes him heroic, but it also sets him up for a fall.

Soyinka reveals Elesin's flaw through his appetite for pleasure. On his final night he demands to marry a young bride, and his focus on this earthly joy hints that his hold on life is stronger than he admits. The Praise-Singer's warnings about how "the hands of women also weaken the unwary" point to the danger. Soyinka uses this to show pride and desire quietly undermining Elesin's resolve well before the crucial moment arrives.

Elesin's tragedy is his failure to die. Distracted and weakened, he hesitates, and the colonial officer Pilkings arrests him before the ritual can be completed. Soyinka structures the play so that the man who boasted he did not fear death cannot, in the end, perform it. Elesin tries to blame the white man and the gods, but Soyinka leaves the strong suggestion that his own love of life held him back — a flaw within the hero himself, which is what makes the tragedy so painful.

Soyinka exposes this weakness most sharply through Elesin's own excuses. Trying to explain his failure, Elesin claims he struggled to "retrieve my will from the power of the stranger", placing the blame on Pilkings and on colonial force. Yet Soyinka has already shown the audience Elesin's love of life and his clinging to his new bride, so the excuse rings hollow. By letting Elesin reach for grand language to cover a private weakness, Soyinka turns his eloquence against him, suggesting that the man who once spoke so proudly is now using words to hide from the truth about himself.

The scale of Elesin's fall is measured by Iyaloja's contempt. The mother of the market, who once honoured him, now tells him bluntly, "You have betrayed us", and accuses him of choosing to "eat the world's left-overs" instead of the honourable death prepared for him. Soyinka uses Iyaloja's hard, plain words to pass judgement on Elesin, turning the community's earlier praise into open condemnation. Her contempt shows how far the once-magnificent horseman has sunk in the eyes of the very people who revered him.

Finally, Soyinka presents Elesin overwhelmed by shame. His son Olunde dies in his place and rejects him as "eater of left-overs", and the broken horseman is left sobbing. When Elesin at last takes his own life in his prison cell, it is too late to restore the honour he has lost. Soyinka uses this bleak ending to complete the tragedy of a great man destroyed less by colonial power than by his own weakness.

Soyinka presents Elesin as a tragic hero: a man of dazzling vitality and pride whose love of life betrays his duty. His magnificence makes his failure all the more painful, and his shame and late death seal one of modern drama's most powerful tragedies.

parts.problemMd:
How is the relationship between Ed and Judy Boone presented in The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-time?

You must consider language, form and structure in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

In The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-time, Simon Stephens presents the relationship between Ed and Judy Boone as tense and emotional, shaped by misunderstanding, guilt, and their shared love for their son, Christopher. Their relationship is damaged but not beyond repair. Through the play, Stephens explores how poor communication, emotional stress, and absence affect their bond, while also showing that they may be able to rebuild some trust through their care for Christopher.

At the start of the play, we learn that Ed and Judy’s marriage has already broken down. Ed has lied to Christopher about Judy, telling him “your mother’s died”. While this seems cruel, it comes from a place of fear and love. Ed wants to protect Christopher from the painful truth of being left. His decision shows how much he struggles with his own feelings and with what’s best for his son.

Judy’s point of view is shown in the letters Christopher finds hidden in Ed’s wardrobe. In these, she admits her mistakes and shows her love for her son. She writes, “I was not a very good mother, Christopher. Maybe if things had been different, maybe if you’d been different, I might have been better at it.” This helps the audience understand that she didn’t stop caring for him — she was just overwhelmed. She also says, “I thought what I was doing was the best for all of us”, showing she still wants to be part of his life.

When Ed and Judy see each other again in London, their emotions run high. Judy is angry that Ed lied to Christopher and says, “What in God’s name did you think you were playing at saying those things to him?” Ed replies by listing all the things he did for Christopher on his own: “I cooked his meals. I cleaned his clothes… And you?” These arguments show how much pain and blame there is between them, but also how much they’ve both struggled.

Even though their relationship is full of tension, we also see moments where they work together for Christopher’s sake. For example, when Christopher refuses to talk to Ed about his Maths A Level, Judy acts as mediator and encourages Christopher to respond to his father. This shows that both parents still care deeply for their son and are starting to cooperate, even if they aren’t close anymore.

Stephens also uses form and structure to explore their relationship. As the play is told through Christopher’s point of view, with help from Siobhan, we see Judy and Ed through his eyes. This makes their actions seem more confusing at times, but also helps us understand how hard it is for Christopher to make sense of adult emotions. Stage directions add more meaning too — for example, when Ed shouts, “I will not have that man’s name mentioned in my house”, it shows how upset he is about Judy’s relationship with Mr Shears. When Christopher starts drumming to block out his parents’ argument, it shows how deeply their conflict affects him.

More broadly, the play shows how hard it can be to raise a neurodivergent child, especially in a world that doesn’t always offer support. Ed and Judy’s relationship breaks down not because they don’t love their son, but because they feel tired, alone, and unsure how to cope. Stephens doesn’t make either parent the villain — instead, he shows them as real people in a difficult situation.

In conclusion, Stephens presents Ed and Judy’s relationship as complicated and emotional. Their past is full of mistakes, but their care for Christopher brings moments of hope. parts.problemMd:
‘Christopher, Ed, Judy and Mrs Shears all try to cope with loss in different ways.’

Explore how different types of loss are dealt with in the play.

You must consider language, form and structure in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

Simon Stephens’s adaptation of The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-time explores the theme of loss in powerful and contrasting ways. Throughout the play, we see how different characters deal with various kinds of loss: the loss of loved ones, trust, stability, and even pets. Stephens uses dialogue, structure, and staging to help the audience understand how complex and personal the experience of loss can be.

At the start of the play, there is a shocking and sudden loss: Wellington the dog has been killed. This event deeply upsets both Christopher and Mrs Shears, but they react very differently. Mrs Shears is overwhelmed and reacts with “Oh no”, showing how much she relied on the dog for emotional comfort. Wellington was more than just a pet — he filled a gap left by people who had left her life. Later, it is revealed that Ed, Christopher’s father, killed the dog. He did this not out of hatred for the dog, but because he was angry and upset about losing his relationship with Mrs Shears. Ed couldn’t deal with his feelings properly and acted out in a violent way. This shows how grief can lead to destructive behaviour when it is not understood or processed.

Christopher, on the other hand, deals with the loss of Wellington in a completely different way. He doesn’t cry or show much emotion. Instead, he decides to investigate: “I want to find out who killed Wellington”. This makes sense for his character, as he sees the world through facts, logic, and patterns. Solving the mystery helps him make sense of something painful. His reaction is also seen when he is told that his mother has died. Instead of showing sadness, he asks, “What kind of heart attack?” and says, “It was probably an aneurysm”. These responses show that Christopher copes with emotional moments by thinking scientifically. It doesn’t mean he isn’t affected, but that his way of managing grief is different from what many people might expect.

Judy, Christopher’s mother, also suffers from loss in the play. She leaves her family, but it’s clear she didn’t stop loving her son. In one of her letters, she admits, “Maybe if things had been different… I might have been better at it”. This shows she feels guilty and regrets not being there. When Christopher appears at her flat in London, she acts immediately: “Come downstairs. Bring Toby. Get into the car”. Even though she left, she still sees herself as a mother and wants to protect Christopher. When her relationship with Mr Shears breaks down later in the play, Judy doesn’t dwell on it — she takes action by moving out and starting again with her son. This suggests that her way of dealing with loss is through physical change and new beginnings.

Another major moment of loss in the play is when Christopher finds out two difficult truths: first, that his mother is alive, and second, that Ed killed Wellington. This causes a deep loss of trust. Christopher says, “Father killed Wellington who is a dog and so that meant that he could kill me”. These words are heartbreaking. They show how betrayal can make someone feel unsafe, even around people they love. As a result, Christopher makes a huge decision: he leaves home and travels alone to London. This journey is full of danger and fear, but he handles it using careful planning and logic. Even when his pet rat, Toby, escapes on the train tracks, Christopher shows bravery and determination. This moment shows how far he is willing to go for those he loves, even in the middle of grief and confusion.

The play’s form and structure also help show the effects of loss. Stephens uses Siobhan as a narrator and guide, helping the audience understand Christopher’s thoughts. Because Christopher finds it hard to express emotions, Siobhan’s voice gives us extra insight into how he feels. The play’s non-linear structure (with flashbacks and quick scene changes) also reflects how grief can feel confusing and overwhelming.

In conclusion, Stephens presents loss as something that affects everyone in different ways. Whether it is the death of a pet, the collapse of a marriage, or the breakdown of trust between father and son, each character must find their own way to cope. Christopher uses logic and routines. Ed struggles with guilt and tries to make up for it. Judy acts quickly to protect what matters to her. parts.problemMd:
How is Christopher presented in The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-time?

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
### Model answer

Stephens presents Christopher as an unusual and deeply honest narrator-hero whose literal, logical way of seeing the world both isolates him and allows him to achieve extraordinary things.

Stephens establishes Christopher’s character through his precise, factual way of speaking. He introduces himself by stating that he knows “all the countries of the world and the capital cities” and “every prime number up to 7507”. The exactness of “7507” rather than a round number captures how Christopher’s mind works in precise facts. He also insists “I do not tell lies”, simply because he “can’t tell lies”, which makes him a completely reliable narrator and invites the audience to trust and sympathise with him from the start.

Stephens also presents Christopher as someone who struggles to understand other people. Christopher admits “I find people confusing”, explaining that “people do a lot of talking without using any words”. By having Christopher describe ordinary social signals, such as a raised eyebrow, as if they were a foreign code, Stephens lets the audience see the world from his point of view and understand why everyday interactions overwhelm him. This honesty about his difficulties makes him sympathetic rather than strange.

The play’s most striking feature is its form: Christopher’s teacher Siobhan reads aloud from the book he has written, and the cast act it out around him. Stephens uses this play-within-a-play structure to put Christopher’s mind directly on stage. The set, often a grid of squares and numbers, reflects the way Christopher organises the world, and his habit of numbering the chapters with prime numbers becomes the structure of the story itself. This form lets the audience experience Christopher’s logical, mathematical way of thinking rather than just hearing about it.

Stephens uses stagecraft to dramatise how Christopher experiences the world. When he is touched or overwhelmed, the stage erupts with noise, flashing lights and overlapping voices, especially during the terrifying journey through the London Underground. These moments use sound and lighting to put the audience inside Christopher’s panic, making them feel his distress rather than simply watch it. Stephens turns Christopher’s heightened senses into powerful theatre.

Despite his difficulties, Christopher is presented as quietly heroic. His investigation into the killing of Wellington the dog, and his solo journey to London to find his mother, show enormous courage for someone who finds the world so frightening. Stephens makes the audience admire him precisely because each small action — asking neighbours questions, getting on a train alone — costs him so much. By staging these ordinary tasks as huge obstacles, Stephens reframes courage as something measured not by how easy an act is, but by how much fear a character overcomes to do it. His refusal to lie also drives the plot: because Christopher cannot accept comforting untruths, he keeps digging until he uncovers his father’s lie that his mother had died, so the very honesty that sets him apart becomes the force that exposes the adults’ deceptions and pushes the story towards its crisis.

Structurally, the play builds towards Christopher’s triumph, and Stephens uses his success in maths to show his growing self-belief. When he learns he has passed his A level he announces simply, “I got an A”, and the plain statement carries enormous pride because the audience knows how much he has had to overcome. His repeated, hopeful question, “Does that mean I can do anything?”, ends the play on a note of fragile confidence. Stephens leaves this question hanging rather than answering it, so the audience is encouraged to believe in Christopher even as it sees how much the world still frightens him.

Through Christopher’s honest narration, the inventive play-within-a-play form and its bold stagecraft, Stephens presents a hero unlike any other. He encourages the audience not to pity Christopher but to admire him, showing that a mind which works differently can be a source of remarkable courage, logic and truth.
