parts.problemMd:
How are Mr and Mrs Shears important in The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-time?

You must consider language, form and structure in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
### Model answer

Although Mr and Mrs Shears appear only briefly, Stephens makes them hugely important, because between them they trigger the play's central mystery and reveal the truth about Christopher's broken family.

Mrs Shears matters first because her dog's death sets the whole play in motion. The opening stage direction — "A dead dog lies in the middle of the stage. A large garden fork is sticking out of its side" — gives the audience a shocking visual image before anyone speaks, and that dog belongs to Mrs Shears, described by Christopher as "our friend". Stephens uses this killing as the inciting incident: Christopher decides "I am going to find out who killed Wellington", and his investigation becomes the spine of the play. Without Mrs Shears and her dog, there is no detective story and no "book" for Christopher to write.

Mr Shears is important in a different way — he is the absent man behind the family's collapse. Christopher's detective logic names him early as his "Prime Suspect", because he "divorced Mrs Shears and left her". Dramatically, Stephens keeps Mr Shears mostly off-stage and talked about rather than seen, which makes him feel like a threatening, mysterious figure. The strength of feeling around him appears through Ed, who refuses to have "that man's name mentioned in my house" and snaps that "that man is evil". This intense reaction signals to the audience that Mr Shears is tied to something painful long before the truth comes out.

Together, the Shears expose the secret at the heart of the play. Through Mrs Alexander, Christopher learns that his mother was "very good friends with Mr Shears", and Siobhan's careful question about whether "your mother and Mr Shears had an affair" confirms it. Stephens uses dramatic irony here: the audience pieces the affair together alongside Christopher, sharing his slow, painful realisation. So the two Shears are structurally vital — Mrs Shears' dog begins the search for one truth, the killer, while Mr Shears turns out to be linked to a far bigger truth: why Christopher's mother really left.

The Shears also matter because they represent the messy adult relationships Christopher struggles to understand. Ed's confession reveals that Mrs Shears "helped me through a very difficult time" after Judy left, and that their friendship broke down because, as Ed bitterly puts it, she "cared more for that bloody dog than for us". This tangle of need, jealousy and resentment is exactly the kind of emotional world Christopher finds confusing. Stephens uses the Shears as a contrast to Christopher's literal, logical mind, highlighting the gap between his clear way of seeing and the complicated feelings of the adults around him.

The way Stephens presents the Shears adds to their importance. Because the whole play is staged as Christopher's "book" being read aloud by his teacher Siobhan, the Shears reach the audience filtered through Christopher's eyes and the words of other characters. We rarely hear directly from them; instead they are described, quoted and judged by others. This method makes them feel less like rounded people and more like pieces in Christopher's puzzle, which suits the detective structure and keeps the focus on how their actions affect Christopher rather than on their own feelings.

So although neither character is on stage for long, Stephens makes Mr and Mrs Shears essential. Mrs Shears' dog launches the plot, Mr Shears unlocks the family secret, and between them they reveal the adult world of love and betrayal that Christopher must slowly learn to navigate.

parts.problemMd:
Ed (talking to Christopher): “You have to know that I am going to tell you the truth from now on.”

Explore the significance of truth and lies in the play.

You must consider language, form and structure in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
### Model answer

Stephens makes truth and lies the moral centre of the play, contrasting Christopher's complete honesty with the damaging lies of the adults around him, and showing that trust can only be rebuilt through the truth.

From the start, Stephens presents Christopher as someone for whom lying is impossible. Through Siobhan reading his words, he explains "I do not tell lies", adding that "It is because I can't tell lies" rather than because he is good. This honesty is part of how his mind works: he needs the world to be factual and ordered. The form of the play reinforces this, since the whole story is staged as Christopher's truthful "book", read aloud by Siobhan, so the audience is constantly reminded that what we watch is his honest account. Stephens uses Christopher's literal truthfulness as a measuring stick against which every other character's dishonesty is judged.

The biggest lie in the play is Ed's. To protect Christopher, he claims "your mother's died", when in fact she has left for London with Mr Shears. Stephens builds this lie in stages — first that she has "had to go into hospital", then that she has died — so the audience watches a loving father bury the truth deeper and deeper. The lie is well-meant but devastating, and it shapes Christopher's whole understanding of his family until he discovers his mother's hidden letters.

The turning point comes when Christopher finds the letters and realises the truth. He states plainly, "Father lied to me. And also he killed Wellington and so that means that he could kill me." Stephens uses Christopher's flat, logical voice to make the moment more powerful: he reasons his way coldly from one lie to a terrifying conclusion. The detective structure of the play means the search for who killed Wellington leads directly to this bigger truth about the family, so the two mysteries are tied together and the audience uncovers both alongside Christopher.

The play's most important scene about truth is Ed's confession. He admits "I killed Wellington, Christopher" and tries to explain himself, but first he makes a promise: "You have to know that I am going to tell you the truth from now on." Stephens gives Ed a long, broken monologue full of pauses, which makes his honesty feel painful and genuine. Ed even admits "It's bloody hard telling the truth all the time", showing that truth-telling is an effort rather than something easy. Crucially, Christopher does not forgive him at once — he screams and pushes Ed away — because trust, once broken by lies, cannot be repaired instantly.

Stephens shows that lies, even kind ones, do real damage, while truth is the only path back to trust. Ed warns that "if you don't tell the truth now, then later on it hurts even more", a line that sums up the play's message. By the end, Ed slowly earns back Christopher's trust through small, honest actions, and the play closes on cautious hope rather than punishment. The structure moves from a web of lies towards gradual honesty, suggesting that relationships survive not by hiding the truth but by facing it.

Through Christopher's inability to lie, Ed's damaging deception and the slow rebuilding that follows, Stephens makes truth and lies the heart of the play. He shows that lies told out of love still wound, and that trust can only grow again on honest ground.

parts.problemMd:
Discuss the presentation of Christopher's relationship with animals in the play.

You must consider language, form and structure in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
### Model answer

Stephens presents Christopher as someone who trusts and understands animals far more easily than people, using his bond with animals to reveal both his loneliness and his need for a simple, honest world.

From early on, Christopher states simply "I like dogs" and insists "I think dogs are important too". Stephens shows that animals make sense to Christopher in a way people do not: they are predictable and do not lie or hide their feelings. This links to his wider character, since he finds human emotions and social rules confusing and frightening. His preference for animals is part of how Stephens presents Christopher's unusual, logical way of seeing the world.

Stephens opens the play with a powerful stage image built around an animal. Before anyone speaks, the audience sees "a dead dog" with "a large garden fork" sticking out of it, and Christopher standing silently beside it. Stephens uses this shocking opening tableau, and the long silence that follows, to make the dead animal the emotional centre of the play from its first moment. By placing Christopher next to the body rather than having him explain it, Stephens shows how much the animal matters to him before we even understand his character, so the audience’s sympathy is tied to Christopher’s care for the dog from the very start.

Christopher's clearest relationship is with his pet rat, Toby. He lists "looking after Toby" among the things he loves most, and even imagines taking the rat into space, saying he "would like it if I could take Toby with me". Stephens uses Toby to show Christopher's caring, responsible side: he looks after the animal faithfully, and the rat becomes a source of comfort and companionship. When Christopher later makes the terrifying journey to London alone, taking Toby with him shows how the animal is a steady, trusted presence in a confusing human world.

Christopher's bond with animals also drives the plot. The play opens with the disturbing image of Wellington, "a dead dog" with "a large garden fork ... sticking out of its side", and it is Christopher's care for the animal that makes him determined: "I am going to find out who killed Wellington." Stephens makes this animal death the inciting incident, and Christopher's sense that the dog deserves justice launches his detective "book". His reaction shows that he feels a strong moral duty towards animals, arguably stronger than the duty the adults around him feel.

Animals matter to Christopher because they never betray him, unlike the people who do. The deepest wound in the play is that his father "killed Wellington", and Christopher's cold logic — that someone who could kill a dog "could kill me" — shows how closely he links cruelty to animals with danger and broken trust. Stephens uses this to make the killing of a dog feel as serious as a crime against a person, because for Christopher animals are honest creatures who deserve protection. The fact that the lie about his mother and the killing of the dog come from the same person makes his sense of betrayal complete.

Christopher's love of animals connects to his love of being alone. He explains that he "really like[s] little spaces so long as there is no one else in them with me", and his dream of being an astronaut is partly a dream of a calm world without confusing people. Stephens stages the play as Christopher's "book", with Siobhan reading his words aloud, so the audience hears his fondness for animals directly in his own honest voice. This form keeps us close to Christopher's feelings and helps us understand why simple, loyal animals matter so much to him.

Through Toby, Wellington and his clear preference for animals over people, Stephens presents Christopher's relationship with animals as a window into his character. Animals give him the honesty, loyalty and calm that he cannot always find in the human world.

parts.problemMd:
Ed (talking about Christopher): “I cooked his meals. I cleaned his clothes. I looked after him every weekend.”

Explore the idea of looking after others in The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-time.

You must consider language, form and structure in your answer.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
### Model answer

Stephens presents looking after others as one of the play's central concerns, showing through Ed, Siobhan and Christopher himself that real care is difficult, practical and often unappreciated, but deeply important.

Ed is the clearest example of looking after others. As a single father, his love for Christopher shows in everyday actions rather than words. In his angry, hurt speech he lists everything he has done: "I cooked his meals. I cleaned his clothes. I looked after him every weekend." Stephens uses this pile-up of short, plain sentences to show how much practical care Ed has given, and how exhausted and unappreciated he feels. The repeated "I" hammers home that, for Ed, love means daily, unglamorous effort that nobody notices.

Stephens shows that looking after Christopher is genuinely hard, which makes Ed's care more real. Judy's letters admit that she "couldn't take it any more" and left, while Ed stayed. Even Ed reaches breaking point: his lie about Christopher's mother and his killing of Wellington come partly from the strain of coping alone for years. Stephens does not present Ed as a perfect carer but as a flawed, struggling one, and this makes his devotion more believable and moving than an easy, idealised love would be.

Christopher's teacher Siobhan looks after him in a gentler, different way. Throughout the play she helps him understand his own feelings and the confusing behaviour of others. Stephens gives her a special role in the play's form: she reads Christopher's "book" aloud and often speaks directly to the audience, guiding both Christopher and us through the story. Her calm, patient support shows a kind of care based on understanding rather than just practical tasks, and she becomes a steady, trusted figure when the adults in his family let him down.

Looking after others is not only something done to Christopher; he does it too. He cares devotedly for his pet rat, listing "looking after Toby" as one of the things he loves most, and refuses to leave the animal behind when he travels. His determination to win justice for the murdered Wellington is also a kind of care. Stephens uses these moments to show that Christopher, so often seen as someone who only needs looking after, is himself loyal and protective towards the creatures he loves. His care is fierce and uncomplicated, a quiet contrast to the messy, strained care the adults around him struggle to give.

Stephens uses the play's structure to show that the role of carer has to be earned back once it is broken. After Christopher learns the truth, he no longer trusts his father, and Ed can only begin to repair their relationship through a promise and a small, careful action. Ed swears, "I promise I will never do anything like that again", and later gives Christopher a puppy he names Sandy. Stephens makes the gift of an animal Ed's way of proving he can be trusted to look after something again, so that the play ends with care being slowly rebuilt rather than simply restored. This quiet, hopeful resolution shows that looking after others depends on patience as much as effort.

Stephens links looking after others to honesty and trust. Ed's care is almost destroyed by his lies, and he can only begin to put things right by promising the truth and slowly proving, through small actions, that Christopher can rely on him again. The play's structure moves from this broken trust towards a fragile, hopeful repair. By staging the story as Christopher's own account, read by Siobhan, Stephens keeps the audience close to Christopher's experience of being looked after — and of learning to look after others in return.

Through Ed's practical devotion, Siobhan's patient guidance and Christopher's love for Toby, Stephens presents looking after others as demanding and imperfect but essential. The play suggests that real care is shown not in words but in steady, everyday actions — and that it depends on trust.

parts.problemMd:
Explore the theme of love in Klara and the Sun.

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
### Model answer

Ishiguro presents love as the most powerful force in the novel, exploring it through Klara's selfless devotion, a mother's desperate love for a dying child, and the question of whether love can ever be copied or replaced.

The clearest love in the novel is Klara's devotion to Josie. As an "Artificial Friend", a solar-powered robot bought to be a child's companion, Klara was designed only to serve, yet her care for Josie grows into something that feels like real love. She watches Josie constantly, learns her habits, and becomes anxious whenever Josie is unwell. Ishiguro tells the whole story through Klara's first-person narration, so the reader experiences Josie entirely through Klara's loving, attentive eyes, and is forced to ask whether a machine can truly love. In a future world where children are given robots instead of human friends, Klara's deep care quietly criticises a society that has begun to hand love over to technology.

Ishiguro also explores a mother's love that is shaped by fear of loss. Josie has been "lifted" — genetically edited to improve her chances in life — and this risky procedure has left her dangerously ill, as it killed her sister Sal. The Mother's love is real but desperate: she secretly plans, with Mr Capaldi, to "continue" Josie in an artificial body if she dies, and even has Klara learn to copy Josie's walk and voice. Ishiguro uses this disturbing plan to show how love can become possessive and frightening. In a society that treats children as projects to be improved, the Mother's love is twisted by the pressure to keep Josie at any cost.

Love in the novel is closely tied to sacrifice. Believing the Sun has the power to heal, Klara sacrifices part of herself to help Josie: she damages the polluting "Cootings Machine" and gives up some of her own fluid, trusting that the Sun will reward her by making Josie well. When she begs the Sun for "special help", Klara insists she would "willingly have given more, given it all", and the repetition shows that her love sets no limit on what she will sacrifice. Ishiguro presents this as an act of pure, selfless love, even though it rests on Klara's mistaken, almost religious faith. The fact that Josie does recover keeps the cause ambiguous, but the love behind Klara's sacrifice is never in doubt, and it contrasts with the anxious, controlling love of the adults around Josie.

Ishiguro contrasts these loves with the simple, hopeful bond between Josie and Rick. Rick is "not lifted", which in this divided society limits his future, yet the two children promise to stay together. Their childhood love is tested by the inequality around them, and the novel leaves their future uncertain. Through them, Ishiguro suggests that genuine human love struggles to survive in a world obsessed with status and improvement, where even children are sorted into winners and losers.

The novel's deepest exploration of love is whether it can be copied at all. Mr Capaldi believes there is "nothing special" inside a person that cannot be reproduced in a machine. By the end, Klara reaches a gentler conclusion: that what made Josie special was not something inside her that could be transferred, but the love others felt for her. Ishiguro uses Klara's quiet realisation to argue that love cannot be manufactured or copied; it lives in the bonds between people. In a world racing to replace humans with technology, this is the novel's most important message about love.

Klara's love is also shown in her ending. Once Josie has grown up and left, Klara is not returned home or repaired but left to run down in a junk Yard. Even so, she feels no bitterness, choosing instead a quiet "slow fade" as she sorts through her happy memories of Josie. Ishiguro uses Klara's calm acceptance to present the deepest love as one that expects nothing in return, asking for no reward even after being discarded. In a society that buys, uses and throws away its Artificial Friends, Klara's loyal, undemanding love quietly exposes how carelessly people treat the very beings made to love them.

Through Klara's selfless devotion, the Mother's desperate love, and the tender bond between Josie and Rick, Ishiguro presents love as the force that makes us human. The novel warns that a society which tries to improve, control or copy love risks losing the very thing that gives life meaning.

parts.problemMd:
Discuss the significance of sacrifice in Klara and the Sun.

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
### Model answer

Ishiguro makes sacrifice central to the novel, using Klara's selfless offering of herself to explore love, faith and what it truly means to be human.

The most important sacrifice is Klara's. Convinced that the Sun has the power to heal, and that the polluting "Cootings Machine" is blocking his light, Klara destroys part of the machine using a portion of her own internal fluid — knowing this may damage her. She even asks the Father to help drain the fluid from inside her own head, calmly accepting that it might leave her slower and less able to think clearly afterwards. Ishiguro presents this as a deliberate, loving choice, and because the whole novel is narrated by Klara, the reader feels the quiet weight of her willingness to suffer for someone she loves.

Klara's sacrifice is powered by an almost religious faith. As a solar-powered machine, she treats the Sun as a living, kindly force, believing he sent "special help" to a beggar and his dog and will do the same for Josie. When she sees Beggar Man, whom she had thought dead, "come back to life" in the Sun's light, she takes it as proof of his power, and this becomes the evidence on which she stakes everything. Ishiguro uses Klara's childlike faith to make her sacrifice deeply moving, even though it rests on a misunderstanding of how the world really works. In a future society that trusts science and data above all, Klara's belief is strange and touching, and it raises the question of whether faith and love matter more than facts.

Ishiguro also shows a darker, more troubling kind of sacrifice in the adults. The Mother is willing to sacrifice almost anything to keep Josie, even planning to "continue" her in an artificial body. She has already, in a sense, sacrificed Josie's safety by having her "lifted" — genetically edited to get ahead, despite the risk that killed her first daughter. Through this, Ishiguro explores how a competitive, status-driven society pressures parents into terrible sacrifices, gambling with their children's lives for the sake of success.

Ishiguro widens the idea of sacrifice through Rick, who is forced to sacrifice his future because he is "unlifted". In this divided society, colleges take only a tiny "less than two percent" of unlifted students, so a child who is not genetically edited is quietly written off before he has begun. Rick is clever and kind, yet the system treats his potential as expendable. Ishiguro uses Rick to show that sacrifice in the novel is not always chosen: the most damaging sacrifices are the ones a cruel social order imposes on those it has already decided do not matter. This makes Klara's freely given sacrifice shine more brightly by contrast.

Klara's whole existence is itself a kind of sacrifice. She is bought to serve Josie, gives all her attention and love, and is eventually moved aside once Josie grows up and no longer needs her. Ishiguro presents Klara's final days in a yard, slowly fading, with striking gentleness: she does not complain, but reflects with contentment on her time with Josie. This quiet ending makes the reader question how a society treats the machines — and perhaps the people — who give everything and are then discarded, raising the uncomfortable thought that a world built on AI labour depends on sacrifices it never bothers to notice.

The significance of sacrifice is that it reveals true love and even a kind of humanity. Klara's willingness to give herself for Josie stands in clear contrast to the controlling love of the adults, and it leads to her gentle conclusion that what made Josie special was the love others had for her, not anything that could be copied. That an Artificial Friend, built only to serve, should be the character most capable of selfless sacrifice is Ishiguro's quiet challenge to a society that assumes machines cannot feel and that worth can be measured. Ishiguro uses sacrifice to argue that love which expects nothing in return is the most human thing in the novel — more human, perhaps, than the choices of the people around Klara.

Through Klara's selfless offering, the Mother's desperate gambles and Klara's own quiet fading, Ishiguro presents sacrifice as the heart of the novel. He suggests that the willingness to give up something for love is what gives life — even an artificial life — its deepest meaning.

parts.problemMd:
How is Klara presented in the novel?

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
### Model answer

Ishiguro presents Klara as an observant, selfless and deeply loving Artificial Friend whose innocence and devotion make her, in many ways, more human than the people around her.

Klara is first presented as extraordinarily observant. As an "Artificial Friend" waiting in a store, she studies human behaviour closely, learning about the world from everything she sees through the window. Ishiguro shows her piecing reality together in fragments, building up an understanding of people from the smallest details of how they move and speak. This unusual way of seeing, conveyed through her first-person narration, makes Klara feel both machine-like and childlike at once, and it draws the reader into her careful, innocent view of the world. In a future society that mass-produces such machines, Ishiguro makes this particular AF feel strikingly individual.

Klara is presented above all as faithful. Once chosen by Josie, she devotes herself completely to the girl's wellbeing, watching over her, worrying about her illness, and never putting herself first. Ishiguro uses Klara's constant attention to show a love that is patient and selfless. In a world where children are given machines as companions because they are lonely, Klara's genuine devotion quietly suggests that she offers more real care than the busy, anxious adults around her.

Klara's innocence is shown through her faith in the Sun. Because she is solar-powered, she treats the Sun as a living, kindly being who can heal, believing he sent "special help" to others and will save Josie. Ishiguro presents this faith with great tenderness, even though it is mistaken, using it to make Klara seem pure and hopeful. Her childlike belief contrasts sharply with the cold, scientific world of "lifting" and genetic editing, and it raises the novel's question of whether such faith is foolish or beautiful.

Klara is also presented as quietly heroic in her willingness to sacrifice herself. She gives up part of her own fluid to damage the polluting Cootings Machine, hoping the Sun will reward her by healing Josie, and calmly accepts that this may leave her weaker. Ishiguro's plain, uncomplaining narration makes this selflessness more moving, because Klara never sees it as a sacrifice at all — only as something worth doing for someone she loves.

Ishiguro also presents Klara through the limits of her understanding, creating dramatic irony the reader must decode. Klara, like Josie, is told that Mr Capaldi is making a "portrait" of Josie, and she does not at first grasp that this so-called portrait is really an artificial body meant to "continue" Josie if she dies. Because the reader sees only what Klara sees, we slowly piece the truth together ahead of her, which makes her trust seem all the more innocent. Ishiguro uses this gap between Klara's literal reading of events and the darker reality to show both her purity and the disturbing way the adults conceal their plans, even from the AF they expect to play a part in them.

Klara's way of seeing is itself part of how she is presented. When she is confused or moved, the world around her appears "partitioned" into separate boxes that she has to assemble into a single picture. Ishiguro uses this odd, mechanical perception to remind the reader that Klara is a machine, yet the emotions she reads in those boxes — "joy, fear, sadness" — are unmistakably human. This tension between her artificial mind and her tender feelings runs through the whole novel and is central to how Ishiguro builds sympathy for her.

Finally, Ishiguro presents Klara with dignity even as she is discarded. Once Josie grows up, Klara is moved aside and ends her days in a yard, slowly fading, yet she reflects on her life without bitterness, content that she did her best for Josie. This gentle ending makes the reader uneasy about how easily this future society uses and then throws away its machines. It also suggests that Klara, who loved and gave everything, may be more human than the people who replaced her with newer models.

Through her sharp observation, faithful devotion, innocent faith and quiet self-sacrifice, Ishiguro presents Klara as a deeply sympathetic figure. In a cold, divided world, her selfless love makes her, paradoxically, the most human character in the novel, and a gentle warning about what people may be losing.

parts.problemMd:
In what ways is Josie important in Klara and the Sun?

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
### Model answer

Josie is important because she is the emotional centre of the novel — the child Klara loves, the focus of her family's fears, and the figure through whom Ishiguro explores illness, love and a divided future society.

Josie is important first because she gives the novel its purpose. She chooses Klara in the store and takes her home, and from then on Klara's whole existence revolves around her. Because Ishiguro narrates through Klara, we only ever see Josie through the loving, anxious eyes of her Artificial Friend, which makes Josie feel precious and constantly watched over. Without Josie there is no story for Klara to tell, and no one for her devotion to fix upon.

Josie is important as the source of the novel's central fear: her illness. She has been "lifted" — genetically edited to succeed — and this dangerous procedure has made her seriously ill, just as it killed her sister Sal. Josie's sickness drives the plot, prompting Klara's desperate appeal to the Sun and the family's secret plans. Through Josie, Ishiguro explores a future where parents gamble with their children's health for the sake of status, showing the human cost of a ruthless, competitive society.

Josie is also important because she raises the novel's biggest question: whether a person can be copied. The Mother and Mr Capaldi secretly plan to "continue" Josie in an artificial body if she dies, and they have Klara study Josie so closely that she can imitate her walk and voice. Ishiguro uses Josie to ask whether there is something unique and irreplaceable in a human being. Her eventual recovery leaves the question open, but it allows Klara to conclude that what made Josie special was the love others felt for her.

Through her relationship with Rick, Josie reveals the inequality of the novel's world. Rick is "unlifted", which limits his future, while Josie has been lifted at great risk. Their childhood promise to stay together is strained by this divide, and the novel leaves their future uncertain. Ishiguro uses Josie and Rick to show how a society obsessed with genetic advantage damages even the closest human bonds, and how children pay the price for their parents' choices.

Josie is also important because, unlike Klara, she is a believably flawed child shaped by her world. At the "interaction meeting" arranged so lifted children can mix, the other guests threaten to "throw her over" to test Klara's coordination, and Josie says nothing to stop them — it is Rick, the unlifted boy, who steps in to defend her. Ishiguro uses this uncomfortable moment to show that even a sympathetic child can be made cruel, or at least cowardly, by the pressure to fit in with her privileged peers. Yet Josie is also capable of real tenderness: when she breaks a promise she tells Klara, "I'm sorry, Klara", with obvious guilt. By making Josie inconsistent and human in this way, Ishiguro keeps her from becoming a mere symbol of illness, and shows how social pressure can warp even a fundamentally kind young person.

Josie's bond with Rick is also important in showing the warmth and creativity the harsh society around her threatens. The two share a private "bubble game", in which Josie draws sketches and Rick fills in the empty speech bubbles, a game "invented a long time earlier in their childhoods". Ishiguro uses this small, intimate ritual to show a genuine human connection built on imagination rather than status, and Klara observes its "growing importance" to them both. Through it, Ishiguro suggests that what is most valuable about Josie — her humour, her imagination, her loyalty — is exactly what a future obsessed with grades and "lifting" risks crushing.

Finally, Josie is important because her growing up shapes Klara's fate. As Josie recovers and matures, she gradually needs Klara less, and eventually Klara is set aside. Ishiguro presents this without blame — Josie is simply a child becoming an adult — but it quietly highlights how the people and machines who love us can be left behind. Josie's journey from sick child to independent young woman gives the novel its shape and its bittersweet ending.

Josie is important, then, as the heart of the novel: the child Klara loves, the focus of her family's hopes and fears, and the figure through whom Ishiguro explores illness, inequality and what makes a person unique. Her story gives the whole novel its meaning.

parts.problemMd:
In what ways is Lennie significant in Of Mice and Men?

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

As one of the novel’s protagonists, Lennie is a deeply significant character in Of Mice and Men and his character reveals key themes such as vulnerability, dreams, power and isolation. Through Lennie, Steinbeck illustrates the harshness of 1930s America and critiques how society treats those who are different.

Lennie is first introduced as a physically powerful character but is vulnerable because of his learning difficulties. Steinbeck uses contrasting imagery to highlight the differences between Lennie and George. While George has “sharp”, “strong” and “slender” features, Lennie is described as “shapeless of face” with “large, pale eyes” which immediately sets him apart. Steinbeck also uses animalistic language to describe Lennie. For instance, it states that he was “dragging his feet a little, the way a bear drags his paws” and that he “bleated with terror”. These comparisons emphasise both Lennie’s physicality and his innocence. His strength, combined with his lack of understanding, makes him both dangerous and deeply vulnerable.

Lennie’s childlike innocence is evident through his love of soft things such as mice, puppies and rabbits, and he even dreams of tending rabbits on the farm he and George hope to own. His repeated desire to “live off the fatta the lan’” is symbolic of the American Dream and his childlike enthusiasm helps keep the dream alive for both him and George. Lennie’s firm belief in the dream offers hope and companionship in a world which is defined by loneliness and economic hardship. This dream becomes even more poignant when considering the context of the Great Depression, a time when many itinerant workers like George and Lennie were left hopeless and rootless.

Lennie is significant because his actions foreshadow later events in the novel. Early in the novel, Lennie, not realising his own strength, inadvertently kills a mouse by petting it too hard. Later, he accidentally kills a puppy given to him by Slim, exclaiming, “I didn’t bounce you hard”. Finally, and most tragically, he kills Curley’s wife in the barn when she allows him to stroke her hair. These events reveal how Lennie’s inability to control his strength leads inevitably to catastrophe. His actions reinforce Steinbeck’s theme of inevitable failure and how even the purest dreams cannot survive in a world governed by brutality and misunderstanding.

Lennie is also depicted as a victim and Curley views Lennie as an easy target for his hatred. Candy explains that Curley “hates big guys” which suggests that Lennie’s physical presence threatens insecure men. During Curley’s attack in the bunkhouse, Lennie only retaliates under George’s command, crushing Curley’s hand in a moment that is both defensive and destructive. Lennie fails to understand the consequences of his strength and this misunderstanding makes him a danger to others and himself. Yet Steinbeck does not portray Lennie as malicious. Instead he ensures readers see Lennie as a tragic figure shaped by a world that has no real place for him.

The novel also shows how society deals with people like Lennie. When he runs away after killing Curley’s wife, he hides in the brush, remembering George’s instructions. A lynch mob forms and although George briefly considers Lennie might be locked up, Slim reminds him that Lennie would not survive such treatment. The threat of institutionalisation, of being put in a “booby hatch”, reflects the limited social care available for those with learning difficulties during the 1930s. Therefore Lennie’s fate is a commentary on the cruelty of a system that punishes rather than protects the vulnerable.

Lennie’s death is one of the most significant moments in the novel. George shoots Lennie as an act of mercy, protecting him from the mob. Lennie dies while imagining the dream, with George describing the farm to him one last time and this allows Lennie to die peacefully, believing the dream is within reach. Steinbeck uses this ending to suggest that Lennie, ironically, comes closest to realising the dream as he dies believing it will actually happen. This reinforces the tragedy that in 1930s America, dreams like theirs were often doomed by poverty and social prejudice.

In conclusion, Lennie is a deeply significant character in Of Mice and Men. He embodies the themes of innocence, vulnerability and broken dreams. Through Lennie, Steinbeck explores how society marginalises the weak and how, in a world full of violence and inequality, even the most hopeful dreams are often crushed. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 40-mark question. parts.problemMd:
Discuss the importance of settings in the novel.

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

In Of Mice and Men, Steinbeck uses setting not only to establish atmosphere but also to reflect the themes of isolation, vulnerability and broken dreams. From the peaceful clearing by the pool to the stark bunkhouse and Crooks’ room, each location in the novel helps to shape the reader’s understanding of the characters’ lives and the harsh realities they face.

The novel begins and ends at the natural clearing by the pool, an idyllic space that Steinbeck describes through rich imagery. The water is still, the trees are leafy and the animals scurry around peacefully. This scene evokes the Garden of Eden and it is juxtaposed with the grim world of the ranch. During the Great Depression, millions of itinerant workers travelled with little more than bedrolls, often camping outdoors like George and Lennie. The “smooth” branch near the pool shows that many others have sat in the same spot and are part of an endless cycle of poverty. However, Steinbeck also uses this same setting as a place of death at the end of the novel and when Lennie returns there, nature reflects the tension and violence which is about to occur. For instance, Steinbeck describes how the heron swallows the water snake, symbolising the survival of the fittest. Here, Steinbeck uses the natural world to show both the beauty and brutality of life.

The bunkhouse is another key setting, reflecting the bleakness of itinerant workers’ lives. Steinbeck describes it as a “long, rectangular building” with whitewashed walls, lacking warmth or comfort. There are no personal possessions, just bunks and a “black cast-iron stove”. The bunkhouse is depicted as a place of masculinity and hierarchy, where Curley asserts dominance and where Lennie is vulnerable. The claustrophobic nature of this space contrasts with the openness of the outdoors, symbolising how the characters are trapped in repetitive, hopeless routines. This reflects the Great Depression, when millions of men like George and Lennie travelled for work but found no security.

The barn is equally important as a setting. It is initially portrayed as a place of warmth and Slim gives Lennie one of Lulu’s pups there. However, this becomes the setting for two major deaths: the puppy and Curley’s wife. When Lennie kills the puppy, Steinbeck uses this to foreshadow the later tragedy of Curley’s wife. The horses sense unease as they stamp their feet and “rattle” their “halter chains”. The barn thus becomes a place of danger and death, reinforcing Steinbeck’s idea that dreams, like Lennie’s desire to tend rabbits, are destined to fail in such a brutal world. It also highlights the fragility of life for people like Lennie and Curley’s wife, who, as someone with learning disabilities and a woman respectively, are both powerless and misunderstood.

Crooks’ room is another symbolic setting. It is a “little shed” off the barn, filled with broken equipment and harnesses, showing both his role as a stable buck and his position in the social hierarchy of the ranch. Crooks sleeps on a “long box filled with straw”, which is worse than the white ranch hands’ basic bunks, revealing how black people were segregated and dehumanised. Steinbeck uses this setting to reflect Crooks’ isolation: he is both physically and socially excluded. Crooks tells Lennie, “A guy needs somebody — to be near him,” reinforcing the novel’s theme of loneliness. His room, like his life, is separated from the rest and is another reflection of racial prejudice in 1930s America.

Time also plays a crucial role in the novel’s setting. The story takes place over just a few days, adding urgency and a sense of inevitability. Events move quickly: the men arrive on Friday, spend Saturday in town and by Sunday afternoon, Curley’s wife is dead. This compressed timeline mirrors the fragile nature of the characters’ dreams and highlights how quickly hope can turn to despair. Further, the novel’s setting in Soledad, meaning solitude, also reinforces the theme of loneliness which is depicted in each setting.

In conclusion, Steinbeck uses settings not simply to describe where things happen, but to deepen the reader’s understanding of the characters and their world. parts.problemMd:
Discuss the theme of responsibility in Of Mice and Men

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

Steinbeck explores the theme of responsibility in Of Mice and Men through the characters’ relationships, the moral choices they make and the wider social context of 1930s America. The theme is particularly evident in how characters respond to the needs of others and the consequences of their actions.

The clearest example of personal responsibility is seen in George’s relationship with Lennie. From the start, George is presented as a reluctant guardian, having promised Lennie’s Aunt Clara that he would look after him. This sense of duty drives George’s every decision. The novel is set during the Great Depression, when economic hardship meant people had to fend for themselves. Most men travelled alone, focused only on survival. George and Lennie’s companionship stands in contrast to this reality, offering a glimpse of a more compassionate way of living that the world around them ultimately rejects. Although he occasionally expresses frustration, "God a'mighty, if I was alone I could live so easy", his actions consistently reveal deep care. Furthermore, Lennie’s mental disability and the lack of support systems reflect the social attitudes of the time. Institutions for the mentally ill and those with learning disabilities were often brutal, and George’s actions can be seen as protecting Lennie from a cruel system. George’s protective behaviour, like instructing Lennie not to talk to the boss, reflects the weight of this responsibility. Steinbeck contrasts George’s loyalty with the usual loneliness of itinerant workers, highlighting the unusual and burdensome nature of this relationship.

Responsibility is also explored in George’s final decision to shoot Lennie. This act is both shocking and compassionate. Rather than allow Lennie to fall into the hands of Curley’s lynch mob, George takes responsibility for ending his life peacefully. By doing so, George spares Lennie from a brutal death and prevents future tragedies. Steinbeck presents this as a heavy moral burden, one that isolates George completely by the end. The choice reflects a deeper, more painful form of responsibility: taking accountability even when there are no good options.

Slim, the "prince of the ranch" is another character who embodies responsible behaviour. He is respected and trusted and his calm authority means others look to him for moral guidance. When Candy’s old dog is to be shot, Slim is the one whose opinion is most valued: “Candy looked a long time at Slim to try to find some reversal”. Slim’s quiet leadership contrasts with Carlson’s blunt insensitivity and his giving of the puppy to Lennie unintentionally sets up the novel’s climax, demonstrating how even responsible acts can have unintended consequences.

Similarly, Candy’s relationship with his old dog is an example of evading moral responsibility. Although he clearly cares for the animal, Candy allows Carlson to take on the task of euthanising it, rather than doing it himself. He later confesses bitterly, “I ought to of shot that dog myself”, a statement that not only reveals his guilt but also foreshadows George’s decision to shoot Lennie personally. Later in the novel, Candy is quick to invest in George and Lennie’s dream, offering his life savings in exchange for security. His eager declaration, “S'pose I went in with you guys. Tha's three hunderd an' fifty bucks I'd put in” suggests he sees the dream as a way to avoid taking charge of his future in a world that has discarded him due to age and disability.

Steinbeck also uses characters who shirk responsibility to explore the theme from another angle, showing how inaction or selfishness can be just as destructive as misguided duty. Curley’s wife, though often portrayed as a victim of loneliness and gender inequality, also demonstrates a lack of awareness, or disregard, for the consequences of her behaviour. She repeatedly seeks out Lennie, despite knowing his unpredictable nature. When she says, “Why can't I talk to you? I never get to talk to nobody” it reflects her need for attention but also her manipulation of a dangerous situation. Her decision to let Lennie stroke her hair directly contributes to the tragic climax. Steinbeck shows how irresponsible actions, even when driven by desperation or isolation, can have fatal outcomes.

In conclusion, Steinbeck uses multiple characters and situations to show how responsibility can be a burden, a moral duty and a force for good or harm. Through George, Slim, Candy and others, he suggests that in an unforgiving world, taking responsibility for others is both noble and tragic. Ultimately, Steinbeck critiques a society that fails to support the vulnerable, leaving responsibility in the hands of individuals who are often unequipped to bear it alone. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 40-mark question. parts.problemMd:
Explore Candy’s relationship with others, including his old dog, in the novel.

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

In Of Mice and Men, Steinbeck presents Candy as a deeply isolated character whose relationships with others reveal the harsh realities of ageing, disability and loneliness during the Great Depression. Candy’s connections, to his dog, to George and Lennie and to the wider group of men, are shaped by his fear of being discarded, but also by his longing for companionship and purpose.

Candy’s most emotionally significant relationship is with his old dog, which acts as a reflection of his own vulnerability. The dog, described as a “dragfooted sheepdog, gray of muzzle, and with pale, blind old eyes” symbolises Candy’s own fate on the ranch: once useful though now seen as worthless. Candy’s reluctance to have the dog put down, even when others argue it is the kindest thing, shows how deeply attached he is. Carlson’s insistence that the dog “ain’t no good to himself” reflects the brutal mindset of the ranch, where people and animals are valued only for their ability to work. Candy’s eventual agreement, and his haunting regret “I ought to of shot that dog myself”, reveal his internal conflict. It also foreshadows George’s decision to take responsibility for Lennie’s death, highlighting the novel’s theme of mercy and duty.

Candy’s relationship with George and Lennie is one of hope and dependency. When Candy overhears them discussing their dream of owning land, he is quick to offer his life savings to be part of it. His excitement is palpable: “S’pose I went in with you guys... I won’t have no place to go, an’ I can’t get no more jobs.” Steinbeck uses this relationship to explore how people on the margins of society — the old, the disabled, the outcast — yearn for connection. Candy’s desperation drives him to cling to this dream, not just for economic security but for emotional belonging. Candy’s position on the ranch is unusual because, unlike most itinerant workers, he has savings which was a rare advantage during the Great Depression. After losing his hand in a ranch accident, Candy received compensation and has since been given an undemanding job. However, Steinbeck shows that even this security is fragile. At the time, there was no meaningful state support for the elderly or disabled and Candy knows his usefulness is limited. Candy sees in George and Lennie a rare opportunity for stability, purpose and dignity and his willingness to contribute financially also shows his deep need to be needed.

However, this bond is ultimately fragile. When Lennie kills Curley’s wife and the dream dies, Candy is devastated. His bitter outburst, “You God damn tramp... Ever'body knowed you'd mess things up”, reveals not just his grief but his powerlessness. Candy lashes out at Curley’s wife, not because he truly blames her alone, but because her death represents the end of his only chance at belonging. This reaction exposes the harsh emotional cost of being denied companionship and the cruel reality of broken dreams.

Candy’s interactions with the other men on the ranch are marked by a sense of inferiority. His age and missing hand set him apart and he often remains on the sidelines. He acts as a source of information for George and Lennie when they arrive, telling them about the characters and the rules of the ranch, but his role is largely passive. He is not respected in the way Slim is, nor is he feared like Curley. When conflict arises, Candy has little influence, and he relies on others to protect or include him. This reflects the broader context of 1930s America, where older workers were easily replaced and left with no support.

Candy’s treatment of Crooks also reveals the limits of his empathy. When Crooks suggests he could join in on the dream too, Candy initially allows it. But when Curley’s wife threatens Crooks, Candy quickly backs down, unwilling to challenge the racial hierarchy. This moment exposes the conditional nature of Candy’s friendship as he is not willing to risk his own fragile place to defend someone more vulnerable. Steinbeck uses this moment to show how even the oppressed can be complicit in maintaining social divisions.

Throughout the novel, Candy’s relationships reflect Steinbeck’s exploration of loneliness, usefulness and the human need for companionship. His bond with his dog is a symbol of his own fate and his hope in George and Lennie’s dream highlights his desire for connection. Yet, Candy is ultimately powerless, excluded by a society that values youth and strength over loyalty and humanity. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 40-mark question. parts.problemMd:
‘Several characters have little or no power at all.’

How far do you agree with this view?

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

Powerlessness is a central theme in Of Mice and Men and Steinbeck presents a world in which several characters are unable to control their own lives. These characters are defined not only by their lack of physical or social power, but also by the wider historical context of the Great Depression, which left many people vulnerable and voiceless. Through figures like Lennie, Crooks, Candy and Curley’s wife, Steinbeck shows how individuals are denied power by disability, race, gender and circumstance.

Lennie is one of the most obviously powerless characters. Although physically strong, his mental disability means that he is unable to understand or control his actions. This leads to him accidentally killing his puppy and, later, Curley’s wife. Steinbeck shows that Lennie is entirely dependent on George, who tells him what to eat, where to go and what to say. When the boss becomes suspicious, George must explain, “He’s dumb as hell, but he ain’t crazy”. Lennie himself says, “I tried not to forget. Honest to God I did, George” showing how little power he has over his own mind. The wider context of the 1930s also adds to Lennie’s lack of power. The Great Depression, high unemployment and the collapse of financial institutions meant that men became itinerant farm workers, forced to travel constantly in search of work. Workers like Lennie and George were at the mercy of bosses who could fire them at any time. There was no provision for those with disabilities, and attitudes towards race and gender further entrenched inequality. Ultimately, Lennie is so powerless that George must take the decision to kill him, believing it the only way to save him from a worse fate.

Candy is another character whose lack of physical strength leaves him without power. After losing his hand in an accident, he is unable to work alongside the other men and is given the job as a swamper. Despite being offered compensation, Candy remains deeply insecure about his position on the ranch. He is unable to stop Carlson from shooting his old dog, and later regrets not taking responsibility himself: “I ought to of shot that dog myself”. His relationship with the dog symbolises his own vulnerability — both of them are old, disabled, and seen as no longer useful. Candy’s excitement at George and Lennie’s dream of owning land reflects his desperation to escape a future where he will be left with nowhere to go.

Curley’s wife is similarly presented as a powerless character, isolated and ignored on account of her gender. As the only woman on the ranch, she is referred to by her husband’s name rather than her own. The men see her as “jail bait” and a “rattrap” and she is often left alone. She reveals her past to Lennie, telling him she could have been in the “pitchers”. Her decision to marry Curley was not based on love, but on escaping a life with no other options. Even in her final moments, she is powerless. Lennie silences her as she screams and she dies without anyone knowing what truly happened. Her death silences her permanently, reinforcing her lack of agency.

Crooks is another character who is denied power by both racism and segregation. He lives alone, apart from the other men and Steinbeck describes him as having “reduced himself to nothing”. When Curley’s wife threatens him by saying, “I could get you strung up on a tree so easy it ain’t even funny”, Crooks retreats entirely, realising how little protection or justice he can rely on. The harsh treatment he receives is typical of 1930s America. At the time, the Ku Klux Klan was prevalent and lynching was commonplace. Despite a moment of connection when he speaks to Lennie and Candy about the dream, Crooks pulls away, saying, “Nobody never gets to heaven, and nobody gets no land”. His hopelessness reveals how racism has stripped him of any sense of possibility or self-worth.

Even George, who appears to have more control than most, is ultimately shown to be powerless in the face of violence and injustice. When Curley decides to hunt Lennie down, George is left with no choice but to act before Curley does. He kills Lennie himself in a moment that is both merciful and deeply tragic, highlighting the futility of their dream and the impossibility of escape.

In conclusion, Steinbeck presents a world in which several characters have little or no power at all. Their fates are shaped not just by individual weakness but by a society that marginalises the vulnerable. Through their stories, Steinbeck critiques a system that devalues humanity in favour of strength, status and survival. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 40-mark question. The argument is clearly focused on the theme of powerlessness, using a wide range of characters to support this claim. parts.problemMd:
Discuss Slim’s relationships with others on the ranch in Of Mice and Men.

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

In Of Mice and Men, Steinbeck presents Slim as a respected and thoughtful figure whose relationships with others on the ranch are characterised by authority, empathy and dignity. Slim’s interactions reveal his moral strength and show how he stands apart from the other men in both status and character.

Slim’s most notable relationship is with the other ranch workers, who clearly admire and respect him. Described as the “prince of the ranch” Slim carries himself with natural authority. When he speaks, “all talk stopped” and Steinbeck refers to the “gravity in his manner” and the “understanding beyond thought” that he possesses. Slim’s high status is also linked to his skill as a jerkline skinner, capable of handling “ten, sixteen, even twenty mules with a single line”. This practical ability, combined with his calm and fair nature, means that Slim’s opinions are treated almost like law: “his word was taken on any subject”. Candy, for example, looks to Slim in desperation, hoping he will stop Carlson from shooting his old dog. This shows how Slim’s opinion is valued above even that of the boss.

Slim’s relationship with George and Lennie is one of quiet understanding and respect. Unlike the boss or Curley, Slim does not question why the two men travel together. Instead, he accepts it as natural and even praises Lennie’s work: “He's a nice fella”. Slim’s kindness is particularly important for George, who opens up to him and shares the story of their escape from Weed. The fact that George confides in Slim suggests a rare moment of trust in a world where men are normally guarded. Slim is also sensitive to the depth of George and Lennie’s friendship, recognising that their companionship is something valuable and unusual on the ranch.

Slim also shows a respectful attitude towards characters who are otherwise marginalised, such as Crooks and Curley’s wife. He speaks to Crooks without using racist language and listens to him when he reports on Lennie’s behaviour, which contrasts with how the other men usually treat him. Similarly, Slim is the only man on the ranch who does not degrade Curley’s wife or objectify her. While he still joins the other men in going to the brothel, Steinbeck presents him as someone who sees people as individuals, not just as stereotypes.

Slim’s calm strength is also evident in his handling of conflict. When Curley accuses him of being with his wife, Slim immediately puts him in his place, causing Curley to back down: “Well, I didn’t mean nothing, Slim. I just ast you”. This moment shows how even the aggressive and confrontational Curley cannot intimidate Slim. Later, when Curley picks a fight with Lennie and has his hand crushed, it is Slim who takes control of the situation. He advises George to make Lennie let go and insists Curley lie about the cause of his injury: “I think you got your han' caught in a machine.” Slim’s ability to de-escalate conflict reinforces his position as a mediator and a man of fairness.

At the end of the novel, Slim plays a crucial role in helping George cope with the consequences of Lennie’s death. After George shoots Lennie to save him from Curley’s revenge, Slim is the only character who understands the difficult nature of George’s decision. He gently leads George away, saying “You hadda, George. I swear you had-da” and offers comfort: “Come on, George. Me an’ you’ll go in an’ get a drink”. This moment highlights Slim’s compassionate nature and the mutual respect between the two men.

Slim’s relationships are shaped by his detachment as well as his dignity. While he treats others with kindness and patience, he remains slightly distant, perhaps because he is more permanent and established than the other itinerant workers. His quiet distance sets him apart, but it also allows him to act as a fair judge of character, someone who sees beyond prejudice and pride. Steinbeck presents Slim as a thoughtful and sensitive man, in order to challenge the stereotypical perception of ranch hands.

In conclusion, Steinbeck presents Slim as a character who, while detached, maintains deeply respectful and understanding relationships with others. His kindness towards George, Lennie, Crooks and even Curley’s wife shows his moral integrity, while his authority over the other ranch hands highlights the respect he commands. Through Slim, Steinbeck challenges the stereotype of the hardened ranch worker and presents a man whose strength lies in his empathy and wisdom. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 40-mark question. parts.problemMd:
Explore the theme of dreams in Of Mice and Men.

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
### Model answer

Steinbeck presents the dream of owning land as a fragile source of hope that gives the powerless men of the ranch dignity and friendship, but which the harsh world of the Great Depression makes impossible to reach.

The central dream is George and Lennie’s plan to own a little place and “live off the fatta the lan’”. Steinbeck presents it almost as a ritual: Lennie begs George to repeat it, and the rehearsed words — Lennie chanting about how he will “tend the rabbits” — turn the dream into a comforting story they tell each other. Set during the Great Depression, when thousands of migrant workers drifted between ranches with no security, this dream of a home of their own is really a dream of stability and independence. Steinbeck uses it to show what these men long for: not wealth, but a place where nobody can sack them and where they belong.

The dream is also what makes George and Lennie different from other ranch hands. George reminds Lennie that, unlike the lonely men who work on ranches, “I got you to look after me, and you got me to look after you”. The balanced structure of the sentence mirrors the equal, two-way bond between them. The dream gives their friendship a purpose and lifts them above the loneliness Steinbeck shows everywhere else on the ranch. It briefly spreads hope to others too: when Candy overhears it, he offers his savings to join, and for a moment the dream seems almost within reach.

Steinbeck widens the theme by giving almost every character a broken dream. Curley’s wife clings to the memory that a man once promised to “put me in the movies” and insists she “coulda been in the movies”. Her dream of fame is presented as a fantasy built on a stranger’s empty promise, and her loneliness comes partly from the gap between that imagined life and her real one as the only woman on the ranch, trapped in an unhappy marriage. Through her, Steinbeck shows how limited women’s choices were in 1930s America and how dreams can become a way of escaping a life that offers nothing.

Steinbeck also uses Crooks to question whether any of these dreams can come true. Crooks has watched many men chase the same fantasy of land, and tells Lennie that “nobody gets no land” because “it’s just in their head”. As the only black man on the ranch, isolated by segregation and forced to live alone in the harness room, Crooks speaks from bitter experience. His blunt realism works as a warning to the reader: in a world this unequal, the dream is a comfort, not a plan. For a moment he is tempted to believe in it too, before Curley’s wife cruelly reminds him of his place.

The dream’s collapse is built into the novel’s structure. Steinbeck repeatedly has the men recite it just before things go wrong, so that hope and disaster are tied together. When Lennie accidentally kills Curley’s wife, the dream dies with her, and George’s decision to shoot Lennie himself is also the moment he gives up the future they planned. By ending the novel with George alone, Steinbeck suggests that in a society that values the strong over the weak, dreams of a better life are almost always crushed.

Through the dream of the farm, Steinbeck explores both the hope that keeps the powerless going and the harsh reality that defeats them. The dream gives the men dignity, friendship and a reason to carry on, but the world of the Great Depression makes it unreachable. Its destruction is Steinbeck’s quiet, angry comment on an America that promised opportunity to everyone but delivered it to almost no one.

References are short and embedded (“the fatta the lan’”, “nobody gets no land”, “coulda been in the movies”), and methods are analysed rather than just named: the ritual repetition of the dream, the balanced sentence that mirrors George and Lennie’s bond, and the way Steinbeck recites the dream just before disaster strikes.
>

The response also moves beyond the literal, reading the broken dreams as a comment on the wider failure of the American Dream, which secures Level 5.

parts.problemMd:
‘Travelling to different places is experienced by some of the characters and the whales.’

Explore the significance of travelling in The Whale Rider.

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

In The Whale Rider, Ihimaera uses journeys — both physical and spiritual — to explore themes of growth, identity, cultural conflict, and the deep interconnection between humans and nature. Travel is not simply geographical; it represents transformation, returning to roots, and the reawakening of traditions.

One of the most powerful portrayals of travel is through Rawiri’s physical journey overseas. Rawiri leaves Whangara and travels to Australia and Papua New Guinea. This journey exposes him to new environments but also deepens his understanding of racism and inequality. For example, while staying at Jeff’s family’s plantation, he witnesses the mistreatment of native workers, particularly the scene where a labourer is left bleeding by the roadside and ignored by his employers. This experience shocks Rawiri into recognising the deep injustices faced by indigenous peoples globally. It is significant because it prompts his spiritual return home, showing that travel can clarify where one truly belongs. His exposure to a world of inequality strengthens his connection to his Māori heritage and compels him to be part of preserving it.

Kahu’s journey, though mostly confined to Whangara, is equally transformative. From birth, she travels between her mother’s family and Whangara every summer, finally settling in the village at age six. Her physical movement mirrors her growing importance as the prophesied leader. The most symbolic act of travel is when she rides the bull whale out to sea. This spiritual journey is life-threatening but deeply significant, connecting her to her ancestor Kahutia This travel is both literal and symbolic — it is a rite of passage that confirms her destiny and reunites the old traditions with the present generation. Her miraculous return from the ocean reinforces her role as saviour of her people and their culture.

The whales' migration serves as a powerful metaphor for ancestral memory and the cyclical journey of life. Led by the ancient bull whale, the pod travels from the Antarctic, recalling the original voyage made with Kahutia Te Rangi. The route they take, especially their turn towards New Zealand, is loaded with symbolism. The old bull whale’s longing for his master causes him to lead the herd towards dangerous waters, despite the protests of the females. This reveals how memory and emotion can override logic and lead to peril. The whales’ journey links the present with the mythic past, demonstrating how the legacy of Paikea continues to shape the present. The journey also reflects ecological dangers; Ihimaera references nuclear testing near Moruroa as a reason why the whales divert their route, subtly showing how human interference disrupts natural migratory paths.

Travelling also highlights generational and cultural divides. Koro Apirana’s reluctance to travel, both physically and ideologically, symbolises his resistance to change. In contrast, Porourangi, who has travelled abroad and experienced other approaches to Māori education, returns with a broader perspective. He wants to prepare his people for “new challenges and the new technology”, while Koro clings to traditional, male-led leadership. Their differing views reflect the central tension of the novel: how to preserve culture while adapting to modernity. Travel, in this context, becomes a metaphor for openness to progress.

The structure of the novel itself echoes the idea of travel and cyclical return. Divided into four sections (Spring, Summer, Autumn, and Winter) this structure reflects the natural passage of time and life. Each season signifies a phase in the narrative and in Kahu’s development, reinforcing the idea that all journeys, even dangerous or painful ones, are part of a larger, natural cycle.

In conclusion, travel in The Whale Rider is deeply significant. Whether through Rawiri’s international experiences, Kahu’s mythic journey on the back of a whale, or the pod’s ancestral migration, Ihimaera uses travel to explore identity, heritage, and transformation. parts.problemMd:
How is Nanny (Nani) Flowers presented in the novel?

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

In The Whale Rider, Ihimaera presents Nanny Flowers as a strong, loving and rebellious figure who both challenges and upholds Māori tradition. Through her humour, wisdom and fierce loyalty, Nanny becomes one of the novel’s most compelling characters, acting as both a protector of Kahu and a challenger to Koro Apirana’s rigid patriarchy.

Nanny Flowers is first introduced as Koro’s wife, but her role quickly becomes far more significant. Despite being married into the tribe, she commands authority and is not afraid to stand up to her husband. Her comic yet assertive remark, “He argues, and I win”, encapsulates the nature of their relationship. This sharp wit undercuts Koro’s authority and shows how Nanny navigates the male-dominated world with her own form of power. Her playful but commanding tone — calling Koro a “paka” — adds humour but also conveys her deep love and exasperation with him.

Nanny is also deeply traditional, particularly in how she honours Māori rituals. When Koro refuses to bury Kahu’s afterbirth at the marae, it is Nanny who takes the initiative, assisted by Rawiri and “the boys”. She performs the sacred task “in sight of Kahutia Te Rangi”, placing the birth cord in the earth and declaring that the ancestor will “always watch over her”. This act positions Nanny as a guardian of both Kahu and the spiritual traditions of her people. Yet, unlike Koro, her traditionalism does not limit her capacity for change. In fact, she uses tradition to support Kahu’s claim to leadership, not deny it.

The characterisation of Nanny Flowers also draws from a lineage of powerful Māori women. She proudly claims descent from Muriwai, the woman who took charge of the Mataatua canoe and saved her tribe. “Now I shall make myself a man”, Muriwai declared, a line that Nanny recalls as proof that women, too, can lead. Later, she reminds Koro of this: “He isn’t any chief. I’m his chief”. Through this, Ihimaera shows how female strength is deeply embedded in Māori tradition, not separate from it.

Nanny’s fierce love for Kahu is unwavering, and she often acts as her protector when others, especially Koro, reject the girl. From the moment Kahu is born, Nanny stands up for her. She undermines Koro’s attempts to erase Kahu’s significance by arranging for her to be named after Kahutia Te Rangi and later orchestrating the secret burial of her afterbirth. Her love is shown not through sentimentality but through action: she raises Kahu, supports her education, and encourages her cultural pride. When Kahu sobs after being rejected by Koro yet again, it is Nanny who comforts her and quietly promises, “You’ll fix the old paka”.

Ihimaera also presents Nanny as wise and perceptive. When Kahu dives into the ocean to retrieve the sacred stone that none of the boys could recover, it is Nanny who realises its symbolic importance but tells Rawiri, “Not a word about this to Koro Apirana…. He’s not ready yet”. Her judgement shows that she understands Koro’s emotional and spiritual limitations, but still nurtures hope for Kahu’s eventual recognition.

Nanny is a comic presence too, often used to diffuse tension in the narrative. Her mock threats of divorce and rivalry with “old Waari” provide warmth and humour, even in serious moments. This humour never undercuts her power, however. Instead, it enhances her status as a matriarch whose authority is earned through love, wisdom, and unwavering loyalty.

In conclusion, Nanny Flowers is presented as a powerful blend of tradition and resistance. Ihimaera uses her to challenge patriarchal leadership, protect Kahu’s place in the tribe, and reflect the strength of Māori women past and present. Her voice, full of sharp humour and emotional wisdom, is essential to the novel’s balance between reverence for the past and hope for the future. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 40-mark question. parts.problemMd:
Discuss the relationship between the brothers, Rawiri and Porourangi, in the novel.

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

In The Whale Rider, Witi Ihimaera presents the relationship between Rawiri and Porourangi as a bond rooted in deep brotherly love, mutual respect and cultural loyalty. Through letters, shared grief, and their united support for Kahu, the novel shows how the brothers remain emotionally close despite physical distance and personal challenges.

From the beginning, it is clear that Rawiri admires Porourangi deeply. As the narrator, Rawiri portrays his older brother in a consistently positive light, describing him as a loving father and a man of “mana”. When Porourangi calls to announce Kahu’s birth, Rawiri is present and immediately protective, stepping in when Koro Apirana reacts with disappointment. Rawiri’s humorous but fond tone sets the foundation for their relationship: “Porourangi said she looks just like me”, Nanny Flowers jokes, which Rawiri repeats without irony.

Their shared grief following Rehua’s death strengthens their bond. Porourangi respects both Rawiri and Nanny by allowing Kahu’s afterbirth to be buried on the marae, a sacred act that Koro Apirana refuses to perform. Rawiri, with the help of the “boys”, joins Nanny in secretly carrying out the ritual, fulfilling Rehua’s wish. This moment reflects the solidarity between the brothers in upholding both family and cultural obligations: “You’re the men who belong to Whangara”, Nanny tells Rawiri, entrusting him with a duty Porourangi cannot yet fulfil.

Despite Rawiri’s later physical absence, the brothers remain emotionally close through letters. While Rawiri travels to Australia and Papua New Guinea, Porourangi keeps him informed about life at home. These letters often show the challenges facing Māori people, but also express personal love — especially news about Kahu, such as “She’s five and started school now” and that she is “still living with Rehua’s folks”. Through these letters, we see Porourangi as a devoted father and responsible elder, while Rawiri’s emotional responses, particularly his homesickness, highlight the strength of their connection.

Rawiri’s return is motivated in part by these updates. A letter from Kahu, which reads, “Don’t forget me”, triggers his decision to go back to Whangara. The emotional pull of family, especially his bond with both Porourangi and Kahu, is portrayed as powerful and inevitable. When Rawiri finally returns, the reunion is filled with warmth, laughter and music, showing how the brothers’ affection remains unchanged by time or distance.

Throughout the novel, the brothers’ relationship is characterised by mutual support. They work together during the crisis with the stranded whales, when Rawiri phones both Porourangi and Koro to get help. When they arrive, the brothers act quickly: “Porourangi gave the orders”, and Rawiri follows his lead without hesitation. This dynamic reinforces their closeness and shared sense of responsibility. It also reflects traditional Māori values of family and leadership, with both men acting as guardians for their community and for Kahu.

There is also a contrast between the brothers that adds depth to their relationship. Porourangi carries the burden of being the tribe’s chosen leader and is often caught between Koro’s expectations and his own personal grief. Rawiri, while less burdened, serves as an emotional anchor — providing support, humour, and empathy. Their roles are complementary, and their shared commitment to Kahu bridges any gaps created by time or geography.

In conclusion, Rawiri and Porourangi’s relationship is a central thread in The Whale Rider. Through moments of shared duty, private communication and mutual support, Ihimaera portrays a bond that is strong, loving and rooted in culture.
