“Put my bag in the front bedroom, Calpurnia,” was the first thing Aunt Alexandra said. “Jean Louise, stop scratching your head,” was the second thing she said.’

Examine the character of Aunt Alexandra in the novel.

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

Aunt Alexandra is a complex and important character in To Kill a Mockingbird as she represents the traditional Southern values of class, gender and racial hierarchy. Through her character, Harper Lee explores ideas of family, prejudice and social conformity. Alexandra both challenges and reinforces the values of Maycomb and her evolving relationship with Scout adds depth to the novel’s treatment of gender and moral awareness.

When Aunt Alexandra first arrives in Maycomb, she is immediately portrayed as imposing and controlling. Her first words are commands: “Put my bag in the front bedroom, Calpurnia… Jean Louise, stop scratching your head”. This shows her need for order and her desire to establish authority within the Finch household. Scout feels imprisoned by her aunt’s expectations, describing her arrival as the moment she “felt the starched walls of a pink cotton penitentiary closing in”. The use of prison imagery illustrates Scout’s resistance to Alexandra’s attempts to impose traditional femininity. Lee presents Alexandra as a product of her time: conventional, proper and deeply concerned with reputation.

Aunt Alexandra is obsessed with family heritage and social status. She believes that “fine folks” are those who have lived on the same land for generations, asserting that “the longer a family had been squatting on one patch of land the finer it was”. This narrow view reflects the rigid class system of the 1930s Deep South, where family history determined social worth. Scout observes that her aunt would “point out the shortcomings of other tribal groups to the greater glory of our own”, which highlights Alexandra’s snobbery and blind loyalty to her social circle.

Her views on class and race are also closely linked. When Scout wants to invite Walter Cunningham to their house, Aunt Alexandra is horrified, saying “he — is — trash” and warning that associating with such people will cause Scout and Jem to pick up their “habits”. This moment reveals Alexandra’s class prejudice and her belief that children should be protected from inferior influences. Likewise, she is disturbed by the children’s close relationship with Calpurnia. Alexandra insists that Calpurnia is no longer needed and is shocked to learn the children have attended her church. These attitudes reflect the racial divisions enforced by Jim Crow laws.

Despite her prejudice, Aunt Alexandra is also presented as caring. She eventually allows Calpurnia to serve her missionary guests after recognising her grace and competence. This small concession signals a softening of her rigid views. Additionally, although she initially believes Atticus’ defence of Tom Robinson brings shame to the family, she shows genuine concern when Tom is killed. Her asking Atticus if the town’s criticism upsets him reveals her inner conflict and perhaps guilt. This emotional moment highlights how even those steeped in prejudice can experience doubt and change.

Aunt Alexandra’s character development is especially visible in her relationship with Scout. Initially, she tries to make Scout behave like a “young lady” criticising her dungarees and tomboy habits. She urges Scout to embrace embroidery and activities that will improve her reputation, such as organising missionary teas. However, by the end of the novel, when Scout is attacked by Bob Ewell, Alexandra’s protective side emerges. She calls Scout “darling” and even brings her overalls, showing a rare moment of acceptance and tenderness. This change suggests that Alexandra begins to value Scout’s individuality over outward appearances.

Scout describes her aunt as having “river-boat, boarding-school manners” and being “an incurable gossip”, yet she also acknowledges that Alexandra “let any moral come along and she would uphold it”. Lee uses these observations to present Alexandra as both comic and serious, as she is someone who clings to outdated customs but also possesses strength and care. She is described as the last of her kind, symbolising the dying values of the Old South that the novel critiques.

In conclusion, Aunt Alexandra is a character who represents the Southern Belle ideal, shaped by a culture of class consciousness, gender expectations and racial prejudice. Through her, Lee examines how these values can be both upheld and questioned within a single individual. Alexandra’s development over the course of the novel, from rigid enforcer of tradition to caring family member, shows that even deeply ingrained beliefs can be challenged by empathy and love. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 40-mark question. This answer would be placed in the top band (Level 5) because it is a well-structured and assured response that shows a critical approach and perceptive understanding of the text. > > **Commentary** > > This essay presents a thoughtful and perceptive exploration of Aunt Alexandra’s character, clearly rooted in the text and fully addressing the contextual demands of the question. The response consistently integrates relevant context, especially relating to gender roles, Southern class values and racial prejudice in the 1930s. The analysis of Alexandra’s views on family status, race and femininity is detailed and mature, with strong close reading of moments such as her reaction to Walter Cunningham and her softening at the novel’s end. Quotes are well-selected and interpreted and the argument flows logically across each paragraph. There is also awareness of how Lee’s narrative methods shape the reader’s response to Alexandra, including Scout’s humorous tone. This is a coherent and insightful response. > **[exam-tip]** > - Focus on **what Aunt Alexandra represents** — social class, gender roles, Southern tradition > - Use **Scout’s reactions** to show how Lee encourages readers to question Alexandra’s views > - Track **how her character changes**, especially in her growing care for Scout > - Weave in **historical context** (Jim Crow laws, gender norms, class hierarchy) as you analyse > - Quote or paraphrase **key turning points**, like her views on Calpurnia and the Cunninghams > - Don’t ignore her **more sympathetic moments** — she’s not one-dimensional

parts.problemMd:
Examine the character of Dill Harris in To Kill a Mockingbird.

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

Dill Harris is a vital character in To Kill a Mockingbird, acting as both a source of humour and a contrast to Scout and Jem. Harper Lee uses Dill to explore themes of childhood, family, imagination and moral sensitivity. Though a relatively minor character, Dill plays a major role in helping the reader understand both the innocence of childhood and the moral awareness that the trial of Tom Robinson provokes.

When Scout first meets Dill, she describes him as a “curiosity” because of his unusual appearance and style: “He wore blue linen shorts that buttoned to his shirt, his hair was snow white and stuck to his head like duckfluff”. From the start, Dill is different from the children of Maycomb, both in appearance and background. This difference reflects the context of 1930s Southern America, where communities were often closed and suspicious of outsiders. Maycomb is depicted as a microcosm of this world and Dill’s status as an occasional visitor from Meridian sets him apart, though he quickly becomes part of Scout and Jem’s inner circle. Scout says, “summer was Dill”, which captures how essential he becomes to their shared adventures and emotional growth.

Dill fuels the children’s imagination, particularly their fascination with Boo Radley. He invents “eccentric plans, strange longings, and quaint fancies” which Scout lovingly compares to a “pocket Merlin”. His enthusiasm contrasts with Jem’s increasing maturity and Scout’s practical nature. Dill’s love of make-believe and tendency to tell tall tales, like claiming his father is dead, adds humour, but it also suggests a deeper emotional need. His lies about his father’s identity, including once saying “I haven’t got one,” hint at his unstable home life and desire to be accepted and valued.

Dill’s emotional vulnerability becomes more apparent when he runs away from home and hides under Scout’s bed. He tells Scout that his mother and stepfather “do get on a lot better without me, I can’t help them any”. Dill’s confession highlights his loneliness and need for attention. His arrival at the Finch house is welcomed by Atticus, who treats him with kindness and responsibility, which contrasts sharply with the emotional neglect Dill experiences at home. In this way, Lee uses Dill to explore the differences in parenting styles and the importance of moral role models during childhood.

Dill’s most significant moment comes during Tom Robinson’s trial, which marks a shift from playfulness to moral seriousness. When Mr Gilmer cross-examines Tom with cruelty and disrespect, Dill begins to cry. He says, “It was the way he said it made me sick, plain sick”. Dill’s sensitivity highlights the impact of racism on a young, innocent mind. Unlike Scout, who is beginning to understand how Maycomb works, Dill is horrified by the normalisation of racial injustice. This response positions him as a character who still reacts emotionally to cruelty while others have become numb. Dill could also be considered a mockingbird figure because he has an unhappy home life. He loses his childish innocence when he sees the ugliness of adult prejudice.

Raymond Dolphus comforts Dill by suggesting that children “cry about the simple hell people give other people — without even thinking”. This reinforces the idea that Dill, though imaginative and naive, sees the truth more clearly than many adults. It also reflects the context of the Jim Crow South, where institutional racism was so ingrained that its violence often went unquestioned by white society. Dill’s inability to accept this injustice signals both his decency and his loss of childhood innocence.

In his relationship with Scout, Dill also reveals his softer side. He declares that Scout is “the only girl he would ever love” and becomes her “permanent fiancé”. Their innocent affection adds warmth to the novel, but also reflects traditional gender expectations of the time. Dill and Jem sometimes exclude Scout from their adventures, which frustrates her and reminds readers of the gender roles that even young children internalise.

In conclusion, Harper Lee uses Dill Harris to explore the emotional effects of broken families, the transition from innocence to awareness and the moral complexity of childhood in a deeply prejudiced society. Through Dill’s eyes, the reader is reminded that justice and empathy often come more readily from children than adults. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 40-mark question. This answer would be placed in the top band (Level 5) because it is a well-structured and assured response that shows a critical approach and perceptive understanding of the text. > > **Commentary** > > This is a perceptive and detailed response that successfully captures Dill Harris’ character. The candidate demonstrates consistent focus on the question, offering a well-structured and coherent examination of Dill’s emotional vulnerability, imagination and moral development. The essay integrates a range of relevant and well-chosen textual references, from Dill’s storytelling to his reaction during the trial. Context is thoughtfully embedded throughout, with accurate references to racial injustice, the Jim Crow South, gender expectations and the closed nature of small-town life. The candidate also explores Dill’s function as a foil to Scout and Jem and effectively argues that Dill is a mockingbird figure. There is balance between narrative moments and thematic discussion, showing full command of AO1 and AO4. > **[exam-tip]** > - Focus on **Dill’s imagination** and how it contrasts with Jem and Scout’s outlook > - Show how Dill’s **lies** and **storytelling** reflect his **unhappy home life** > - Explain how Dill’s **sensitivity** in the trial scenes marks a **loss of innocence** > - Make clear why Dill can be seen as a **mockingbird figure** > - Weave in **context** about the **1930s**, the **Jim Crow laws** and **family roles** > - Use Dill’s **emotional reactions** to racism to highlight **Lee’s moral message**

parts.problemMd:
‘The law is central to this novel.’

How far do you agree with this view?

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
| ### Model answer

The law is central to To Kill a Mockingbird, functioning not only as a plot device but as a lens through which Harper Lee explores justice, morality and social prejudice in 1930s America. However, the novel also suggests that moral justice can exist outside of legal boundaries, showing that while the law is crucial, it is sometimes not always enough.

Atticus Finch, the moral centre of the novel, is a lawyer who believes in justice and equality before the law. He defends Tom Robinson, a black man falsely accused of raping a white woman, Mayella Ewell. Although Atticus does not usually take on criminal cases, he agrees after being asked by Sheriff Heck Tate, knowing that he will lose. This decision reflects his belief in the importance of giving Tom the best possible defence, regardless of race. He tells Scout: “The one thing that doesn’t abide by majority rule is a person’s conscience”. This shows that, for Atticus, the laws of morality must sometimes guide legal duty.

Tom’s trial is the clearest demonstration of the limits of the law in a racially segregated society. Despite clear evidence that Tom could not have committed the crime as his left arm is useless, he is still found guilty. The all-white jury’s decision reflects the deep racial prejudice ingrained in Maycomb and in the legal system of the southern states of America. This echoes the real-life Scottsboro trials, in which nine Black men were wrongly convicted by biased, all-white juries, despite overwhelming evidence of their innocence. Like Tom Robinson, they were failed by a system that should have protected them.

Yet, there are small signs that the law is beginning to change. One juror in Tom’s trial hesitates, which indicates that Atticus’ argument made some impact. Jem, devastated by the outcome, asks, “How could they do it, how could they?” Jem’s emotional response shows a child’s growing understanding of the law and his disappointment in its failure to deliver justice. Harper Lee uses the trial to show how legal institutions can shape young people’s moral education.

Scout also gains awareness of the law throughout the novel. At first, she sees Atticus’ job as just part of normal life, especially when Walter Cunningham pays legal fees with produce rather than money. But by the end of the novel, she has developed a deeper understanding. When Sheriff Tate insists on protecting Boo Radley by claiming that Bob Ewell “fell on his knife”, Scout agrees, saying that exposing Boo would be “like shootin’ a mockingbird”. This moment symbolises Scout’s growth as she recognises that sometimes moral justice must outweigh legal procedure, especially when the law might harm the innocent.

Atticus himself struggles with this dilemma. When he thinks Jem may have killed Bob Ewell, he insists that the law must take its course. However, when it is revealed that Boo Radley saved the children, Atticus accepts Tate’s fabricated account, agreeing that subjecting Boo to the spotlight of the legal system would do more harm than good. This moment reflects a mature understanding that justice is not always best served by strict legal action. As Tate states, “Let the dead bury the dead”, implying that the community’s sense of morality can sometimes override legal truth.

The law is also shown to be intertwined with prejudice and power. The legal system fails Tom Robinson not because of a lack of evidence, but because of his race. Atticus’ defence is logical, ethical and legally sound but it cannot overcome Maycomb’s racist values. This highlights the limits of a law that is meant to be blind but is shaped by social bias. The novel critiques the way legal systems reflect the flaws of the societies they serve.

In conclusion, the law is central to To Kill a Mockingbird, not just in the literal sense of the courtroom scenes, but in how it shapes the characters’ understanding of fairness, truth and justice. However, Lee also shows that legal justice does not always align with moral justice. Through Atticus, Scout and Jem, the novel encourages readers to consider when following the law is right and when it might be more ethical to challenge or interpret it differently. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 40-mark question. This answer would be placed in the top band (Level 5) because it is a well-structured and assured response that shows a critical approach and perceptive understanding of the text. > > **Commentary** > > This is a sophisticated and focused response that fully addresses the question and consistently integrates relevant textual and contextual knowledge. The candidate presents a clear and convincing argument that the law is central to the novel while also recognising its limitations. The analysis explores the character of Atticus as a moral figure within the legal system and effectively discusses the trial of Tom Robinson as a turning point for both Scout and Jem’s development. Contextual links to Jim Crow laws, racial injustice and the Scottsboro trials are woven seamlessly throughout the essay. The contrast between legal justice and moral justice is well developed, particularly in the analysis of Boo Radley’s protection. Textual references are used selectively and precisely. The structure is coherent, with each paragraph contributing to the overall argument. This is a confident and insightful top-band response. > **[exam-tip]** > - Focus on how **Atticus**, as a lawyer, represents the **ideal of legal justice** > - Show how the **trial** reveals the **failings of the legal system** in a racist society > - Explore the contrast between **legal justice** and **moral justice** (e.g., concerning Boo Radley) > - Use the context of the **Jim Crow laws** and **Scottsboro trials** to deepen your analysis > - Track how **Jem and Scout’s understanding of the law** evolves across the novel > - Use **short quotes** to support clear, developed ideas about how the law is shown

parts.problemMd:
How does Lee present Atticus Finch in To Kill a Mockingbird?

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
### Model answer

Harper Lee presents Atticus Finch as the moral centre of To Kill a Mockingbird: a father and lawyer whose empathy, integrity and quiet courage make him the conscience of a prejudiced town.

Lee first presents Atticus as a moral teacher. He tells Scout that you never really understand a person until you “climb into his skin and walk around in it”. The metaphor of climbing into someone’s skin makes empathy sound active and physical, something you choose to do rather than simply feel. Because the novel is narrated by an adult Scout looking back on her childhood, this lesson carries weight: the reader sees that it shapes the woman she grows into. As a single father raising two children in 1930s Maycomb, where strict ideas about discipline and family were the norm, Atticus’s gentle, reasoning approach already marks him out as different from the town around him.

Atticus’s empathy becomes principle when he agrees to defend Tom Robinson, a black man falsely accused of attacking a white woman. He has no illusions about his chances. He tells Scout that in a Southern court, when it is a white man’s word against a black man’s, “the white man always wins”. This is a clear-eyed admission of how the Jim Crow South worked, where segregation and prejudice meant a black defendant could not get a fair trial. In his closing speech he still reminds the jury that a courtroom should be the one place where all men are treated as equals, whatever their colour. Atticus takes the case knowing he will lose, telling his children that “simply because we were licked a hundred years before we started” is no reason not to try. Lee uses the gap between his certainty of defeat and his decision to fight to show that, for Atticus, doing right matters more than winning.

Lee also uses Atticus to redefine courage itself. After Mrs Dubose dies, he explains that real courage is not “a man with a gun in his hand” but knowing “you’re licked before you begin but you begin anyway”. This definition reflects directly on his own role in the trial. Lee reinforces the idea through the mad-dog scene, in which Atticus reluctantly shoots the rabid Tim Johnson with a single shot. The diseased dog works as a symbol of the madness of racism spreading through Maycomb, and Atticus is the one steady enough to face it. Tellingly, he never boasts about his marksmanship; the children have to learn from Miss Maudie that their father was once the best shot in the county. His refusal to show off makes his courage quieter and, Lee suggests, more genuine.

What makes Atticus admirable is that he is the same person everywhere. Miss Maudie tells the children that “Atticus Finch is the same in his house” as he is on the public streets, capturing the idea that his private and public selves never differ. Lee often builds Atticus through the testimony of other characters like this, which makes his goodness feel earned rather than simply announced by the narrator. He hopes to raise Jem and Scout without catching “Maycomb’s usual disease”, his phrase for the casual racism around them. By calling prejudice a disease, Atticus suggests it is something children absorb from a sick society, so that resisting it takes real, deliberate effort from a parent.

Lee does not present Atticus as faultless. His firm belief in the basic goodness of his neighbours is tested when the all-white jury convicts Tom despite the evidence, and some readers feel his calm patience underestimates how dangerous the town’s racism really is. Even so, his restraint is part of who he is: he insists on treating everyone, including the Ewells who later attack his children, with a dignity they never return. Rather than weakening him, his disappointment makes him more human — a good man trying to hold on to hope in an unjust world.

Through Atticus, Lee argues that real integrity means doing what is right whatever the cost. He is presented less as a flawless hero than as a model of conscience: empathetic, principled and quietly brave in a community that rewards none of these things. In a novel set in the racially divided Deep South, he stands as Lee’s example of the person Maycomb could become, if only it had the courage to climb into another’s skin.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> This is a 40-mark question. This answer would be placed in the top band (Level 5) because it is an assured, well-structured response that shows a perceptive understanding of how Lee presents Atticus and integrates context throughout.
> 
> **Commentary**
> 
> The response stays sharply focused on how Lee presents Atticus — moving through his empathy, his principled defence of Tom Robinson, his redefinition of courage and his consistency — rather than narrating the plot. Textual references are short, well chosen and embedded (“climb into his skin”, “the white man always wins”, “Maycomb’s usual disease”), and the analysis of method is developed rather than just spotted: the skin metaphor, the mad dog as a symbol of racism, and Lee’s habit of building Atticus through other characters’ testimony.
> 
> Context (AO3) is woven into the argument rather than bolted on: the Jim Crow South, segregation and 1930s attitudes to family all support points about Atticus instead of sitting in a separate paragraph. The answer also shows discrimination by acknowledging the limits of Atticus’s optimism, which lifts it securely into Level 5. To push further still, a student could analyse Lee’s adult-Scout narrative perspective a little harder.
> 
> **Other arguments you could consider**
> 
> - A response could focus on Atticus as a parent, comparing his honest, reasoning approach with Aunt Alexandra’s concern for family name and appearances.
> - A response could explore the more critical reading of Atticus as an idealised figure whose faith in gradual change does little to challenge Maycomb’s racist systems directly.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Answer “how” Lee presents Atticus — name her methods (metaphor, symbolism, other characters’ viewpoints), don’t just describe what he does.
> - Keep quotations short and embedded; a phrase like “the white man always wins” is worth more than a long copied-out speech.
> - Weave context into your points — link Jim Crow segregation to specific moments like the trial, never as a separate paragraph.
> - Show range: cover Atticus as father, lawyer and neighbour, not only the courtroom.
> - Use the mad-dog scene to show Lee’s symbolism — Atticus facing the rabid dog mirrors him facing the town’s racism.
> - A confident answer notes Atticus’s limits as well as his virtues; examiners reward a balanced, thoughtful view.
> - Plan five or six points before you write so a 40-mark answer stays focused and covers the whole novel.

parts.problemMd:
Re-read If—.

**If—**

If you can keep your head when all about you

Are losing theirs and blaming it on you,

If you can trust yourself when all men doubt you,

But make allowance for their doubting too;

If you can wait and not be tired by waiting,

Or being lied about, don’t deal in lies,

Or being hated, don’t give way to hating,

And yet don’t look too good, nor talk too wise:

** **

If you can dream — and not make dreams your master;

If you can think — and not make thoughts your aim;

If you can meet with Triumph and Disaster

And treat those two impostors just the same;

If you can bear to hear the truth you’ve spoken

Twisted by knaves to make a trap for fools,

Or watch the things you gave your life to, broken,

And stoop and build ’em up with worn-out tools:

** **

If you can make one heap of all your winnings

And risk it on one turn of pitch-and-toss,

And lose, and start again at your beginnings

And never breathe a word about your loss;

If you can force your heart and nerve and sinew

To serve your turn long after they are gone,

And so hold on when there is nothing in you

Except the Will which says to them: ‘Hold on!’

** **

If you can talk with crowds and keep your virtue,

Or walk with Kings — nor lose the common touch,

If neither foes nor loving friends can hurt you,

If all men count with you, but none too much;

If you can fill the unforgiving minute

With sixty seconds’ worth of distance run,

Yours is the Earth and everything that’s in it,

And — which is more — you’ll be a Man, my son!

** **

— Rudyard Kipling

Compare the ways the writers present the experience of growing up in If— and one other poem from the anthology.

You should make reference to language, form and structure.

Support your answer with examples from the poems.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
### Model answer

Chosen second poem: **Poem at Thirty-Nine** by **Alice Walker**

Both poems present growing up as something deeply shaped by a parent: Kipling's If— offers a father's advice on how to become a man, while Walker's Poem at Thirty-Nine looks back on what a father taught a now-grown daughter.

Both writers root growing up in the bond between parent and child, but they face in opposite directions. Kipling writes as a father directly addressing his son, ending "you'll be a Man, my son!", so the whole poem is a lesson in how to grow up well. Walker instead writes as an adult child, opening "How I miss my father", looking back on his influence. The contrast is clear: Kipling looks forward to the child's future, while Walker looks back with love and loss on a father who has died.

The two writers present what growing up requires very differently. Kipling makes it a test of virtues, building condition upon condition through the anaphora of "If you can…" — to "keep your head", to "meet with Triumph and Disaster / And treat those two impostors just the same". The relentless repetition makes maturity sound like a demanding checklist. Walker presents growing up more gently, as absorbing a parent's example: her father "taught me how" to manage money and "that telling the truth / did not always mean / a beating". Both show growing up as a kind of learning, but Kipling's is a stern code while Walker's is warm and personal.

Both poems present growing up as gaining independence, yet they shape it differently. In If—, independence means self-mastery — holding "on when there is nothing in you / Except the Will". Walker shows independence as becoming her own person: she learned to "escape / the life he knew", and now cooks and lives "just like him" but in her own way, "seasoning none of my life / the same way twice". Walker's growing up frees her from her father's path even as she carries his influence.

Both writers also present growing up as learning to cope with hardship, but they value endurance and freedom differently. Kipling makes maturity a matter of grim resilience: the grown man must "never breathe a word about your loss" and "stoop and build 'em up with worn-out tools", so growing up means hiding pain and pressing on whatever happens. Walker presents coping not as silent suffering but as winning the freedom to live her own way; the closing image of her "chopping wood, / staring into the fire" shows a calm, self-possessed adult, not one braced against the world. Kipling's growing up hardens the child into a stoic; Walker's frees the child into herself.

The forms reinforce this difference. Kipling uses regular eight-line stanzas and a steady rhyme scheme, and the drilling repetition of "If" drives the poem forward like a code of manhood, suggesting that growing up is about discipline and control. Walker uses free verse with very short, broken lines that tumble down the page, suggesting a freer, more natural kind of growth and a mind moving through memory. The reader feels Kipling's growing up as something earned through effort, and Walker's as something absorbed through love.

Both poems close with a parent's pride, but the tone differs sharply. Kipling's promise — "Yours is the Earth" — is triumphant and forward-looking, a reward for growing up correctly. Walker imagines that her father "would have grown / to admire / the woman I've become", a quieter, sadder pride mixed with grief, since he is gone. Kipling's growing up is a challenge still to be met; Walker's is a journey already travelled and mourned.

In the end, both writers present growing up as shaped by a father's influence, but where Kipling offers a confident, forward-looking set of rules for becoming a man, Walker reflects back with tenderness and loss on the woman her father helped her become. Together they show growing up as both a lesson taught and a bond remembered.

> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
> **Commentary**
> 
> The answer compares the two poems throughout rather than treating them separately, moving between them on shared ideas — the parent-child bond, what growing up requires, independence, form, and the closing pride. References are short and embedded from both poems ("you'll be a Man, my son!", "How I miss my father", "the way it is done"), and methods are analysed: Kipling's anaphora and regular form versus Walker's free verse and broken lines.
> 
> The response keeps a clear comparative line of argument and gives roughly equal weight to both poems, which is what secures Level 5 on this paper. There is no need for context here — the focus stays on the writers' methods and effects.
> 
> **Other arguments you could consider**
> 
> - A response could compare the tone of authority, contrasting Kipling's commanding voice with Walker's reflective, conversational one.
> - A response could explore how each poem defines success in growing up — Kipling through self-control, Walker through freedom and self-expression.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Compare the poems throughout, moving between them on each idea, rather than writing about one and then the other.

parts.problemMd:
Re-read Prayer Before Birth.

**Prayer Before Birth**

I am not yet born; O hear me.

Let not the bloodsucking bat or the rat or the stoat or the

club-footed ghoul come near me.

** **

I am not yet born, console me.

I fear that the human race may with tall walls wall me,

with strong drugs dope me, with wise lies lure me,

on black racks rack me, in blood-baths roll me.

** **

I am not yet born; provide me

With water to dandle me, grass to grow for me, trees to talk

to me, sky to sing to me, birds and a white light

in the back of my mind to guide me.

** **

I am not yet born; forgive me

For the sins that in me the world shall commit, my words

when they speak me, my thoughts when they think me,

my treason engendered by traitors beyond me,

my life when they murder by means of my

hands, my death when they live me.

** **

I am not yet born; rehearse me

In the parts I must play and the cues I must take when

old men lecture me, bureaucrats hector me, mountains

frown at me, lovers laugh at me, the white

waves call me to folly and the desert calls

me to doom and the beggar refuses

my gift and my children curse me.

** **

I am not yet born; O hear me,

Let not the man who is beast or who thinks he is God

come near me.

** **

I am not yet born; O fill me

With strength against those who would freeze my

humanity, would dragoon me into a lethal automaton,

would make me a cog in a machine, a thing with

one face, a thing, and against all those

who would dissipate my entirety, would

blow me like thistledown hither and

thither or hither and thither

like water held in the

hands would spill me.

** **

Let them not make me a stone and let them not spill me.

Otherwise kill me.

** **

— Louis MacNeice

### Model answer

Chosen second poem: **War Photographer** by **Carol Ann Duffy**

Both poems present fear of human cruelty, but MacNeice's Prayer Before Birth voices the terror of an unborn child dreading the world, while Duffy's War Photographer shows a man haunted by the suffering he has witnessed.

Both writers present fear of what human beings do to one another. MacNeice's unborn speaker fears that "the human race may with tall walls wall me, / with strong drugs dope me, with wise lies lure me", listing the ways people harm each other. Duffy's photographer carries the fear and pain of real atrocities, summed up in the bleak half-line "All flesh is grass", which reduces human life to something that quickly withers. Both poems are filled with dread of human violence, but MacNeice fears it in advance while Duffy's photographer has already seen it.

The writers use very different speakers to create fear. MacNeice gives a voice to a child "not yet born", which is strange and unsettling, making the fear feel universal — every human enters this frightening world. Duffy uses a third-person account of one ordinary man whose "hands, which did not tremble then / though seem to now", a small physical detail that shows fear surfacing only later, in safety. MacNeice's fear is a desperate plea against a world not yet faced; Duffy's is the slow, haunting aftershock of horror already witnessed.

Language and sound heighten the fear in both. MacNeice uses heavy repetition and pounding internal rhyme — "on black racks rack me, in blood-baths roll me" — so the sounds themselves feel violent, like blows. Duffy uses sudden, clipped sentences and place names — "Belfast. Beirut. Phnom Penh." — whose flatness makes the suffering feel endless and matter-of-fact. Both control sound carefully: MacNeice to make fear feel overwhelming, Duffy to make it feel cold and inescapable.

The forms shape the fear differently. MacNeice builds his poem as a prayer, each stanza beginning "I am not yet born", and the stanzas grow longer and more frantic, the lines tumbling and breaking as the fear mounts towards the final cry, "Otherwise kill me." Duffy uses controlled, regular stanzas, and this calm order is itself disturbing, suggesting how easily the world packages suffering — "five or six" images — for a comfortable Sunday reader. One form enacts panic; the other enacts a chilling detachment.

Both poems also fear powerlessness, the fear of being unable to act or feel. MacNeice's deepest dread is of being reduced to something without feeling at all, begging "Let them not make me a stone", as if losing his humanity would be worse than death. Duffy's photographer is powerless in a different way: he can record horror but cannot change it, and in the end "stares impassively" from the aeroplane, drained and numb. Even the reader is powerless to truly care, feeling only fleeting "tears between the bath and pre-lunch beers". MacNeice's speaker pleads to be killed rather than emptied of feeling, while Duffy's photographer has already been hollowed out, so both writers present numbness as a fate more frightening than death itself. For MacNeice the fear is of being turned to stone; for Duffy the fear is that everyone, witness and reader alike, already has been.

Finally, both poems fear that people lose their humanity. MacNeice dreads being made "a cog in a machine, a thing with / one face", terrified of becoming inhuman. Duffy fears the opposite kind of inhumanity in the reader, whose "eyeballs prick / with tears" but who ultimately "do not care". Both writers present a deep fear that cruelty and indifference will strip people of their humanity, whether the unborn child's or the comfortable reader's.

In the end, both poems present fear of a cruel, dehumanising world, but MacNeice voices the raw terror of a child about to be born into it, while Duffy shows the quieter, lasting fear of a man who has already seen its horrors and a world that looks away.

**Blessing**

The skin cracks like a pod.

There never is enough water.

** **

Imagine the drip of it,

the small splash, echo

in a tin mug,

Sometimes, the sudden rush

of fortune. The municipal pipe bursts,

child for streets around

parts.solutionMd:
### Model answer

Chosen second poem: **Search For My Tongue** by **Sujata Bhatt**

Both poems present community, but Dharker's Blessing shows a whole neighbourhood drawn together by a sudden flow of water, while Bhatt's Search For My Tongue presents a more personal sense of belonging to a language and culture.

Dharker presents community as a crowd united by shared need. When the pipe bursts, "every man woman / child for streets around / butts in", and the list of containers — "brass, copper, aluminium, / plastic buckets" — suggests a whole mixed community rushing together. Bhatt's idea of community is quieter and inward: it lives in the "mother tongue", the language that ties her to her people and homeland. Both poems show belonging, but Dharker's is a public, physical gathering while Bhatt's is the private bond of shared language and roots.

The writers use religious language to show how precious community is. Dharker calls the gathered people a "congregation" and the water "the voice of a kindly god", turning the neighbourhood's rush for water into something sacred and shared. Bhatt treats her mother tongue almost as a living, sacred part of herself, something she fears losing when forced to "speak a foreign tongue". For both writers, what binds a community — water or language — is something holy that gives life meaning.

Language and imagery create very different moods. Dharker's writing is bright and joyful: "silver crashes to the ground" and children scream "in the liquid sun", the light imagery making the moment feel like a celebration. Bhatt uses a startling extended metaphor of a tongue that can "rot" and "die" but then "grows back", a "bud" that "blossoms out of my mouth". Dharker's images are about a shared outer event; Bhatt's are about an inner struggle to hold on to belonging.

Both poems also use sound, and the image of "tongues", to capture what binds people. Dharker's community finds its voice in "a roar of tongues" and a rush of "frantic hands", the noise turning a crowd into one excited body, a shared voice. Bhatt's poem is full of tongues too, but they belong to a single speaker holding "two tongues in your mouth"; the same word that means a roaring crowd in Dharker means private heritage in Bhatt. The shared image links a loud public community to a quiet personal one, showing belonging can be heard in a street or felt on a single tongue.

The forms reflect these differences. Dharker's poem builds to one long, breathless central stanza, the lines piling up to mirror the crowd surging together — the structure itself becomes a gathering. Bhatt actually weaves another language into her poem, including lines of Gujarati, so the form embodies the two cultures she belongs to. One structure shows a community coming together in a single rush; the other shows a speaker holding two communities, two tongues, inside herself.

Both poems also present community through the body, which makes belonging feel physical and real. Dharker fills her crowd with "frantic hands" reaching for water and "naked children" whose "small bones" remind us how bodily and vulnerable this shared moment is. Bhatt locates her community inside the body too, in a tongue that can "rot and die" yet "blossoms out of my mouth", so belonging to a culture is something she physically feels in her mouth. For both poets, community is not an abstract idea but something lived in the body, whether a crowd's grasping hands or a single speaker's living tongue.

Finally, both poems present community as something fragile and precious. In Blessing, the water and the joy it brings are sudden and temporary, and the focus on the children's "small bones" reminds us how vulnerable this community is. In Search For My Tongue, the speaker fears her mother tongue — and so her belonging — will be lost, until it reassuringly "blossoms" back. Both writers show that belonging to a community, whether of place or of language, is something that can be threatened and must be treasured.

In the end, both poems celebrate community, but Dharker presents it as a joyful, physical coming-together around a shared blessing, while Bhatt presents it as a deeper, more personal belonging carried in language and identity.

### Model answer

Chosen second poem: **Half-caste** by **John Agard**

Both poems present identity as caught between two cultures, but Bhatt's Search For My Tongue explores identity through language, while Agard's Half-caste challenges the labels other people use to define mixed identity.

Both writers present a divided or double identity. Bhatt imagines having "two tongues in your mouth", the "mother tongue" and "the foreign tongue", to show a speaker living between two languages and cultures. Agard's speaker is described by others as "half-caste", a single word that tries to split his identity in two. Both poems explore what it means to belong to more than one culture, but Bhatt looks inward at her own fear of loss, while Agard looks outward, confronting the people who label him.

The writers use extended images to capture identity. Bhatt's central metaphor is a tongue that can "rot and die" yet "grows back", a "bud" that "blossoms out of my mouth", showing that her cultural identity cannot be lost. Agard turns the insult "half-caste" into a series of images that mock it, asking whether "when light an shadow / mix in de sky" you get "a half-caste weather". Both use vivid imagery, but Bhatt's reassures her that identity survives, while Agard's exposes how absurd it is to call a person only "half" a being.

Language itself becomes a statement of identity. Bhatt weaves Gujarati into her poem, printing whole lines in her mother tongue, so the form proves her identity has survived. Agard writes in Caribbean Creole — "Explain yuself / wha yu mean" — using non-standard spelling and grammar as a proud assertion of who he is. For both poets, the very language of the poem is an act of identity, refusing to be erased by a dominant "standard" culture.

Both poems are also framed as a reply to an outsider who has questioned the speaker's identity, putting the listener on the spot. Bhatt begins "You ask me what I mean" and immediately turns the challenge back with "I ask you, what would you do", making the reader share her dilemma rather than judge it from outside. Agard speaks directly to his accuser throughout and ends by ordering them to "come back tomorrow" to hear the rest of his story on his own terms. Both poets refuse to let their identity be defined by the questioner, taking control of the conversation about who they are.

The tone each poet takes towards identity is strikingly different. Bhatt's tone is anxious and inward, full of dread that her identity will "rot and die" and that she will have to "spit it out", a private fear of disappearing. Agard's tone is defiant and witty from the start, mocking the label rather than fearing it: he jokes about having to "cast half-a-shadow" and throws in the scornful aside "ah rass", using humour as a weapon. Bhatt quietly defends an identity she is frightened of losing; Agard loudly attacks the prejudice that tries to diminish his.

The forms shape the argument. Bhatt's poem moves from fear to reassurance: the structure carries us from the tongue that seems to "die" to the moment it "blossoms", so the shape enacts the recovery of identity. Agard builds his poem through repetition and a challenging, questioning structure, repeating "Explain yuself / wha yu mean" so that he turns the tables on the accuser. One form dramatises an inner journey; the other stages a confrontation.

Finally, both poems end with confidence about identity. Bhatt closes in triumph as her mother tongue "blossoms out of my mouth", showing identity cannot be suppressed. Agard ends by demanding the listener return "wid de whole of yu mind" to hear "de other half / of my story", insisting on being seen as a whole person. Both writers refuse to let their identities be reduced or lost, ending on a note of self-assertion.

In the end, both poems present identity as something to be defended and celebrated, but Bhatt explores it through the survival of her mother tongue, while Agard fights back against the labels others use to divide and diminish him.

### Model answer

Chosen second poem: **Hide and Seek** by **Vernon Scannell**

Both poems capture childhood from a child's-eye view, but Fanthorpe's Half-past Two shows a boy lost in a timeless innocence, while Scannell's Hide and Seek shows a child's excitement turning to lonely abandonment.

Both writers recreate a child's way of seeing. Fanthorpe invents compound words like "Gettinguptime" and "Timeformykisstime" to capture how a small child experiences the day, not by clock-time but by events. Scannell uses the second person and the present tense — "Call out. Call loud: 'I'm ready! Come and find me!'" — to put us inside the child's mind during the game. Both use language to make the reader feel childhood from the inside, though Fanthorpe focuses on a child's confusion about time while Scannell focuses on the thrill of hiding.

Both poems show adults failing children. In Half-past Two, the teacher punishes the boy but, "Being cross, she'd forgotten / She hadn't taught him Time", so he is trapped by an adult's carelessness. In Hide and Seek, the child's friends abandon him — they "scuffle, and they're gone" — leaving him alone in the cold shed. Both writers show childhood as a vulnerable state in which children are let down by the bigger people around them.

Both use rich sensory detail to capture the child's world. Fanthorpe's boy escapes "Into the smell of old chrysanthemums" and "the silent noise his hangnail made", a dreamy, timeless place beyond adult rules. Scannell's child is wrapped in physical sensation too — "The sacks in the toolshed smell like the seaside", "the cold bites through your coat". Both root childhood in vivid, bodily experience, but Fanthorpe's sensations are magical and freeing while Scannell's grow cold and uncomfortable as the wait drags on.

Both poems also show childhood running on a child's own sense of time rather than the clock. Fanthorpe's boy cannot read "half-past two" and so escapes into a "clockless land" where adult time stops altogether, making his childhood a freedom from the clock. Scannell's child has no clock either, only feeling — "It seems a long time since they went away" — and that slow, dragging time is what turns his game sour. For both writers, childhood is measured by feeling, not minutes, but the same freedom from clock-time frees one boy and traps the other.

Both poems also present childhood as a state of powerlessness, though the children seem to have very different amounts of control. Fanthorpe's boy is helpless before an adult world he cannot understand: he "couldn't click its language" of clocks, and at the end is "slotted… back into schooltime" like an object moved by others. Scannell's child appears to be in charge, even ordering himself about with confident commands — "Push off the sacks" — yet his triumphant "I've won!" is met by an empty garden, so his control is an illusion. Both poems show that children, whether confused or confident, are finally at the mercy of a world run by others.

The structures move in different directions. Fanthorpe's poem lets the boy "escape" into "the clockless land for ever", and although he is returned to "schooltime", the ending keeps a sense of wonder and lost innocence. Scannell's poem builds suspense and then collapses into a chilling twist: the child emerges to find "The darkening garden watches. Nothing stirs." The shift from excited present-tense commands to that silent, empty ending turns a game into a small tragedy of abandonment.

The two poems end on very different notes. Fanthorpe's tone stays tender and slightly magical, presenting childhood as a place of innocent imagination, where "time hides tick-less waiting to be born". Scannell's ends bleak and lonely, the final question — "But where are they who sought you?" — leaving the child, and the reader, with a sense of being forgotten. One poem celebrates the freedom of the childish mind; the other exposes childhood's hidden fears.

In the end, both writers present childhood through a vivid child's-eye view in which adults let children down, but Fanthorpe finds in it a magical, timeless innocence, while Scannell uncovers loneliness and abandonment beneath a simple game. Together they show childhood as both wonderful and frighteningly fragile.

Support your answer with examples from the poems.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
### Model answer

Chosen second poem: **Poem at Thirty-Nine** by **Alice Walker**

Both poems explore powerful memories of a parent, but Lawrence's Piano is overwhelmed by a longing to return to childhood, while Walker's Poem at Thirty-Nine remembers a father with warmth and a sense of what he gave her.

Both poems show a memory suddenly triggered. In Piano, a woman "singing to me" carries the speaker "back down the vista of years" to a childhood scene. In Poem at Thirty-Nine, the everyday act of "Writing deposit slips and checks" makes the speaker "think of him". Both writers show how ordinary present moments can unlock the past, but Lawrence is pulled helplessly backward while Walker reflects more calmly.

Both remember a parent through tender, specific images. Lawrence pictures himself "A child sitting under the piano" pressing "the small, poised feet of a mother who smiles as she sings", a warm, safe memory. Walker remembers her father teaching her "how" to write slips and that "telling the truth / did not always mean / a beating". Both memories are loving, but Lawrence's is wordless and sensory while Walker's centres on the lessons and values her father passed on.

The poems differ on what memory does to the speaker. Lawrence calls the song's pull "insidious", admitting it "Betrays me back" until "the heart of me weeps", as if the memory overpowers his adult self. Walker's memory strengthens her: she has grown into someone who cooks and lives "just like him". For Lawrence memory is almost a weakness that unmans him; for Walker it is a source of identity and pride.

The senses work differently in each poem's memory. Lawrence's memory is triggered and ruled by sound: the "insidious mastery of song" overwhelms him and the "tinkling piano" of the past drowns out the present, so memory is something heard and helplessly surrendered to. Walker's memory lives instead in active doing, especially food: her father "cooked like a person / dancing" and "craved the voluptuous / sharing / of good food", and she keeps him alive by cooking herself. Lawrence is washed back into the past by a sound he cannot resist; Walker carries her father forward through what she does with her hands.

The forms suit each mood. Lawrence uses regular rhyming couplets and long, flowing lines, and the soft sounds — "the boom of the tingling strings" — lull the reader like the music itself, mirroring how he is swept away. Walker uses free verse with short, broken lines that feel thoughtful and unhurried, as if she is turning the memory over piece by piece. One form drowns the speaker in feeling; the other lets her examine it.

The two poems also treat childhood within memory very differently. Lawrence longs to climb back into his own childhood, confessing that "The glamour / Of childish days is upon me" until his grown-up "manhood is cast / Down", as if memory drags the adult back into being a boy. Walker keeps her adult self firmly in the present, remembering her childhood lessons only to measure how far she has come, "the woman I've become". For Lawrence memory pulls him back into childhood; for Walker it shows how childhood made the adult she is proud to be.

The endings show the difference clearly. Lawrence's speaker is finally overwhelmed: "I weep like a child for the past", collapsing into helpless nostalgia. Walker ends looking forward as much as back, imagining her father "would have grown / to admire / the woman I've become". Lawrence's memory leaves him grieving for what is lost; Walker's leaves her grateful for what remains.

In the end, both poems show how deeply a parent lives on in memory, but Lawrence presents memory as a flood of nostalgia that reduces a grown man to tears, while Walker presents it as a warm inheritance that has shaped who she is. Together they reveal memory as both a comfort and a source of longing.

### Model answer

Chosen second poem: **Half-past Two** by **U A Fanthorpe**

Both poems present a child left alone, but Scannell's Hide and Seek builds towards painful loneliness and abandonment, while Fanthorpe's Half-past Two turns a child's solitude into something dreamy and almost magical.

Both poems isolate a child because of others. Scannell's boy hides so well that his friends give up: their words "scuffle, and they're gone", leaving him alone in the dark shed. Fanthorpe's boy is kept behind after school and then forgotten, left by himself in the schoolroom. Both children are alone through the carelessness of others — distracted friends, a distracted teacher — but Scannell's loneliness grows frightening while Fanthorpe's becomes strangely peaceful.

The writers present the experience of solitude very differently. In Hide and Seek, the cold and dark close in: "The floor is cold", "the cold bites through your coat", and the child grows uneasy. In Half-past Two, the boy drifts happily "Into the smell of old chrysanthemums" and "the silent noise his hangnail made", escaping into his own world. Scannell makes solitude physically uncomfortable; Fanthorpe makes it dreamy and safe.

The two poets also position the reader very differently through who they address. Scannell writes in the second person, so "you" are the one hiding in the dark shed; this direct address traps the reader inside the loneliness, making the abandonment feel like our own. Fanthorpe keeps to the third person, watching "he" from a gentle distance, so the boy's solitude feels observed with tenderness rather than suffered. One poet shuts us inside the lonely child; the other lets us look on him kindly.

Both use sound, and silence, to capture loneliness. Scannell fills the ending with an eerie stillness: "The darkening garden watches. Nothing stirs. / The bushes hold their breath." The silence is heavy and threatening. Fanthorpe's boy enters a "clockless land" of "silent noise", a quiet that frees rather than frightens him. The same idea — a child alone in silence — produces dread in one poem and wonder in the other.

Commands shape the mood of each solitude too. Scannell drives his poem with tense imperatives — "Don't breathe. Don't move." — so the child's aloneness feels strained, full of warnings and pressure. Fanthorpe's boy faces no such commands; he simply drifts "beyond onceupona", "Out of reach of all the timefors", and the absence of any instruction makes his solitude feel like release. Scannell's lonely child is braced and anxious; Fanthorpe's is loosened and free.

The child's own feelings about being alone also change in opposite directions. Scannell's boy starts out enjoying his solitude, proudly imagining the others "thinking that you're very clever" for hiding so well, so being alone first feels like winning. Fanthorpe's boy begins frightened, "too scared at being wicked" to speak up, yet his enforced solitude slowly softens into calm wonder. Scannell's child slides from a happy aloneness into miserable loneliness, while Fanthorpe's moves the other way, from fear into peace, so the same state of being alone carries the two children to opposite emotions.

The structures shape opposite outcomes. Scannell builds suspense through the game and then delivers a bleak twist: the boy emerges triumphant — "I've won!" — only to find everyone gone, his victory hollow. Fanthorpe's boy is also returned to the ordinary world when the teacher remembers him, but he keeps the memory of having "escaped into the clockless land for ever". One structure ends in loss; the other in a kind of secret gain.

Finally, the poems give the child's solitude opposite meanings. Scannell's ending — "But where are they who sought you?" — leaves the child genuinely abandoned, exposing the hidden cruelty in childhood. Fanthorpe presents being alone as a brief, magical release from adult rules, something the boy "never forgot". For Scannell loneliness is a wound; for Fanthorpe being alone is a doorway into imagination.

In the end, both writers place a child alone and forgotten, but Scannell turns that solitude into painful, frightening loneliness, while Fanthorpe transforms it into a dreamy, timeless escape. Together they show how a child's experience of being alone can be either a small tragedy or a quiet wonder.

Let me not to the marriage of true minds

### Model answer

Chosen second poem: **La Belle Dame sans Merci** by **John Keats**

The two poems present opposite visions of love: Shakespeare's Sonnet 116 celebrates love as constant and unchanging, while Keats's La Belle Dame sans Merci warns that love can be a dangerous illusion that destroys.

The poems make opposing claims about what love is. Shakespeare defines true love as steadfast: "love is not love / Which alters when it alteration finds", insisting that real love never changes. Keats shows love that is all change and ruin, leaving his knight "Alone and palely loitering" after his encounter. Shakespeare praises love's constancy; Keats dramatises love's power to deceive and abandon.

Both use vivid imagery, but to opposite ends. Shakespeare calls love "an ever-fixèd mark / That looks on tempests and is never shaken" and "the star to every wandering bark", images of guidance and permanence. Keats surrounds love with images of decay — "The sedge has withered from the lake, / And no birds sing" — and a "lily on thy brow", suggesting sickness and death. One poet's love is a steady star; the other's leaves a barren, dying landscape.

The two poems also show love having opposite effects on the lover. Shakespeare's faithful lover stays strong and unmoved, a love that "looks on tempests and is never shaken", so devotion makes a person steady whatever storms come. Keats's knight is wrecked by love instead: it leaves him "haggard and so woe-begone", marked with a deathly "lily on thy brow", as if love has drained the life out of him. The same force that makes Shakespeare's lover constant makes Keats's lover sick and ruined; love builds one up and destroys the other.

Time is central to both. Shakespeare insists "Love's not Time's fool", that real love "bears it out even to the edge of doom", surviving even death. Keats's love is destroyed in a moment: the knight enjoys only fleeting pleasure before the "faery's child" leaves him wasted and aged before his time. Shakespeare's love conquers time; Keats's love is conquered by it, fading as quickly as it came.

The two poems also treat the senses and pleasure of love very differently. Shakespeare keeps love almost abstract and unbodily, admitting that even "rosy lips and cheeks" must fade while true love does not, so physical beauty matters little to him. Keats fills his love with rich sensual detail — the lady "found me roots of relish sweet" and "made sweet moan" — yet that very sweetness is the trap, luring the knight to ruin. For Shakespeare love rises above the senses; for Keats the pleasures of the senses are exactly what make love so dangerous. Shakespeare's lover is safest when he ignores beauty and feeling, while Keats's knight is destroyed precisely because he gives in to them, so the two poets draw opposite lessons from the body's part in love.

The forms mirror the messages. Shakespeare's tight sonnet, with its steady rhyme and confident final couplet — "If this be error... I never writ, nor no man ever loved" — enacts the very constancy it praises. Keats uses a ballad form with short, haunting final lines in each stanza, and the circular structure, which ends where it began with "And no birds sing", traps the knight in endless suffering. One form is balanced and assured; the other is eerie and unresolved.

Finally, the poems take opposite stances. Shakespeare's sonnet is a confident celebration, holding up perfect, faithful love as an ideal worth everything. Keats's poem is a warning, showing love as a beautiful but deadly enchantment — "La Belle Dame sans Merci / Thee hath in thrall!" — that leaves its victims among "pale kings" and "Pale warriors". Shakespeare tells us what love should be; Keats shows us how love can destroy.

In the end, the two poems present love as opposites: Shakespeare's Sonnet 116 celebrates a constant, time-defying devotion, while Keats's La Belle Dame sans Merci warns of a deceptive, destructive passion. Together they capture both the ideal of love and its dangers.

Alone and palely loitering?

The sedge has withered from the lake,

** **

O what can ail thee, knight-at-arms,

So haggard and so woe-begone?

** **

With anguish moist and fever-dew,

And on thy cheeks a fading rose

Full beautiful — a faery’s child,

Her hair was long, her foot was light,

And her eyes were wild.

And made sweet moan.

** **

And nothing else saw all day long,

For sidelong would she bend, and sing

A faery’s song.

** **

She found me roots of relish sweet,

And sure in language strange she said —

‘I love thee true’.

** **

She took me to her elfin grot,

And there she wept and sighed full sore,

And there I shut her wild wild eyes

With kisses four.

** **

And there she lullèd me asleep

And there I dreamed — Ah! woe betide! —

The latest dream I ever dreamt

On the cold hill side.

** **

I saw pale kings, and princes too,

Pale warriors, death-pale were they all;

They cried — ‘La Belle Dame sans Merci

Thee hath in thrall!’

** **

I saw their starved lips in the gloam,

With horrid warning gapèd wide,

And I awoke and found me here,

On the cold hill’s side.

** **

And this is why I sojourn here

Alone and palely loitering,

Though the sedge is withered from the lake,

And no birds sing.

** **

### Model answer

Chosen second poem: **Sonnet 116** by **William Shakespeare**

Keats's La Belle Dame sans Merci presents love as a deadly danger that destroys a knight, while Shakespeare's Sonnet 116 presents love as the opposite — a safe, steadfast force that protects against danger.

Keats fills his poem with danger from the start: the knight is found "Alone and palely loitering", already a victim. Shakespeare instead presents love as a refuge from danger, "an ever-fixèd mark / That looks on tempests and is never shaken". For Keats, love itself is the danger; for Shakespeare, love is what keeps us safe when the "tempests" of danger come.

The writers use nature imagery in opposite ways. Keats surrounds the knight with sickness and death — "a lily on thy brow", "a fading rose", "no birds sing" — a dying world that warns the reader of danger. Shakespeare uses imagery of guidance and security — love is "the star to every wandering bark" — suggesting love steers us safely through danger. Keats's nature withers with threat; Shakespeare's offers protection.

Keats shows danger as seductive and hidden. The "faery's child" seems loving — "she did love", "I love thee true" — before she destroys him, so the danger lies in love's deceptive beauty. The danger is sweetened with gifts of "honey wild, and manna-dew", pleasures that lull the knight before the trap closes. Shakespeare denies that real love can deceive: it "alters not", remaining honest and unchanging. Keats warns that love's danger is that it lures you in; Shakespeare reassures that true love never betrays.

Keats also presents the danger of love as a kind of enslavement of the body. The knight is shown physically weakened and sick — "So haggard and so woe-begone" — and the warning voices reveal "pale kings" with "starved lips", love's victims wasted away. Shakespeare answers that true love is the one thing time and decay cannot touch: it is no "fool" of time even as "rosy lips and cheeks" fade. Keats shows love's danger eating away the body; Shakespeare shows real love standing firm while the body declines.

The two poems also move in opposite directions, and this shapes how we feel the danger. Keats's knight is left frozen and still, doomed to "sojourn here / Alone and palely loitering", so love's danger ends in helpless paralysis. Shakespeare's love, by contrast, presses steadily forward and endures, refusing to bend "with the remover to remove", so it actively resists the danger of change. Keats's danger leaves its victim stuck and going nowhere; Shakespeare's love keeps moving and holding firm, which is exactly why it is safe.

The forms hold the danger differently. Keats's ballad has a circular structure — it ends as it began, "And no birds sing" — trapping the knight in endless ruin, so the danger feels inescapable. Shakespeare's sonnet builds to a confident couplet that defeats the danger of time, as love "bears it out even to the edge of doom". Keats's form leaves danger unresolved; Shakespeare's form masters it.

Finally, the poems differ in purpose. Keats's poem is a warning, showing the "pale kings" and "Pale warriors" already destroyed by this danger and the knight doomed to join them. Shakespeare's is reassurance, promising that true love stands firm against every danger. One poem shows love as a trap; the other shows love as a shelter.

The tone of each speaker also shapes how danger feels. Keats's knight speaks in a faint, exhausted voice, his words slowing to the dread of "Ah! woe betide!" as he recalls the danger that ruined him, so danger sounds like haunted regret. Shakespeare's speaker is bold and certain, dismissing any doubter with "I never writ, nor no man ever loved", daring the reader to prove him wrong. Keats's hushed, broken tone makes danger feel like a wound that never heals; Shakespeare's confident tone makes love sound strong enough to stare danger down.

In the end, Keats presents love as a beautiful but deadly danger that ruins those it enchants, while Shakespeare presents love as a safe, steadfast force that withstands danger. Together they show love's two faces: a hidden threat and a sure protection.

### Model answer

Chosen second poem: **If—** by **Rudyard Kipling**

Both poems centre on the bond between father and child, but Walker's Poem at Thirty-Nine looks back lovingly on a father from a grown child's view, while Kipling's If— speaks as a father giving advice to his son.

The poems present fathers from opposite sides. Walker writes as a daughter remembering: "How I miss my father", looking back with love and loss. Kipling writes as a father directly addressing "my son", looking forward to the man he hopes the boy will become. One poem is a child's tribute; the other a father's guidance.

Both show fathers passing things on. Walker's father taught her practical and moral lessons — "how" to write deposit slips, and "that telling the truth / did not always mean / a beating". Kipling's father offers a whole code of virtues through the anaphora of "If you can…", urging self-control and resilience. Both fathers shape their children, but Walker's teaches by warm example while Kipling's instructs through stern command.

The tones differ sharply. Walker's feelings are tender and a little sad, full of affection — she now cooks "just like him" and imagines he "would have grown / to admire" her. Kipling's tone is firm and demanding, more proud than tender, promising "you'll be a Man, my son!" only if the long list of conditions is met. Walker's father is mourned and loved; Kipling's speaks with bracing authority.

The poems also feel very different about whether the father is present. Walker's father is gone, and her affection is shadowed by absence and regret — she wishes "he had not been / so tired" when she was born, so her love is mixed with loss. Kipling's father is fully present, speaking straight to a living son with a future still ahead of him. Walker's tender feelings come from looking back at someone she can never reach again; Kipling's come from a father still able to shape the child before him — love remembered against love being given.

Both poems also admit the father is not perfect, but handle this differently. Walker quietly acknowledges that her honesty hurt him — "many of my truths / must have grieved him" — yet she forgives and treasures him all the same. Kipling's father makes huge demands, almost impossibly high, asking the son to "meet with Triumph and Disaster / And treat those two impostors just the same". Walker shows love that accepts a father's faults; Kipling shows a father whose love comes wrapped in tough, exacting standards.

The forms suit each relationship. Walker uses free verse with short, broken lines that feel personal and reflective, like a mind moving gently through memory. Kipling uses regular, rhyming stanzas and the relentless repetition of "If", a controlled form that mirrors the discipline the father is teaching. One form feels like loving memory; the other like a lesson learned by heart.

Both poems end on the father's lasting influence. Walker's closes with a grown woman shaped by her father's example, "cooking, writing, chopping wood", carrying him in who she has become. Kipling's ends with the promise of inheritance — "Yours is the Earth" — the reward for living by his father's code. Both show a father living on in his child, whether through remembered love or through hard-won character.

The endings also leave us with different feelings about each father. Walker closes on a warm, hopeful image of her father imagined approving of the woman she has become, "staring into the fire", so her feelings settle into peace and pride. Kipling closes on a single triumphant line, "you'll be a Man, my son!", so his feelings rise to a proud climax built on conditions met. Walker's poem ends in gentle, settled love; Kipling's ends in a burst of pride — quiet tenderness against loud, demanding hope.

In the end, both poems explore the powerful bond between father and child, but Walker presents feelings about a father through a daughter's loving memory, while Kipling presents a father's own voice shaping his son. Together they show fatherhood from both sides of the relationship.

Re-read War Photographer.

**War Photographer**

In his darkroom he is finally alone

with spools of suffering set out in ordered rows.

The only light is red and softly glows,

as though this were a church and he

a priest preparing to intone a Mass.

Belfast. Beirut. Phnom Penh. All flesh is grass.

** **

He has a job to do. Solutions slop in trays

beneath his hands, which did not tremble then

though seem to now. Rural England. Home again

to ordinary pain which simple weather can dispel,

to fields which don’t explode beneath the feet

of running children in a nightmare heat.

** **

Something is happening. A stranger’s features

faintly start to twist before his eyes,

a half-formed ghost. He remembers the cries

of this man’s wife, how he sought approval

without words to do what someone must

and how the blood stained into foreign dust.

** **

A hundred agonies in black and white

from which his editor will pick out five or six

for Sunday’s supplement. The reader’s eyeballs prick

with tears between the bath and pre-lunch beers.

From the aeroplane he stares impassively at where

he earns his living and they do not care.

** **

— Carol Ann Duffy

Compare the ways the writers present suffering in War Photographer and one other poem from the anthology.

You should make reference to language, form and structure.

Support your answer with examples from the poems.

**[30 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
### Model answer

Chosen second poem: **Prayer Before Birth** by **Louis MacNeice**

Both poems present human suffering caused by people's cruelty, but Duffy's War Photographer shows the real suffering of war and the world's indifference to it, while MacNeice's Prayer Before Birth voices an unborn child's fear of the suffering to come.

Both locate suffering in human cruelty. Duffy's photographer records "a hundred agonies in black and white", the suffering of real war zones. MacNeice's unborn child fears "the human race" will "on black racks rack me, in blood-baths roll me". Both writers blame people, not nature, for suffering, but Duffy shows suffering already happening while MacNeice dreads suffering yet to come.

Both make suffering vivid through powerful imagery. Duffy reduces human life to "All flesh is grass", a bleak image of how easily people are destroyed, and shows how "the blood stained into foreign dust". MacNeice piles up violent images and sounds — "blood-baths", "black racks" — so the suffering feels relentless. Duffy's suffering is specific and real; MacNeice's is imagined and universal, but both make it disturbing.

Both poems also turn suffering people into objects. Duffy lays the photographs out like dead bodies, "spools of suffering set out in ordered rows", so real human pain becomes neat stock to be sorted. MacNeice fears being turned into "a cog in a machine, a thing with / one face", his humanity stripped away. Both writers suggest that the worst suffering is being reduced to a thing — a row of images, or a part in a machine — rather than treated as a person.

Both poems also reach for religious language to weigh this suffering. Duffy compares the photographer to "a priest preparing to intone a Mass", as if recording suffering were a solemn, sacred duty in a careless world. MacNeice shapes his whole poem as a desperate prayer, the unborn child crying "O hear me" to some power that might spare him suffering. Duffy uses religion to show one man taking suffering seriously; MacNeice uses it to show a soul pleading to be protected from suffering — in both, faith-language marks how grave the suffering is.

A key idea in both is the world's failure to care. Duffy's reader feels a brief pang — "eyeballs prick / with tears" — then forgets, "between the bath and pre-lunch beers", while those who suffer "do not care". MacNeice fears a world that would "freeze my / humanity". Both writers suggest that the deepest suffering comes from people losing their compassion.

The forms shape the suffering differently. Duffy uses controlled, regular stanzas, and this calm order is itself unsettling, mirroring how the press neatly packages "five or six" agonies for a comfortable reader. MacNeice uses a building prayer structure, each stanza beginning "I am not yet born", the lines growing more frantic as the fear of suffering mounts. One form is coldly ordered; the other rises towards panic.

Finally, the poems respond to suffering differently. Duffy's photographer is numbed and helpless, staring "impassively" from the plane, unable to make anyone care. MacNeice's speaker resists, begging for "strength" and ending with the defiant cry that he would rather be killed than made cruel: "Otherwise kill me." Duffy shows suffering met with weary detachment; MacNeice shows it met with desperate resistance.

Place and movement add to the sense of suffering in both poems. Duffy lists distant war zones in clipped, full-stopped names, "Belfast. Beirut. Phnom Penh", so suffering feels scattered and endless across the world. MacNeice's child fears being pushed about by cruel forces, dreading those who would "dragoon me into a lethal automaton", so suffering feels like being driven against your will. Duffy spreads suffering across real places we choose to forget; MacNeice imagines suffering as a loss of freedom — both make the pain feel inescapable.

In the end, both poems present human suffering as the product of cruelty and indifference, but Duffy exposes the real suffering of war and a world that looks away, while MacNeice voices an unborn child's terror of the suffering people will inflict. Together they force the reader to confront our shared responsibility for human pain.
